WILSON (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, I desire to bring to the attention of the Government the fact that about an hour ago I received a number of telegrams from my city in reference to the paper shortage. It is stated that the newspapers in Saskatoon will have to cease publication unless some arrangement is made to secure a supply of paper. I should like to know whether the Government have taken any action in the matter, and what they intend to do to relieve the situation.
Sir HEiNRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance):	The newspaper publishers of
Canada have had a committee looking after the newsprint question, and negotiations have been under way with a view to obtaining necessary supplies for the newspapers. An agreement was reached last October under which the mills and the newspapers arrived at certain prices, not on the basis of Governmental paper control, but as a matter of ordinary business arrangement between the mills and the newspapers. That agreement provided not only for the supply of newsprint at a fixed price which had been agreed upon up to the end of June, but also for a supply for the Canadian press from then on at the usual trade rates as fixed by the pulp and paper manufacturers as applicable to the export trade. I regret very much to have to inform the House that last Saturday the newspaper publishers interested came to Ottawa and reported that they had been unable to provide for proper newsprint supplies and that there was grave danger of a large number of Canadian papers- some 27 in all-having to suspend publication, not because they were not willing to pay the price but because the commodity was not available for them. Telegrams have been sent out to the different manufacturers of newsprint and the matter will be taken up to-morrow morning with those manufacturers. I hope to be able to give
my lion, friend more definite information after that meeting.
Has the minister suggested to the newspaper proprietors the propriety of reducing the size of their newspapers?

DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL [DOT]STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
The House resumed, from Monday, May 31, the debate on the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this
late stage of the debate it will hardly be expected that much can be added by way of argument either for or against the proposals which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has given to the House in the resolutions which accompanied1 his speech, or indeed either for or against the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
In the remarks I am about to address to the House I shall endeavour, therefore, not to go into particulars to any great ex-, tent in regard to the resolutions, but rather seek to emphasize in bolder outline than has been possible in the course of the discussion which has taken place, the differences in attitude and point of view which seem to .separate hon. gentlemen opposite who are supporting the Budget from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who are supporting the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding).
But, before directing attention to the differences which exist between us and which have been so manifest in this debate, may
1 say just one word, with many others who have spoken, in regard to an opinion which we all hold in common and that is a word of congratulation to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), on the manner in which he has presented the Budget to this Parliament, on the arrangement of the Budget itself, the information it contains, and the purpose which he has had at heart in presenting it to the House. I think we all realize that upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance at this session of Parliament there has fallen a burden' heavier indeed than that which has fallen on the shoulders of any previous Minister of Finance. He has not only had to take account of the vast expenditures which have been incurred in the ordinary course of the increasing obligations of this country, but he has also had to take into account all the extraordinary expenditures which have to be met in consequence of the war. As my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's mentioned, in presenting previous Budgets during the period of the war, the Minister of Finance of the day has been able to count upon the sentiment of patriotism and enthusiasm throughout the nation to back up any suggestions he might propose to this Parliament. But now the war is past, and instead of the urge of patriotic endeavour the present Minister of Finance has the afteT-math of the war to contend with and he has to present to the House in their stern reality conditions consequent upon the, enormous expenditures which have been incurred in the last few years, the liabilities which they have involved and the herculean efforts in the matter of sacrifice which will be necessary before these obligations can be met. I think that in presenting the Budget in the manner in which he did, going fearlessly and fully into the liabilities of the country, not seeking to conceal in any particular our obligations or to make them appear less than they are, but presenting to us the facts in their true light and significance he has enabled us to comprehend the situation with which we are now confronted. For that reason, as well as for the splendid manner in which he presented the Budget itself, we owe him our hearty congratulations.
I think, too, that the hon. the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated on having professed at least a desire to accomplish certain things. He has said that he hopes that it will be possible in future to raise the revenue that is required without resorting to any further loans. Every hon. member, and every citizen of this country, will

believe that that is a right, a proper, a good and a necessary policy. We may have little consciousness of the full extent of our liabilities, but we all do know that with these liabilities what they are, unless it is going to be possible to meet obligations out of current revenue we are heading towards an abyss of bankruptcy in this country from which it will be impossible to recede. So it is wholly to the public interest, it is wholly to the good of the nation, that the Government have determined-and indeed they would be culpably negligent if they did not so determine-not to have further public loans for the purpose of meeting our obligations.
The Minister of Finance, I think, has also been wise in intimating that he hopes to raise the required revenue by taxation upon luxuries rather than upon the necessaries of life. Whether or not his proposals will accomplish that end I shall deal with in a moment, but in so far as he is endeavouring to place the burden of taxation upon the shoulders of those who are best able to bear it, he is following the sound and proper line of finance.
I think he has been wise also in urging that so far as possible taxation should be in a direct rather than in an indirect form. Though it is not so pleasant a form of taxation, in the long run it is going to result in greater good to the country. It is right that we should know exactly what we are paying out so that we may take the course . that is wisest both from a personal and from a public point of view.
So that in these particulars-in giving us a true statement of the facts, in promising that there shall be no further loans, in seeking to make taxation direct rather than indirect, in promising to place a tax upon luxuries, and also in recognizing that taxation upon incomes is a form of taxation that is preferable to that of indirect taxation-the Finance Minister's professions have been in the right direction, and I believe his purpose has been in accord with his professions.
But, Sir, if he has failed to accomplish his purpose, and if he has failed to carry out his intentions it is because he has found himself a member of a government which has a particular policy of its own for the raising of taxation, and he has been prevented from going as far as he would have liked in the direction he has professed. The fault and the criticism which we on this side have to find are not with ithe good professions and the good intentions of my hon. friend, but
TMr. Mackenzie King.]
rather, that at this time in the history of Canada, at this time in the history of the world, the Government has as respects the Budget, done some things which it ought not to have done, and has left undone other things which it ought to have done. Sir, let me speak for a moment about the things which it has left undone and which it ought to have done.
My hon. friendl '(Sir Henry Drayton) spoke at considerable length about the necessity of economy and retrenchment. Nothing could 'be more deserving of praise than profession of economy and retrenchment, unless it be the practice of those virtues. But when we turn from the professions of my hon. friend to examine the practices of the Government of which he is a member, we find that we are a long way from seeing an earnest of that economy and retrenchment which he would have us believe is the motive which the Government has at heart. I shall not attempt now to mention the particulars in which the Government has shown a great indifference-I might almost say a wanton indifference-to extravagance in public expenditures, because these matters have been admirably dealt with in the many speeches made by hon. gentlemen on this side. I refer in particular to the speeches of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster), my hon. friend from Guysborough and An-tigonish (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), and my hon. friend from Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) who spoke last night. If I might I would suggest that hon. members read these speeches carefully, and see wherein the Government has been extravagant and indifferent, and .then take note of what has been said in reply by hon. gentlemen opposite. Why, Sir, some very strong accusations have been made against the ministry from this side of the House, accusations so strong that one could hardly believe that they could pass unchallenged for a single moment. But unchallenged they have passed up to the present time.
I shall mention two or three of these things in order to give my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, who has not yet spoken in this debate, or some of his colleagues who may speak on his behalf, if he himself does not speak, an opportunity of making an explanation concerning them.
First of all, take the expenditures for last year. I shall not go into the expenditures during the war period because we are all prepared to admit that those expenditures -however vast they may have been, how-

ever carelessly and recklessly they may have been administered in many particulars-are part of the war period which has passed, and that nothing will foe gained by going at too great length into them. But we have a right to consider what has been done since the war, and especially have we that right in view of the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite, after promising that they would hold office only for the purposes of the war are retaining office now for the sake of office. We have a right to ask therefore-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will my hon. friend state when that promise was made, and by whom?

My right hon. friend asks me when the promise was made *that the Government would retain office only for the purposes of the war, and by whom. My right hon. friend knows that I have not at hand at the moment the different speeches made by himself and his colleagues-*
Oh, oh.

-and he knows therefore that I am not in a position at the moment to quote chapter and verse, but I will give him this answer: The people of the Dominion, when they were listening to the speeches of the Prime Minister and of those who sit around him as his colleagues to-day were clearly and definitely under the impression that by their utterances they meant that they were forming the present coalition Government solely for the purpose of carrying on, and helping to win the war, and that when that purpose was accomplished the elements of which the ministry was composed would revert back into the natural groups from which they had come-
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

-and that the people of this country would be given an opportunity of returning to power a government which would be in a position to frame peace policies for the period of reconstruction. May I say to my right hon. friend and to his colleagues that if, in the remarks they addressed to the people of this country at the time they were appealing to them for their support, they meant anything different; if they had in their hearts and in their minds what the Minister of Marine intimated yesterday he had in his mind, a mental reservation-if anything of that kind is conceivable it discloses the extent
of the deception which they were practising upon the people of Canada at that time. What are words after all? The devil can quote Scripture for his purposes. It is the intention, it is the impression that you seek to convey, that counts; and hon. gentlemen opposite-both those of Conservative persuasion and those who at the time professed to be of Liberal persuasion-led this country to believe that the two parties should unite for the purpose of winning the war, and that when that purpose was accomplished they would go to the country and give the people a chance to return a representative parliament.
I am happy to think that there were at least some members of the Government who from a sense of honour felt it incumbent upon them to leave the Administration. On what ground? On the ground that they entered the Government solely for the purpose of winning the war, and on the distinct understanding that when that was accomplished their contract was completed and they were at liberty to retire. Those hon. gentlemen at least had no intention of deceiving the country; they at least had no doubts in their own minds as to what the people understood at the time-they have lived up to the professions they made and the pledges they gave.
Well, Sir, inasmuch as we have had from the question of the Prime Minister a further evidence of the intention of the Government-openly professed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) recently to hang on to office regardless of the wishes of the people, may I give reasons to the House and to the country why such an intention should be frustrated if it is at all possible to prevent this Government continuing to administer our national affairs?
One reason why an appeal should be made to the country is because these hon. gentlemen have the war habit of mind, and so long as they remain in office they will persist in it. What do I mean by "the war habit of mind"? It is the habit of mind which believes that everything should be done by the autocratic will of the ministry, regardless altogether of the wishes of Parliament; it is the habit of mind which allows lavish expenditures to be accounted for by chance. And I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, and more particularly to the people of Canada, facing as we are the great questions of the day, that so long as this present Administration remains in office, so long will that war habit of mind continue to actuate the Government in their

management of public affairs, especially as regards extravagance in public expenditures.
What evidence have we of that tendency? As I have said I do not purpose to speak of the actual period of the war, but to take the post-war period. As an example I refer to the expenditure for the last current year as given in the Auditor General's Report. And in that connection let me develop the thought which my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) brought out so clearly last week. He showed that the addition to the public debt during this year of peace was $395,000,000, or more than $1,000,000 a day. That is the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite as contrasted with their professions of a desire for economy. Notwithstanding all our public debt we are faced with an increase of over $1,000,000 a day on the ordinary expenditures of the country. Such is the record of the Administration since the Armistice, as reported in the last volume of the Public Accounts.
Then take the record of the Government in regard to appointments-which are another prolific source of expenditure. We would have expected that with the large number of appointments made during the war period, there would have been, after the Armistice, a rigorous cutting down of those large war staffs. But we find, in answer to a question asked in this House as to how many appointments had been made to the permanent and temporary staffs of the Civil Service since the Armistice, that at the date the answer was given, several weeks ago, there had been added 4,176 permanent appointees and 22,954 temporary appointees, or a total of 27,130 added to the Civil Service list by the commissioners of the Civil Service during this peace period. In other words, 50 civil servants a day have been added to the Civil Service since the Armistice, or as my hon. friend said in presenting the information,-27 regiments of 1,000 each had been appointed by the Civil Service Commission in this period of peace. There is an example of the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite in contrast with their professions of economy and of retrenchment.
Then we have the moneys that 'have been *unaccounted for,-and here is a statement that has been made from this side time and time again. The Auditor General's Report, brought down only two or three days ago, repeats the story contained in the reports of the two previous years, that a sum of $121,000,000 of public money paid out during the war, has been unaccounted for up to the present time, and that the

Auditor General himself has been unable to get any explanation regarding this huge sum, although he has made request in writing for an accounting of it. There is the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite as contrasted with their professions.
In addition to the failure to account for moneys which have been paid out in accordance with the votes of Parliament, we have also instances of moneys used for purposes other than those for which they were appropriated by this House. That is a violation of one of the fundamental principles of Government: the control of parliament over the public expenditures. When Parliament votes a sum of money for a particular purpose, it is supposed to be used for that purpose. But according to the statements given to us in the Public Accounts money that was voted for the demobilization of our forces, in other words, money voted for military purposes for the security of this country, has been used for publicity purposes to help establish a press bureau which would be of service to hon. gentlemen apposite. There again we have a contrast of the professions of lion, gentlemen opposite with their practice.
Further, we have the indifference of the Government in the matter of requiring leaders for contracts. As has been stated here on several occasions, our laws require, in order to protect the public in matters of public expenditure, that when the Government is about to award contracts it shall call for tenders so that the lowest tenders *may be accepted. We had recently an exhibition of that indifference in regard to one item which I shall mention-although I might mention a great many-the expenditure for the mercantile marine which is being built by the Government. Contracts amounting altogether to $70,000,000 were awarded, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) in defending his Estimates admitted on the floor of this House that in not a single instance had the Government called for tenders or sought to award those contracts by public tender. And what is true in the case of those contracts is true also of thousands of other contracts which have been awarded by the different departments of the Government-awarded with absolute indifference to the laws which have been placed on the statute book for the protection of the Treasury.
Then, again, we have the indifference of the Government to the supervision of Parliament in the matter of expenditure. As an instance I may cite the case that came

up in the House last week in regard to the appointment of a minister plenipotentiary to Washington. Was Parliament given any opportunity to pass upon the expenditures that will arise in connection with that appointment? All we were told was that the Prime Minister himself had read the correspondence, and had had some one else read it, and that no member of this House .should see a line of it, although already a contract had been entered into which will involve large expenditures, which expenditures the Government will force .through this House by virtue of the majority at its command.
Then let me refer to the moneys which have been loaned to foreign countries. Last night we had a pretty strong indictment of same hon. members and their friends in regard to contracts awarded out of the credits extended to foreign countries. Some $70,000,000 or more have been loaned to countries like Roumania and Greece for [DOT]the purpose of enabling them to [DOT]buy supplies of various kinds. Whether or not these credits are worth anything remains to be seen; but it was shown conclusively last night by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Arch-ambault) that the Government had not hesitated to ask companies of which some hon. members on the other side are members or officers to supply goods to these countries, and had not hesitated to pay handsome sums from the public treasury for such goods sent abroad on the credit of the Dominion. That is a form of procedure which, possibly, can he defended by the letter of the law, but I asik my hon. friends opposite: in their efforts with regard to charity, where should charity begin in times such as these if not at home? We have need of economy; we have need of retrenchment in every particular. Instead of spending money lavishly and without the security that is necessary, the Government owes it to the people of this country to see that every dollar that goes out of the public treasury, spent for materials of any kind, is spent wholly and absolutely in the public interest.
Then, I might refer also to the Estimates of the present year, but it would take considerable time to go into the details. Members on this side have referred to item after item that we could well afford to cut down. Surely no member of this House would have found any fault with the Estimates of the Department of Militia and Defence had they been at a lower figure this year than they were a year ago. But
what is the difference? We are called upon this year to vote $4,000,000 more for the Department of Militia and Defence than we were asked to vote last year. Is that going in the right direction? I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance: Is that retrenchment? Is that the economy of which he approves?
May I put a question to the hon. gentleman? How does the vote for Militia and Defence this year compare with the vote for the year immediately preceding the war?

My hon. friend has asked me for a comparison between this year and the year before the war. He knows that I have not the figures with me as to the period before the war, but if I had, that would not affect matters one way or the other. The figures that are important are those which indicate which way we are tending. Are we going in the direction of economy, or have we since the war been going in the direction of increased expenditure? The figures of the Auditor General's Report show that whereas last year we spent a sum which was fairly large oti Militia and Defence, this year the Government are asking us to spend an additional $4,000,000 on that account. I say to my hon. friends opposite that if they had come down to the House with four millions struck off the amount of last year, they would have fulfilled to a better degree the wishes of the people of this country.
So Mr. Speaker, while we can compliment the minister on his fair professions and good intentions, we cannot do other than condemn the Government on its record in the matter of economy and retrenchment as having moved entirely in the wrong direction. Just to summarize what I have said: the Government has vastly increased the ordinary expenditure-increased it by over a million dollars a day according to the last statement brought down. It has vastly increased the appointments, both temporary and permanent, to the Civil Service-increased them at the rate of fifty civil servants a day. It has left unaccounted for $121,000,000 or more of public moneys which have been paid out. It has spent money for purposes for which it was not appropriated by Parliament. It has spent public money on contracts without calling for tenders in accordance with the law of the country. It has given money in loans and credits to foreign countries on very doubtful security and in a manner which will help its own friends rather than [DOT] further the best interests of this country.

And, instead of decreasing the public expenditure for the current year, it has ehown in many' particulars a tendency to increase the expenditure and to be indifferent to the necessity of retrenchment. That is one count which we have against hon. gentlemen opposite.
But, .Sir, looking further at the Budget : looking at the resolutions which my hon. friend has brought down, may I say perfectly frankly to him that what we most object to in his Budget is that it protects privilege and war profiteers instead of protecting the consumers of this country? We had expected, at this time of all times, a people's Budget; we have instead a profiteer's Budget; that is apparent when we come to analyse it. I say that for this reason: when we study the incidence of this taxation we find that in practically everything the minister has proposed there are increased burdens placed upon the consumers, not the upper classes, so-called, but the middle or poorer classes; and there is, on the other hand, a, careful protecting and safeguarding of those who are in a position of privilege in this country.
We had a right to expect, having regard to the professed desire o! hon. gentlemen opposite for economy, some statement from the Minister of Finance to the effect that the Government had devised machinery whereby the people throughout the country who had failed to pay their income tax in the last year or two would be obliged to make good their failures. We all know that the income tax has not been collected as fully and carefully as it should have been. Last summer, at the convention which the Liberal party held in this city of Ottawa, a resolution was passed, which was brought to the attention of the Government-a resolution condemning the Government for the non-enforcement of the income tax law. It was in these words:
This Convention condemns the Government because it has not enforced the income tax law in such a manner as to make it produce the revenue which such a tax should produce if properly collected.
The Government, Mr. Speaker, had that resolution before it. The Minister of Finance knew that that criticism was being made, not by one political party only, but by people generally throughout the country. As I have said, we had therefore, reason to expect and hope that when the Minister of Finance came down with his Budget he would also come down with the announcement that as respects the men and 
possibly some women in this country who had not paid the income tax, the Government had devised machinery under which all arrears of taxation would be carefully and fully collected.
Not only have the Government safeguarded some of their friends in that particular; but in regard to war time wealth, the wealth which was accumulated during the period of the war, have they had one word to say in the Budget proposals? One would never know that a single man had made an extra dollar during the period of the war, from what has been said by the Finance Minister in his address or by what is indicated in his Budget. There are several reasons why the Government should have taken account of war time wealth- that is to say, wealth that was made in the period of the war, out of the war, as	a	consequence of the	sacrifices and of the necessities of the people during that time. I say there is more than one reason why the Government should have taken note of that. The first reason is that the Government should have been taking account of it during the war; the Government while the war was going on should have been making some effort to secure from those who were profiting and profiteering during that period sums of money which would help to meet the expense of war. That was not done. Every day of delay means increased difficulty in reaching that particular source of wealth. By not introducing a resolution this session in regard to war time wealth, the Government make it increasingly difficult, if not almost impossible, to reach that source of wealth at any subsequent session or at any subsequent time. And my hon. friends tell us that they are going to stay in office for another couple of years-stay in office for another couple of years and further protect during that period those who have profited so largely during the war.
But, Sir, there is a third reason why the Government should have made some effort to collect from those who profited during the period of the waT, and that is that such a course as that is only right and just. Think of it, Mr. Speaker; think of vast fortunes being amassed during the period of the war, when mem were giving their lives and incurring .sacrifices in the service of the country. Think of the Government allowing the heaviest burdens to rest on the shoulders of the people generally, on the shoulders of those who already have endured great sacrifices, and not seeking to

lighten those burdens by making a levy on war fortunes. It would be better for every man who has made a fortune out of the war to give that fortune over to the State. It would be a thousand-fold better for him, for his children and for his children's children were he to do that, for I can see no good that will come to any home or family that gains a new status and builds up a new place in society out of fortunes that have been reaped through the blood of men and sacrifice of human lives.
I shall not trust to my own words to express the indignation which I believe the people will feel in regard to this indifference on the part of the Government. Let me read the words of a well-known Canadian woman, one who is greatly interested in social and industrial questions, a speaker of great ability, and one whose voice has been heard championing many causes of right, justice and popular liberty. I find in one of the May numbers of this year-I have not the exact date-of the Calgary Albertan, this article:
Government which conscripted life has not proved strong enough to conscript the war wealth. Mrs. Nellie McClung-
Oh, oh.

I hear some hon. gentlemen opposite laughing. Some day they will listeft to Mrs. Nellie McClung, and to the voice of the women on whose behalf she is speaking:
Mrs. Nellie McClung, the noted authoress, of Edmonton, was asked toy The Albertan yesterday to give her opinion of the new taxes proposed in the Budget and last evening wired the following:
The money has to be raised, of course, and, personally, I can do without silk stockings and georgette blouses, but I did hope that some of the war debt could be dug out of the war profiteers and the people who boldly proclaimed that they were not "running their business for the glory of God." The new taxes will not be any hardship for those. They will simply add it to the price of their products, and let the people pay, as usual. But it will bear heavily on the salaried and professional people, who are now burdened to the limit. To them it will mean a further lowering of the standards of living, and they will become more than ever the new poor. I would have liked to see the Government make drastic reduction in the' tariff, and cease to protect wealthy manufacturers, sugar people and others and show a real strength in throttling the big interests. The present Budget does not aim to do this. I am disappointed. I thought a Government that felt strong enough to conscript life would be strong enough to do anything.
That is tihe view of a woman in regard to the attitude which the Government have taken in protecting those who have made vast fortunes out of the war and in throwing the burden of taxation upon the common people.
Let me give another voice, the voice of the men who served overseas, as stated by the president of the Great War Veterans' Association. Hon. members have doubtless noticed that within the last few days the Great War Veterans' Association have been considering the effects of this Budget; they -have felt so exasperated at the attitude taken by the Government in intimating they intend to hold on to office irrespective altogether of the views of any class of people in this country, that the Great War Veterans' Association are now sending to the different branches of their organization communications indicative of the attitude of those who hold executive positions, and asking that resolutions be passed telling the Government that the time has come for them to get out of office.
But what do the Great War Veterans say in regard to these taxes? This is a quotation from a message sent by Mr. R. B. Maxwell, Dominion President of the Great War Veterans' Association of Canada, to all branches of his association urging them to call mass meetings for the purpose of demanding a general election. In this message he gives the reasons why the Great War Veterans think a general election is- desirable. This is what he says in particular reference to the Budget that has been brought down:
Parliament now requires that those who served in the war shall share in the payment of the major portion of the war debt despite the fact that war-accumulated wealth remains practically unmolested.
There, in one sentence, is the charge which they make against hon. gentlemen opposite. In this Budget which the Government have brought down, the Government have left war-accumulated wealth practically unmolested.
Lest it may seem that I am going a little far in suggesting that war-aceumula/ted wealth should be held as a first charge for meeting expenditures which have arisen out of the war, may I give to the House a few extracts from a memorandum submitted, not by any special committee chosen for any special purpose, but by 4 p.m. a department of the British Government to a committee of the British House of Commons in regard to this question of war wealth? I do this just to illustrate the nature of the sources from which it might be possible to draw in helping to meet the vast expenditures with which the country is confronted at
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

Perhaps my hon. friend will wait until I am through, -when I shall 'be pleased to answer any .questions he may lask. At present, I desire to continue this argument. I have said *that the reason we take exception to the Budget which my hon. friend has brought down is the fact that it does not recognize these great public needs, these great public rights. It has lost -sight .altogether of what the profiteers owe to the community -and to the State at this particular .time, .especially in view of the conditions that have been developing during the past-few years.
*Sir, I wish also to say that another reason for our exception to the Budget is that it reveals the outstanding f-abt 'that fh.e Government 'has no policy for dealing with the high -cost of living. Mr. .Speaker, if there is any question which is paramount in Canada to-day, -and which transcends all other considerations, it -is the important question of the high Cost of living. We could not expect hon. gentlemen opposite to solve 'that question. Certainly not; but we at least had ia right to .expect that they would -take some step towards a solution of the -problems which .the high cost of living involves, and that they would have had some suggestion to offer which would, if adopted, have helped to relieve the burdens which men, women and children in this country are bear-

ing to-day. But rwhiat have they done? Instead of alleviating the high cost of living as it affects the great mass of consumers they have added to it. They have increased the cost of living and made it more difficult for the people of Canada to jive than it has been heretofore. To an invisible tariff they have added a visible tariff on a great multitude of commodities, thereby increasing the cost of living to the vast body ot consumers. From one end of Canada to the other, in every home, there has been considerable difficulty in coping with the isituation. Go where you will, you will find this the baffling problem that taxes the ingenuity of the great majority of the people. As I say, Mr. Speaker, instead of meeting the high cost of living as it wtas obviously the duty of the Government to have met it, by reducing the tariff on the necessaries of life, they have added this visible tariff in the nature of an excise to the invisible tariff Which talready exacts its toll from the people in regard to commodities in general use.
But they have done more than that. They have not been satisfied with merely adding one tax but they have heaped tax upon tax on many of the necessaries of life that enter into daily consumption.
So far as this Budget affects luxuries, we can heartily endorse all that the Government proposes. It is proper that luxuries should be taxed and taxed just as much as they will stand, but, as has been pointed out by one hon. member after another on this side of the House there are many articles, such as boots and shoes, clothing, the different articles required in the daily food of poor people, canned goods for example, which are taxed and over taxed. Consider this excise tax in relation to the cost of living. Take clothing for instance. The cloth say is brought from the Old Country, and on it a tariff tax is paid when it enters Canada, a tax which is based on the par rate of exchange, although the pound sterling has fallen in purchasing value. The result is that instead of the tax being paid on the actual value of the commodity, it is levied on the higher arbitrary rate, which results in additional protection being given to the Canadian manufacturer on this particular article. Then when that commodity gets into the hands of the wholesaler or of the manufacturer who passes it to the wholesaler, an excise tax is levied not merely on the value of the commodity itself but also on the extra taxes that have been put upon it. Upon passing from the wholesaler to the retailer another 
excise tax is placed upon it and then, from the retailer to the consumer, yet another tax is placed upon it. By the time this commodity, in the nature of a necessity, reaches the	consumer,	it is	carrying	notonly its own value but tax upon tax	upon tax and	that is	the
way the Government is solving the problem of the high cost of living. We find that under this Budget the consumer not only has to pay the tariff on many necessaries of life, but hie burden is added to by these different excise taxes.
There is another ill effect which the Budget is going to have on the poorer people in this country in that it is going to encourage the manufacture of shoddy goods. Quality is quite as important as quantity and there is probably no way in which you can hit a man harder than to give him poor value for his money. It will be recalled that Charles Kingsley in describing shoddy material, used the term "cheap and nasty." The poor man who has a hard enough struggle already to provide food and clothing for his children will feel that he cannot afford this extra tax and will be forced to buy this wretched shoddy material.
Instead of caring for and protecting the consumers the Government have left them to their fate. One thing I was surprised to see in regard to this matter was that while a tax is put upon the goods obtained by the consumer there is no tax upon the goods that are being sent out of the country. Why? Because in that instance it helps the manufacturer. He, not the [DOT]consumer, is the chief consideration with the Government, Again, the more you export out of the country, the less there is for the consumer. Look it all over and you see all along the line the interests of the privileged classes carefully taken care of while the interests of the great bulk of the people have not been safeguarded.
But not only has the Government failed to make any contribution towards the solution of the high cost of living, it has shown its absolute incapacity to bring down any proposal, or to denote any policy in the Budget to assist in securing increased production. We have heard hon. gentlemen opposite ge't up in turn and say that the only salvation of the country is increased production; that it is only by increased production we can solve the high cost of living, and get the money to imeet high taxation. Yet in the Budget proposals there is nothing to further that increased production which is needed most of all. To increase production

you must take some of the duties off necessaries and thus lower the cost of living. Then you will make men happier, more ready to work, more ready to put their zeal into the particular lines of production in which they .are engaged. But you must also take the duties off the instruments of production. The Government has not done this. It has not taken any duties off the necessaries of life; it has not taken any duties off the instruments of production. On the one hand, it has no policy to cope with the high cost of living and on the other it has no policy to bring about increased production, which through reduction of duties on the necessaries of life and on the instruments of production is demanded on every side. It is demanded by all classes of people in this country.
Go where you will in Canada to-day and you will find that people are not getting the necessaries of life such as food, clothing and shelter, in the quantities in which they should be able to secure them, Take a young man or woman making his or her own way in the world, starting out in life. Is it good public policy, is it in the interest of human well-being that struggles should be made more difficult than necessary for these young people? If in any way the Government can help to make possible an increase in the number of homes it will be contributing to the happiness, contentment and prosperity of the country. Take homes that are already established in the crowded cities, Montreal and Toronto, for instance, where you have one house close against another or one tenement above another; or in the lonely regions whether on the prairies or in the recesses of the mountains where you have isolated homes; or in those more favoured localities where there is neither overcrowding on the one hand nor isolation on the other; in almost every one of these homes, whether you find there only two persons living together, or a large family, or three generations, you will find the joys of home life diminished, and anxieties increased, by reason of the great advance in the cost of living;	The one thing necessary is,
for the Government to do what lies in its power to bring relief from that anxiety, to make possible a greater degree o,f happiness and comfort than now exists. This it can only do by making possible greater production in those basic industries which provide what is necessary in the way of food, clothing, and shelter.
Take	the requirements of industry
itself. What is all industry? Industry is 189
nothing other than the transformation of natural resources, through a variety of processes, into commodities and services available for human use. It starts with the great basic industries of agriculture, fishing, lumbering, mining. These primary basic industries are those that have to be developed in the first instance. After their development, whatever of wealth is produced from that original source becomes converted by further processes of transformation-through the application of labour, and through the application of tools and machines, to assist in furthering production-into commodities and services of one kind and another available for human use. One result as:	that unless
you make possible the increase of production in the basic industries to the largest extent possible you are only handicapping all the subsequent processes and the ultimate development of wealth. So we say that in regard to the instruments of production applied to the natural resources of the country, there should be as little in the way of handicap as it is possible to have. The more readily available the instruments of production aire, the greater will be the wealth produced from those primary industries; and as greater wealth is produced from the primary industries so will greater wealth be available for the secondary industries, and consequently available to the consumer of commodities. In that way the volume of trade will be increased and the volume of prosperity will also be increased. That is why it is so important that in an effort to increase production the Government should have brought forward some constructive policy.
I can imagine my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, saying when I suggest that some of the war-time wealth might be taxed, " It is poor policy to tax capital, because capital is the goose that lays (the golden eggs." Well, I can appreciate his not wishing to tax capital, hut I wonder if it has occurred to hon. gentlemen opposite that if there is one form of capital that is most essentially capital it is the instruments Of production that are used for carrying on further production. Instruments of production for the basic industries are the real capital that is necessary along with labour, >to create further wealth; and as long as customs duties are kept on the implements of production of the basic industries so long you are simply taxing the capital that is necessary to produce further wealth.



Now, not only is it in the interest of industry generally that there should be the utmost freedom of production in the primary industries but it as especially in the interest of the manufacturing industries. As I have saiid the wealth that is to be used or further transformed in manufacturing, has to come in the first instance from these primary industries. If it is not obtained there it cannot be obtained at all. As it is increased in volume there, so it will increase the volume of these other industries. There is also this further circumstance: Wages have been going up, salaries have been going up. They cannot go up indefinitely if our manufacturers are to hope to be able to compete with the manufacturers of other countries. There are real wages and there are nominal wages. Nominal wages are what a man gets in terms of money; real wages are what he can buy with hie money. If real wages are not increased a man is no better off no matter how much he gets in the way of increase in nominal wages; and real wages will increase only as the necessities of life become more plentiful and it becomes possible to obtain, at lower cost, the food, the clothing and the warmth and shelter that is necessary. As these things become available in larger quantities so will a man's real wages increase. Now if manufacturers, if the owners of transportation systems, if those who employ men at wages and on salaries hope to be able to meet the world competition it will only be by so increasing the development of the natural resources of the country and the basic industries that wealth will be made more and more plentiful, and that thereby it will be made possible for the wage-earning and the salaried classes to obtain what is needful through the real wages which they Teceive.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the same increase is equally desirable in the interests of trade and commerce. It is not less in the interest of increased production and manufacturing than in the interest of trade and commerce, that there should be a large volume of trade. I think I am perfectly right when I say that in trading profits are made not on the price but on the volume of trade. It is the turn-over that counts-and the greater the number of transactions, the better it will be for the man who is fortunate enough ter be carrying on a particular business. Now what is the effect of the taxation which the Government, is proposing? It is for the most part in the nature of a restriction upon trade; it is making it more difficult

for those who are engaged in trade and commerce to carry on their commerce in the volume to which they were formerly accustomed. The turn-over will not be what it hitherto has been. And if the turnover is checked at one point it is going to check the man further down; and so instead of making for prosperity, the effect of any taxation that restricts development in trade is simply to turn back the hands of the clock, to hamper the production of the real sources of wealth from which all wealth is ultimately to come. I might go at some length into the requirements of trade and commerce in that regard, but I think the point as stated will be sufficient of itself.
Let me, however, develop this further thought-an all-important one at this time- that development of the basic industries of this country is absolutely necessary on the score of a wise, economic development of the future of industry and trade in Canada. The kind of wealth and the kind of production is just as important as the quantity of production, and in many respects more important. Statistics will show unmistakably that in Canada the trend has been relatively away from production in agriculture to the production of commodities along other particular lines. In other words, instead of fostering a natural development in industry in this country, the Governmental policies in Canada have been fostering a highly artificial trend in development. We have been building up cities and towns at the expense of rural life. That is something that cannot be denied; and I say that that is not only against the interests of rural life but is against the interests of the manufacturers, it is against the interest, of all who live in cities and towns.
Let me give the House a few statistics in this regard as to the development of Canada in the last few years. We have not available any census statistics other than those taken in 1901 and 1911, but they show that in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick between those years the urban population had increased very considerably while in those provinces and Prince Edward Island the rural population decreased materially. In Quebec the urban population increased in that period by 314,383, while the rural population increased by only 39,951. In old Ontario the urban population increased by 392,511 in 10 years, or a total of 1,328,489, but the rural population actually decreased 52,184 in the same period, leaving a total of 1,194,785. This

tendency for the urban population to increase at the expense of the rural has been greatly intensified in the province of Ontario during the period of the war owing to the artificial stimulus given to industries connected with the war.
In the western provinces, which are rural above everything else, in 1901, taking the provinces together, 75.39 per cent of the population was rural, and 24.61 was urban; while in 1916-there is a later census in the West-the figures are 64.31 per cent for the rural population and 35.69 per cent for the urban. This is an abnormal and unhealthy division of population where 15 per cent of the available agricultural land is not yet under cultivation.
The census of 1911 shows that the urban population of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta increased 92 per cent in ten years; but the rural population increased only 52 per cent. The census of 1916 shows that this tendency towards expansion of the cities has increased. In Saskatchewan the rural population decreased from 84.37 per cent to 72.79 per cent between 1911 and 1916.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the significance of those figures is very great indeed. What is needed at the present time above all else? During the war the cry that went out to the world was first, for more men; then the cry was, for more munitions; then for more ships; then for more food, and'more food, and more food. And it is the cry for more food that the world is hearing today. It was the lack of food that ultimately brought the German and Austrian armies to their knees. It was starvation that ended the war as effectively as anything else. To-day the need of the world above all other things is for increased quantities of food, and the problem of the high cost of living will never be solved until there is that increase. Yet these statistics that I have read show that the trend in this country during the last couple of decades has been .all in one direction: Increasing the demand for food in the urban centres, while reducing relatively the numbers of those who are capable of producing food in the rural districts. I cannot but believe that a development of that kind is certain to be inimical to any country in the long run, and that it is not a wise national policy which abnormally stimulates development in one direction, while retarding it in a direction which seems all-important from the national point of view.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) I think recognized that this would be one of the most difficult arguments for 189-r
him to meet in the course of his campaign on behalf of the special interests, and he undertook to tell us the other day that it was no use trying to deal with this movement from the country into the towns, that civilization was tending that way, that it was inevitable. I think we get the crux of the situation in the attitude we take towards this problem if we really believe that it is in the interests of national development to be indifferent to this movement away from the land to the urban centres, that it is the urban centres that must at all costs be developed at the expense of the rural districts, why, certainly we are likely to advocate a policy that will further that end. But, on the other hand, if we believe that the interests of both the rural and the urban centres will be best served by keeping a maximum number of people on the land to produce the necessaries of life in as large quantities as possible, then our views towards the fiscal and other great problems of the country will be determined accordingly. Let me read what the Minister of the Interior said in regard to this development. His remarks will be found in the unrevised Hansard of May 25, at page 2774:
But, this diminution which has come to Canada, to the United States and to every country in the world-and it is terribly 'aggravated in Great Britain by reason of their fiscal policy, undoubtedly,-this general diminution in rural population is inevitable; no change of policy can ever alter it. Why? Well, it seems to me that the reason is obvious. The farmer produces food; that is the great product to the turning out of which he applies his energy. As the world advances in population, people do not eat any more food individually; the need1 of food increases just as the population advances and no more. But as civilization advances the other needs and indulgences of mankind multiply an hundredfold. Transportation needs,1, clothing needs, entertainment needs, all these requirements advance by leaps and bounds, whereas food remains relatively stationary. Consequently a larger proportion of the world's people are engaged in making these other products and rendering these other services than are engaged in the growing of food. Do what we will, we would be foolish to try to 'beat back logic itself, and the whole trend and movement of the age.
That is a hopeless attitude to adopt, and I am surprised that one who is usually so careful in following out an argument to the last point should have slipped, into some of the errors which my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has made in that statement. He says that the people's demand for food has not increased, but that their demand for clothing has, and that that is something we need more and more of as we go along. Well, I would ask my hon. friend: Where

is the wool and where is the cotton to come from which are, -so essential for clothing unless from the products of the farm?

speechtext: The hon. gentleman will see that I used the word "mainly." That, I said, was "mainly" the product of the farm. It is true that the raw wool is also, but it would be a stretch of the imagination to believe that cotton is a product of the farms of Canada.

My hon. friend was not speaking of Canada alone, he was speaking also of the United States and of England. I would like to bring to the attention of my hon. friend that all the things essential to life-food, clothing, shelter, warmth-are derived from the basic industries-agriculture, mining, lumbering, fishing. These things are fundamental. When we follow out what my hon. friend has said, what does it come to? That the thousands of men going into the different callings of transportation, of mercantile life, and other city activities mean that so many more men have to be fed in the urban centres and that fewer men remain in the country to supply the needs of the augmented	urban population.
That is what it comes to, this artificial development; society is making less possible all the time the production of the necessary commodities in the required quantities. I can see nothing but misfortune for any nation or any country that permits a development of that kind to proceed. My hon. friend spoke about England and talked about the increase in the slums. He pointed out that there was a great deal of unemployment in these slum areas of the cities. Well, that is an inevitable effect of the turning of development from the land into urban centres, where the development is not natural and proper. Let me quote to my hon. friend words of great truth as well as of great beauty, which I take from Goldsmith's Deserted Village-they are familiar to him, I am sure. These words view in one stanza the situation that we are trying to view as a whole:
111	fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, Where wealth accumulates and men decay. Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade, A breath can make them as a breath has made; But a bold peasantry, their country's pride, When once destroy'd, can never be supplied.
That, Sir, is a fundamental consideration of which we should take account at this time. We do not want to see in Canada an aristocracy of wealth grow up in our large cities, and men leaving the rural .areas, a great plutocracy and aristocracy com-

bined on the one side, and men decaying and villages and rural life deserted on the other. What we want is a bold peasantry; what we want is men who love the soil, who love contact with nature. We need them, as I have already said, if we arc to maintain our human society in a proper degree of strength and vigour. It was with that consideration in view that at the Liberal Convention held last summer, in addition to a resolution with regard to the tariff, to which I shall refer in a moment, the following important resolution on encouragement to agriculture was laid down as one of the planks of the Liberal platform :
In the interest of agricultural production and development it ia expedient to encourage cooperation and induce greater investment in farming; therefore, it is deemed expedient to utilize the national credit to assist co-operative agricultural credit associations to provide capital for agriculture at the lowest possible rates.
With the object of reducing the high cost of living by eliminating as far as possible the waste and expense in handling food products between the producer and consumer, it is expedient to extend the principle and system of Canadian Government elevators and to provide interior and terminal cold storage warehouses equipped for the assembling, assorting, preparing, storing and grading of food products in order that co-operative organizations and others may have available to them reliable, modern equipment, for the distribution of farm products in superior condition and at lessened cost either for domestic consumption or for export. And that cold storage transportation facilities should be provided, at the cost of operation, for the shipment of food products throughout Canada and for the carrying to the markets of the world the surplus farm products of this country and delivering them in such condition that will make Canadian foodstuffs a standard of quality for the world's market.
That, in the interests of agriculture, in aid of greater production on the land, and for the conservation of the soil in Canada, it is expedient for the Government to arrange for the distribution of fertilizers at the lowest possible cost.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party in its advocacy of measures that it believes to be in the interests of agriculture is not seeking in any way to care primarily for the interests of one class as against the interests of another. As I have said to-day,
I firmly believe that the welfare of every city dweller is dependent absolutely upon the well-being and welfare of the people who dwell in the country, and only as we increase and improve agricultural development shall we make possible a happier lot for the masses of the people in the cities; shall we make possible a reduction in the cost of living; shall we make possible the . obtaining of food supplies at a price which will enable us to get the labour fiat is

necessary for the carrying on of the manufacturing industries.
There is another reason why I think we should encourage the people as far as we can to live in the country. The greatest of all assets to a nation is the health of its people. There is no denying that country life makes for the health of the human being, as life in the city does not begin to do. To the extent that the people are engaged in rural occupations; to the extent that they are in close contact with nature, -in fishing, in mining, in lumbering, in agriculture, in any of these great basic industries-to that extent will they be stronger and healthier. For that reason I should like to see an energetic policy of rural development instituted in this country which would help to make rural life as attractive as it possibly can be made. Let me illustrate what I mean iby a simple example. The Government has had voted large sums of money which it is prepared to lend to munigipalities for the purpose of putting up dwellings for working men in cities and towns. That may he good as far as it goes, but something much better would be the erection all over this country of cottages on farms where men and women could live with their families, working as farm labourers and farm helpers, if you like, having their own cottages, their own homes, and assisting the farmers in the production of necessities for the people in the cities and towns. Anything that will encourage the people to go on the land; anything that will help to make farm life enjoyable and prosperous, will help to develop a prosperous and vigorous people.
Having regard to the vast losses which we sustained during the war, to the numbers of men -who were killed, and to the large numbers who suffered physical injury of one kind or another or impairment of health, it becomes most important that the Government should give as much attention as it possibly can to the conservation of human life. We talk a great deal about the conservation of natural resources, -but, Sir, the conservation of human life is equally important. May I here refer to another most important plank in the platform of the Liberal party as laid down at the convention of last year? The following resolution on the conservation and improvement of physical standards of Canadians was moved, as I recall it, by one of the women delegates:
Whereas the Great War and the greater epidemic have taken an appalling toll of Canadian life ; and
Whereas human life and physical efficiency are the nation's greatest assets; and
Whereas the conservation and improvement thereof should be the country's first care;
Therefore this gathering of Liberals in convention assembled pledges itself to a vigorous prosecution of the measures best calculated to conserve the life and improve the physical standard of our Canadian citizenship.
As I said a moment ago, human life is much more important than wealth; health is of greater concern and a more important capital than money. But what is being done at the present time along preventive lines? I know that hon. gentlemen opposite have established a Department of Health, and in that work they have had the co-operation of members on this side of the House. But thus far we have seen very little as a result of what is being done by that department. May I urge the department to consider this matter of the health of the people, not in any small way, but as part of a great national policy such as I have been endeavouring to indicate during the course of my remarks this afternoon, based upon the wisdom of bringing people into contact with nature; the desirability of enabling as many as possible to find their places of residence, their homes, where their health is likely to be benefited to the greatest degree?
Let me read a line or two from an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Star of May 13. The subject with which it deals is a very important one in connection with the production of wealth, which we are considering at the present time. I am putting it on the material ground, for the meantime, of increased production, because it is only as labour and capital are applied to the natural resources of the country that we have an increase of production. This article is headed: "More Deadly Than War," it says:
Dr. C. D. Parfitt, of Muskoka, tells the special committee on pensions at Ottawa that Canada lost more lives from tuberculosis than in battle with Germans.
The editorial continues:
The figures Dr. Parfitt gives are alarming. In five years 35,684 Canadian soldiers were killed in battle in Europe, and during the same period 42,920 Canadians died of tuberculosis in Canada. The incidence of tuberculosis was 120 per cent greater in the Canadian than in the British Expeditionary Force, suggesting that the people of this country are peculiarly susceptible to the ravages of the disease.
The greatest war of all time has come and gone, with its tanks and poison gas, and many deadly weapons perfected by science, yet it ha9 failed to equal in destruction of life the steady ravages of tuberculosis. Its sum of misery, with families broken up, lifework cut

off, strong men bent under bereavement, and talent filched from the public service, makes a smaller heap than is the regular loot of the White Plague.
The contrast between the nation at war and the nation at peace is now being realized in Canada, and it means the lifting of a deadly weight off the minds and hearts of the people. But judged in terms of life and death, a more 'deadly weight crushes down upon the public. 3t places also a burden upon the conscience of all. Canada took effective action to bring her men home from the deadly trenches; what is Canada doing to save her women and children from tuberculosis ?
That is not my question, but a question put by a paper which is friendly to the Govemmemt. What is Canada doing to save her women and ehidiren from tuberculosis? Five per cent or one twentieth of our population who earn a livelihood, regardless of their calling in life, are absolutely wholly and continuously, physically incapacitated from performing the duties pertaining to their profession, trade or labour, by disease which is and should be preventable. Place the total population of Canada at 8,000,000, and generally speaking, we estimate one half of this to be male. If it is further estimated that of the male population, at least two-fiths or 1,600,000 are wage-earners, and if you calculate that 5 per cent of this number, because of disease which is capable of prevention, are totally and continuously unable to earn, you can readily understand what a loss this means financially. In order to ascertain what this means, let- us suppose the average earnings to be at the rate of S3 per head per day. Five per cent of 1,600,000 of a population represents 80,000, and this multiplied by $3 each would give $240,000 per day. First you have the loss to the families of the wage-earners, second, the profits lost to employers as a result of these 80,000 people being forced to remain idle, and third, loss of production to the nation at a time when conservation plays such an important part.
As regards the saving o! life, approximately 200,000 babes are born every year in Canada, and an average of 120 out of every 1,000 of these die before they are one year old from conditions which may and should be, in large measure, prevented. This in itself deprives the nation of 24,000 potential native-born citizens a year. There are between 10,000 and 15,000 deaths annually in Canada from tuberculosis.
My reason for touching on these questions of health at this point is as I have indicated, that the Government have told us

that what is needed at the present time above all is increased production. We can have increased production only as we have increased labour, increased willingness to produce and increased instruments of production wherewith to labour. It is going to be increasingly difficult to- have the immigration we had in former years, because Europe cannot spare her people as she formerly did. Is it not then the part of a wise, sane and -far-seeing policy to try to develop our national life in a manner which will best conserve our human life as well as best increase the production of the necessaries of life for the masses of the people?
I come now to some references which have been made to the National Policy. Hon. gentlemen opposite have sought to revive and stimulate throughout the country interest in the so-called National Policy of protection and to recount all it is alleged to have done for Canada. Without arguing the question one way or the other as to what the National Policy did or did not do, may I submit this consideration to the people of Canada as an all important one, in any consideration of a fiscal policy, namely, the condition of Canada as it was when the National Policy was introduced and as it is to-day in regard to possible future development. 'When the National Policy was introduced into Canada in 1878 or 1879, we had no export of manufacturers vvoTthy of the name, and we had little in the way of a home market. When Sir John A. Macdonald appealed to the House of Commons to support his policy of protection of manufactures, he did so on the ground that what we needed was a home market for our manufactured goods; that we needed to stimulate individual industries; that we needed to give an infant industry an opportunity to grow and develop. The infanlt industry of the day of the inauguration of the National Policy has become the giant iron and steel merger of which we have heard mention in this House recently. Is the iron and steel merger, running up into millions, if not billions of dollars, an industry comparable with the kind of industry which Sir John A. Macdonald wished to stimulate? All that I am anxious to point out at the moment is that as times change, conditions come to the fore of which full account should be takenp From the moment the National Policy was introduced to the present time, efforts have been constant to improve conditions for a number of special industries in this country? Look at the vast expenditures that

have been made on railways and on canals and shipping; look at the transportation within the country itself and across the seas; see what the Government are doing at the present time in the matter of stimulating the merchant marine; take the work of the Department of Trade and Commerce in having trade commissioners in different parts of the world; take the credits the Government are giving to foreign countries -all of these 'are ways of helping special interests to develop their particular industries. I am not saying that these are not good, but I am pointing out that they all help to give a larger market to the manufactures of this country, and to the extent that they do so, the consumers of this country are placed at a greater disadvantage than they would be if these great advantages were not given to particular interests.
If we are going to consider one interest, let us consider all interests. That
5 p.im is what we say is desirable in developing an industrial policy. No one would say that it was unwise to further internal and export trade; but if it be wise to help and stimulate one industry in its world development, it is equally wise to stimulate all the industries of the country. Let me read what Sir John A. Macdonald said when he introduced the National Policy. These are his words, respecting Canada in the seventies, as he uttered them in Parliament:
a young and struggling country, just emerging from the first struggles with the forest. We have but little realized capital as yet. The manufacturers of the country, with a few small exceptions have scarcely taken root.
!He quoted with approval John Stuart Mill. And here I might direct the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to the question he asked the other * day as to whether John Stuart Mill had or had not supported protection. This is what Sir John A. Macdonald quoted from John Stuart Mill:
The only case in which, on mere principles of political economy, protecting duties lean be defensible is when they are imposed temporarily (especially in a young and rising country) in hope of naturalizing a foreign industry in itself perfectly suitable to the circumstances of the country.
Those are not my words, but the words of Sir John A. Macdonald quoting John Stuart Mill. The point 'I make is: That any argument .as to what was necessary and what was the best policy for Canada in 1879 must be considered to-day in the light of the changed conditions.
Sir John A. Macdonald in the statement I have just quoted refers to the fact that Canada was then a young country with practically no home market for her manufactures and certainly with no export market at all. Let me give my hon. friends the contents of a communication which I think will appeal to them as authoritative, and which will indicate the change that has taken place in Canada since the National Policy was first introduced. .When my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and I had the pleasure of visiting 'the Maritime Provinces in tihe early part of this year, we were most generously received toy the Commercial Club of St. John, o'f which, I think, the hon. .member for St. John is president. He was away .at the time, but the vice-president and other officers of the Commercial Club showed us great courtesy and asked us if we would accompany them to St. John harbour to see 'the nature of the .shipping at that port. We spent the morning going over the harbour and looking at the different ships that were lying at .anchor there. The point that these gentlemen wished to bring .especially to our attention was that the facilities at St. John were wholly inadequate to meet 'the demand which was imposed upon 'them by the amount of shipping that was toeing done at that .port. It was in the month of January, and at that time every wharf was lined with ships. Lying at anchor in the harbour were some thirteen or fourteen ocean liners that had to wait their turn to get accommodation. Those ships were there from every quarter of the globe. They were there to take Canadian goods, the natural .and manufactured products of Canada, to the markets Of the world. They were there to carry our products to Europe, Africa, Australia and .
