Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a picture of the development of trade and industry in this country as it is at the present time. This was the month of January. You will observe that the ships were to sail to practically every part of the world, to Africa, to Australia, to Brazil and to the northern and southern parts of Europe, and this was only from one of our ports. It all denotes trade that lias been facilitated by the 'Government. It must 'be apparent that the great body of consumers in this country are entitled to at least some consideration when their taxes are going in very large measure to help ta make possible this vast development of export trade. The photographs which were promised in the letter came in the course of a day or two, and when one looks at them one sees railroad terminals jammed with cars. Everything that can be done to increase and further develop this vast trade may be desirable, hut as was pointed out by some hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate, and particularly by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), iit is impossible to have trade going in one direction and expect to continue doing business un-_ less you have cargoes in the opposite direction as well. Many of these ships came to Canada in ballast, bringing nothing valuable to our shores; that is not a condition that can be maintained indefinitely. If we want to build upon a sound basis we must develop those industries which we are best qualified to develop, and to the greatest extent possible encourage exchange of products with other nations.
All I am arguing for is that in our national policies we shall not have a circumscribed or narrow vision; but that we shall look to the necessities and interests of all classes and groups and not to the particular interests of any group or class. As I listened to the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meigben) who expounded the Government's policy, it seemed to me, that

he had fallen into the common error of those who become advocates of protection of looking primarily to special interests as of vital concern. His mind seemed focussed on particular interests to ithe exclusion of industry as a whole. He spent a great deal of time citing from the reports of special committees which he said had been appointed by the Asquith Government to report upon the condition of particular industries in England. He sought to emphasize the findings of these committees because some members of them urged increased protection. But my hon. friend forgot to make a survey of British industry as a whole. It is perfectly true that certain industries in England have not the position they formerly had, but the question we must ask is: "What was England's position as a whole during the war; was she not able not only to finance herself and the different nations allied with her, but to carry the war through to a successful issue?" It is possible that the steel and iron industry of England is not at the moment what it once was. But what about England's shipping industry? Englishmen say that so long as England is an island she has to keep command of the seas through her merchant marine, and she has to protect it by her navy. As a result when the war came on England was supreme in that realm and it was her merchant marine together with her navy that saved her and helped save the rest of the world. England with her merchant marine could go to any quarter of the world to get the supplies she needed to feed her people, and to produce the needed armaments.
You can always get men to say that from the point of view of a particular, industry it is desirable to protect it and you do not need to go to England for an example of that. If you focus your mind on any particular industry or profession or business you will find some who are interested in it favour the application to it of the protective principle. But when you leave a particular industry and cast your eye over all industries you will realize that while protection may be necessary in special cases,-its application generally is not equally beneficial. You prove nothing if you- take one example and leave out all other considerations. There is a little book which was published in the Middle Ages in England known as Seldon's Table Talk in which a youth says to his father that he can prove by the kind of logic that his father has been using that he is perfectly entitled to marry his own grandmother. His father has been
saying that a certain thing has been done in one case and therefore it ought to be done in another. When questioned by his father as to how he could argue as he did the son replied: "You married my mother; why should I not marry yours?" So it is in regard to the logic of my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who siays that because certain industries considered by themselves would be the better for protection, therefore other industries in other countries are in need of it. speechtext: Hear, hear.

My hon. friend smiles but he does' not take into account the agricultural, the fishing, and the mining industries, which are surely of some importance in England. There is also the shipping industry and others which might be mentioned. 'Surely these are examples enough for my hon. friend. The whole carrying trade of England is involved. It is a matter 'of relativity having .regard to possibilities and opportunities for future developments. I could give my hon. friend a parallel to much that he has given us. Last year in England I took occasion to examine somewhat carefully the workings of joint industrial councils and I was told that in practically all the industries in England where they have joint industrial councils their members were united in a demand for increased protection for their particular industry. EVery day there were demands from bodies interested in particular trades such as the textile trade and others, saying: "We would like increased protection for this industry by itself." When I spoke to one of the English members of Parliament and	asked what
attitude the Government	were	likely
to take in regard to the matter, his reply was: "That is all right as long as we are dealing with individual industries, but these matters are not settled by individual industries; they are settled in Parliament where all industries have a voice. When they look at their own particular industry they say that it ie desirable to give that industry special consideration but when they are confronted in Parliament by

men who are representing different industries it becomes a different question." When you get a vast body of opinion to view the question from its many different angles, .you begin to see the necessity of give and take and the wisdom of not deciding what the policy of the nation shall be on the basis of one, two, or three particular industries because the question must be decided on the basis of what is the proper policy for all. That is the security which is found in our parliamentary institutions; that is why self-government stands ior government of the people as a whole. While it is desirable that the interests of every industry should be safeguarded, Parliament must take into consideration the general interests of the community-it is the good of the whole body politic that has to be considered.
I was surprised to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) make the comparison he did between England and Germany at the commencement, of the war. He spoke of the condition of preparedness that Germany was in by reason of her vast industries and wealth. If there is one thing more than another which the war has revealed it is that the aim of Germany was not merely political domination but industrial domination, and that what made possible the action of Germany was the combination of plutocracy, autocracy and militarism, the combination of the Ballins and Krupps and men of that kind who had built up vast industries to the exclusion of the rights of the great body of the common people and the autocratic aristocracy that controlled the State.
There would have been no war had Germany been cast in a different mould; but they developed in Germany that love of power, that worship of wealth which made men blind to every consideration of human well-being. So, when Germany took her ruthless step she did it for the purpose of achieving industrial and political conquest throughout the world. But she was beaten by those who* took a different course. She was beaten by those nations that did not favour the special few-either in the matter of wealth or in the matter of privilege-but which had regard for the common weal and for common well-being. Sir, it was the autocratic Government in Germany, combined with the autocratic control of industry, that made the war possible. If the German Government had not been modelled on the basis of autocracy, if her industry had not been constructed on a basis of autocracy, the war would never have been

possible-it was the combination of the two for an object that would further their joint ambition that made possible the step which Germany took.
What is wanted in the world to-day is not autocracy either in government or in industry. What is wanted in the world and in this country to-day is the democratization of government and the democratization o*f industry. I say that any government that will assume, office as this Government did, and say that it intends to hold on to office-despite the demand of the people to the contrary-is an autocratic government.
Hear. hear.

I say that the Government, being an autocratic government, in seeking to maintain its friends in their positions of privilege, is trying to build up that combination of autocracy in government and autocracy in industry which must prove disastrous to the wellbeing of a state. In industry there are four factors which are entitled to consideration: Labour is entitled to consideration as well as capital; the community is entitled to consideration as well as managerial ability, and all four are necessary to the carrying on of industry. Give to the workingmen of the country a larger voice in the determining of policies which affect the conditions under which they have to work and earn their wages. Give to the community a larger say in regulating prices, in preventing profiteering, and in restricting combines, and our industrial future will be safe and secure.
But, Sir, in ease I have not answered my hon. friend (.Mr. Meighen) sufficiently in regard to w-hat he quoted from these .special reports, let me give him an authority which I hope he will respect. It relates to what I said a moment ago about considering the well-being of all instead of the well-being of a privileged few. When my right hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was Acting Prime Minister, he asked permission to place on Hansard-.because of its great importance- a document of vast significance. It was the declaration of the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference in regard to the economic conditions of the world. Let me read what my right hon. friend said in asking permission of the House to place this document on record. Here is my right hon. friend's statement as reported in Hansard! of May 3, 1920:
I desire to call the attention, of hon. members to a certain matter, and- with the assent of the

House, to make a motion thereon. The reason therefor is 'briefly this: I hold in my hand a declaration made by the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference on the economic conditions of the world. It 'is a recent compilation by an authority which is at the centre of things in Europe, and which has very wide sources of information, and being a pronouncement of that body on the present economic conditions in the world', it seems to me that it would be well to give it as great publicity and attention as possible. The motion I propose to make is that this declaration, which is not a very lengthy one, be recorded in Hansard so that it may come into possession of members of the House and be studied by them. I think it would have an even wider effect by being so published; it would be drawn to the attention of the press of the Dominion generally. It would be of the very greatest benefit to our people throughout the whole country if the statements contained in the declaration were brought to their attention and studied. They go to the very foundation of existing troubles and they end with a certain number of recommendations, or suggestions, and it would he a most excellent thing if we all took them into our consideration.
Now wftiat does this declaration of the Supreme 'Council of the Peace Conference say? I have not the time to read it all, but does it say-as my hon. friend, the Minister of the Interior, says-"Protect this particular industry and restrict trade so far as possible," or does it say, "Make trade as free as you can between different countries and industries thereby helping world development in freedom of exchange?" I shall quote from the document itself. Here are some pertinent passages:
In the sub-joined review of the position, the conference indicates* the lines on which it considers that a solution of the problem can best be found. ...	.
The first step to the reconstruction of Europe is to complete the process of demobilization in all countries, to resume the full employment in peaceful pursuits of the whole of the ablebodied population, and to encourage by every means the normal interchange of their products.
Then elsewhere it says:
-the output of factories and manufacturing industries throughout the world is below the standard which prevailed before the war, and far below the demands now made upon them. The net result of under-production arising from these various causes is an acute shortage of the essential supplies on which the economic life of Europe depends. . . .
This situation requires to be met with the same courage as was displayed on both sides during the war. The energy which was then thrown into the production of foodstuffs must be revived and redoubled in order to restore the situation. It must be made a point of honour with the tillers of the soil in every country to show that peace can extract from nature more than war. Europe must take measures to provide herself more largely with the food she requires in order that she may resume her full activities, and much can be effected if the necessary preparations are made without delay. . . .
In regard to industry generally, each Government must take steps to impress on its people that the limitation of production directly assists the upward movement of prices, and that it is by increasing production that they can best help to solve the problem. Every proposal which may assist in this direction deserves the closest attention. ...	[DOT]
Governments must co-operate in the reconstruction of the common economic life of Europe, which is vitally interrelated, by facilitating the regular interchange Of their products and by avoiding arbitrary obstruction of the natural flow of European trade. . . .
The demand not only for foodstuffs, but for clothing, boots and other manufactured articles, is in most countries far in excess of the supply, while luxuries of every kind command a readier sale than at almost any previous period....	.
It is essential to the recovery of Europe that the manufacture of additional paper money and Government credits should be brought to an end, and this must be effected as soon as the war expenditure has been terminated.
Excessive profit making, commonly known as profiteering, has resulted from the scarcity of goods. Deflation and a check upon the continuous rise of prices will do much in itself to end the conditions that make profiteering possible. But it is essential, in order to obtain the co-operation of all classes in the increase of production, that each government should take such steps as are appropriate to the circumstances of its own people to assure and guarantee to the workers that the burdens that they are called upon by their efforts to remedy are not aggravated by those who would exploit the economic difficulties of Europe for their own personal ends	
That the states which have been created or enlarged as the result of the war should at once re-establish full and friendly co-operation, and arrange for the unrestricted interchange of commodities in order that the essential unity of European economic life may not be impaired by the creation of artificial economic barriers.
There is the report which my right hon. friend, when Acting Prime Minister, caused to be placed on Hansard. There is the report of the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference which he says goes to the very foundations of existing troubles. And the whole tenor of that report is to make the natural flow, or interchange, as between different countries and different industries just as free as it can possibly be made.
Now, Sir, let me speak more particularly in reference to the amendment of my hon. friend ('Mr. Fielding) which is before the House. Unless I have altogether failed in making apparent what I believe to be most necessary in this country at the present time, not only because of Canadian needs but also because of the world situation today, it will be evident that above all else we should have a policy which will help reduce the high cost of living and increase production. If we take the resolution of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), we shall immediately see

that its whole aim and purpose is to call upon the Government to take immediate steps here and now to relieve the problem of the high cost of living by reducing the duties on the necessities of life, and to make possible increased production by reducing the duties on the instruments of production. That purpose is stated in general terms, but that is the real significance of the amendment.
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to take considerable satisfaction in pointing out the differences in points of view to which expression has been given by hon. members on this side of the House when speaking on the fiscal question; and their party press has been deliberately trying to emphasize those differences. They seem to think it is remarkable that in a large body of men representative of every section of the country and engaged in different activities there should be differences in point of view in regard to what attitude should be taken by the Government toward one industry or another under certain circumstances, or regardless of circumstances altogether. Let me say to my hon. friends opposite that weakness does not lie in differences in point of view where there is an honest expression of opinion, it is not uniformity of opinion that marks the robust and vigorous mind. The weakness that is truly weakness is that type of mind which will not admit into the regions of its thought any views other than those which agree with its own, and which therefore cannot entertain any really honest differences of opinion. The only weakness which I can see in the expression of opinion whatever it may be, is where opinions are expressed that are not in the public interest, and which are dictated by personal considerations. But let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that if it is united action they are looking for, they will not have very long to wait; as soon as this amendment is put to the vote they will find that every member on this side of the House without exception will vote in favour of it.
Why is that? Because the amendment expresses what is the view entertained generally by the people of this country. It is perfectly true that the amendment does not express all that every member on this side of the House would like it to express; it does not go the length of certain of my hon. friends on this side who incline towards an extreme of free trade, if you will, or towards an extreme of protection. I am perfectly free to admit to hon. gentlemen opposite that on this side of the House we have some
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
men who hold quite extreme views on the fiscal question one way and the other. But this I would point out, that while individually they hold extreme views, they are men enough to give up those extremes and unite on ground which is common and which they feel to be in the public interest; and so long as they are prepared to do that, so long are they serving the public interest. It is out of differences of opinion-strong differences of opinion if you will, held by men of one particular attitude of mind and by men of another particular attitude of mind that in the last analysis we resolve what is best in tHe public interest. Nothing is ever gained in the long run by countenancing extremes, and sooner or later all men realize that the only road of progress is by taking the moderate course.
So while hon. members on this side of the House, as I have said, may not all agree in detail -with everything that hon. friends opposite would like them to favour in regard to fiscal matters, nevertheless they are, I believe, agreed on this -that what is most needed is expressed in the amendment: an immediate reduction in customs duties in a manner which will help relieve the high cost of living, and also free the instruments of production, so as to make possible an increase of production in this country.
And, Sir, they had a right -to expect that the Government would introduce something of this kind, for two reasons: In the first place, because at a previous session the Government had intimated that legislation to that end would be introduced. But what has the Government done to fulfil its promise? It has taken the promissory note of one minister and in exchange for it has given the promissory note of another minister. But of what use are the promissory notes of the Government? As my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said in his resolution, they have failed to implement the promise which they made at a previous session that a general revision of the tariff would be made at the following session.
Let me read from the amendment these words which constitute its substantive part:
"That in view of the continued increase in the high cost of. living, of the greatly increased burden of taxation, of the hardship which many of the people suffer from these causes, and the unrest naturally arising therefrom; and in view of the desirability of adopting measures to increase production and effect such relief to consumers and producers as may be within the power of Parliament, the House is of opinion that, pending a wider revision of the tariff,

substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation should be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance; first, diminishing the very high cost of living which -presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country."
My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) asked: Why did the Opposition not bring in the tariff platform laid down by the Liberal party at its last convention? I will give my hon. friend the answer. In bringing in this amendment the Opposition were -anxious to have the Government realize thait they were placing before the Government that which could be done here and now, and that which should be done here and now. Had the Opposition brought in the platform of the Liberal party regarding -the tariff as laid down at the convention, my hon. friend would have been the first to get on his feet and say to hon. gentlemen "the Opposition have brought in a platform which is intended as a party platform, and which they know very well that we on this side cannot be expected to carry out at a particular session." My hon. friend would have said that we had designedly brought before this House something which it was impossible to have immediately carried out, and that in that way we had been trying to play fast and loose with the Administration.
I tell my hon. friend that we are wholly sincere when we say that the people today are demanding an immediate reduction of the duties on these necessities of life, an immediate reduction of the duties on instruments of production These two things should be done here and now. They are a fundamental part of the Liberal platform as laid down at the Liberal convention. We say to the Government: -Do not delay; act immediately in reference to this resolution.
Now, Sir, let me say again that the whole effort on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite-and it is an old trick and a common one-has been to point to the differences between the opinions expressed by individual members and to say nothing whatever about the ground which is held in common and for which all are prepared to fight. They have made a great deal -of the differences of opinion expressed in this debate, but they have said very little about the unanimity of opinion that- prevails in regard to this particular resolution.. The same kind of tactics have been adopted
with reference to what took place at the Liberal convention. Were there differences of opinion at the Liberal convention in regard: to the tariff? Certainly there were. What would any hon. gentleman expect of a gathering composed of representatives from all parts of Canada representing all the different provinces, all the different industries and classes in the community; men and women from the Prairie Provinces; from the rural districts and urban centres of Ontario and Quebec; men and women from British Columbia and from the Maritime Provinces? There they were assembled for three days, discussing questions of interest to this country representing all the different interests and views of the people of the particular districts whence they came. They discussed the tariff issue; they came there for the purpose of discussing it amongst other things. It was known for months that the convention was to be called and that the drafting of a platform on the question of the tariff as well as on other questions would be one of its most important concerns. Was that gathering like a collection of Egyptian mummies? Was it of men whose minds were all cast in the same mould? Was it of men whose individualities and personalities shrivelled and shrank into nothing under the glance of a Prime Minister or the edict of a Government? No; they were free men, discussing freely their views, trying to arrive at a common basis of understanding in regard to what was most in the interests' of the people as a whole. You had there exactly what you have here,-some taking extreme views in one direction, others taking extreme views in another direction. But, Sir, you had the splendid spectacle of that vast assemblage of men and women standing up as one and approving the platform of the Liberal party.
If my hon. friends opposite wish to know .wliat was the resolution, with regard to the tariff adopted at that convention and where I stand in reference to that resolution, let me read it to them at this point.. Let me do so more particularly for this reason: The Minister of (Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) the other day read .from a paper published in the Maritime Provinces, the name of which he did not give, an article in which it was said that in the Maritime Provinces I was advocating free trade. I have never advocated free trade anywhere. I told my hon. friend at the time that what I did in the Maritime Provinces was to read from the platform of the Liberal Party as laid down at that

convention. But my hon. iriend went on to say that I had said one thing in the Maritime Provinces, and he gathered that when I got up to speak here I would say something else and that possibly when I went out to the West I would say something different there,-in other words, that I would , be "all things to all men." Well, it is perhaps natural for my hon. friend and some of his associates who call themselves Liberals but who sit as members of a Tory administration under the name of Unionists 'to think that they can be all 'things to all men. It would,, take a greater than St. Paul to play that role with satisfaction in the administration opposite. I have no desire to imitate anv behaviour of that kind. Hon. gentlemen are only deceiving themselves if they think that they can be all things to all men; that they can remain Liberals and yet hold the views expressed by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) during the course of this debate and ap-plauded so vigorously by so many hon. gentlemen apposite. I have only one message to give from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I would not be worthy of the trust reposed in me by members of the party with which it is my privilege to be associated in the position that at the moment I hold, were I to be one thing at one time and another thing at another time. Sir, I was chosen for the responsible duties that I am seeking to discharge at the Liberal convention at which the platform of the Liberal party was laid down, and by that platform I intend to stand or fall. The resolution on the tariff was as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest Importance: First: diminishing the very high :ost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; Second: reduicing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the' Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food: farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should he made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries),
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution when returned to power.
Supplementing that .resolution i.s a resolution on reciprocity proclaiming the faith that the Liberal party had in that , arrangement as it was introduced, expressing regret that opportunity was not afforded to this country to obtain the benefits of it, and expressing the hope that the time might yet come when some of the benefits that were hoped for by that measure might yet be gained for the people of Canada. Just in this connection may I direct the attention of the House to what my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) said the other evening. He asserted that most of the things that were asked .for under that reciprocity agreement had been granted by the Government of the day. Wel'1, if that is true, what will the Canadian .people think of the utterances [DOT] olf hon. gentlemen when in the campaign of 1911 they defeated that agreement on the ground that it was against the interests of Canada? I tell him that their attempt to-day to mislead the people in regard to any of the features of 'this platform are just as misleading and just as unpatriotic as were their endeavours to mislead the public in .regard to the results they allege would be brought about by the reciprocity agreement.
Let me further point out that there is not a line in the resolution adopted by the Liberal convention which has not appeared in resolutions proposed in Parliament from this side .prior to 'the time that the convention was held. Theire is not a line in the resolution which was not approved and which had not 'the sanction of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, or which -was not advocated by him prior to his death.	Indeed, at the
very time that he was taken from us he was preparing to give battle to hon. gentlemen opposite on the very" issues that are laid down in that platform. The last public address by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, only two or three weeks before his death, was in the main one approving a resolution passed by Eastern Ontario Liberals in words almost identical with the resolution which was adopted at the Liberal convention. If anything were necessary by way of sustaining the wisdom of a policy such as that which is true to the traditions of Liberalism, it would be, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has pointed out, the way in which the

Liberal policy which was introduced in 1896 resulted in the prosperity of this country. When the Liberals of 1896 introduced their platform, criticisms were levelled against it much in the nature of the criticisms that have been made against the platform of the Liberal party as adopted at its recent convention. How did that policy work out? True, in some particulars things were not done which might have been done; but let me read to hon. gentlemen, not the words of any one on this side of the House, but the words of an authority whom they will not call in question in regard to what the Liberal party did while in office towards carrying out this policy, and let us see whether or not there is reason to fear that, in the future, should the guidance of affairs be entrusted to the hands of Liberals and those of progressive thought, the affairs of the country will not prosper thereby.
I have in my hand a volume written by Sir John Willison, entitled "Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Liberal Party." Sir John Willison is, I think, at the present time president of the Canadian Reconstruction Association, and hon. gentlemen opposite know that association and understand its purposes. This is what Sir John Willison has to say in regard to the Liberal policy as it was introduced and as it was carried out. The quotation commences on page 288:
These then were the trade issues which entered into the contest of 1S96, and this the position of the controversy when the Liberal party came into office in Canada. There was undoubtedly uneasiness among manufacturers and some fear among all classes who were concerned in industrial operations and interested in financial and banking institutions that revolutionary tariff legislation would be introduced, investments prejudiced or destroyed, the business of the country thrown into confusion, labour displaced, and commerce embarrassed and depressed. It is the work of a day to create a protectionist system. It is a delicate and difficult undertaking to scale down duties, and establish freer trade conditions without doing damage and injustice to industries which have been created by tariff legislation. The Liberal ministers were bound in unmistakable pledges to proceed with caution and with deliberation, and they thoroughly understood that violent and inconsiderate action would create commercial instability and panic, revive protectionist sentiment, and discredit the cause of tariff reform. They therefore instituted a tariff commission, which met the manufacturers, traders and producers at various centres throughout the country. The commissioners gave earnest and sympathetic consideration to all reasonable representations, and in the main, the [DOT] protected interests presented their arguments in cordial, candid, and straightforward fashion. They took it for granted that while the ministers were most concerned to promote the welfare of the masses of the people, they would prefer to benefit rather than to injure established industries, and that enterprise would be

recognized and investments protected in so far as the interests of capital and labour and the stability of the commercial fabric demanded. These tariff hearings did much to restore public confidence, and to prepare the country for a progressive but safe and moderate measure of tariff adjustment.
On April 25th, 1897, the new tariff was brought down in Parliament, and it is not exaggeration to say that no fiscal measure of more far-reaching significance was ever framed by a Canadian Ministry. It gave substantial relief to consumers and producers.
It gave what we are seeking to-day-a tariff in the interests of consumers and producers, a tariff that will bring relief to both consumers and producers.
It was a bold step in Imperial unity. It introduced the principle of minimum and maximum tariffs, and practically adopted the Davies resolution of 1892 in favour of preferential treatment of British products. In brief, the_ iron and steel duties were reduced from $1.50 to $1.00 a ton, and the bounty increased by $1.00 a ton. The taxes on barb wire and binder twine were abolished. Corn was placed on the free list. The flour duty was reduced. There was a reduction equal to 22 per cent of the duties on refined sugar. Duties on the raw material of many farm necessaries were reduced. The tax on uncleaned rice was increased, as were also the taxes on liquor and tobacco. There was a general substitution of ad valorem for specific duties, and this also involved substantial reduction of imposts. The classifications were reduced and simplified. Provision was made that the duties on goods produced under trusts and combinations could be summarily reduced or abolished. There was also, as the distinguishing feature of the measure, an immediate reduction of 12 J per cent on British goods, and provision for a further reduction to 25 per cent on July 1st, 1898. In a few cases, particularly in cottons, the duties were increased, but this seemed to be necessary in order to give fair scope for the reduction of 25 per cent on goods admitted under the special tariff. This special tariff was not, as then framed, a direct discrimination in favour of Great Britain. The German and Belgian treaties, which will be discussed later, disabled Canada from such direct discrimination in favour of the mother country. It was therefore provided that the minimum tariff should apply to any country which admitted the goods of Canada at rates as low or lower than were prescribed by the specia' schedules. This limited the application of the special tariff to Great Britain and New South Wales, and providing Canada could secure relief from British favoured nation treaties, accomplished the purpose of the Canadian Government. It is convenient to say now that in 1898 West India sugar was admitted into Canada at the lower rate of taxation, and that in 1900 the duties on British goods were further reduced from 25 per cent to 33J per cent below the figures of the general tariff.
The country received the general provisions of the new tariff with marked favour and the British preference with positive enthusiasm. The Conservative attack was directed against the constitutional aspects of the measure rather than against its readjustments of the scale of taxation. It is true that at the moment it was denounced as a deadly blow at important Canadian industries. But when it was found that

trade prospered, industries flourished, and new life was infused into all the channels of Canadian commerce, ground was shifted, and it was thought better to describe the new fiscal policy as a practical ratification of the old protectionist system. In fact, the measure has never been subjected to any consistent line of attack. It is sometimes denounced as unduly favourable to the United States, sometimes as calculated in its practical operation to crush out Canadian industries in order to facilitate British imports, sometimes as unmitigated protection. There is no doubt that the principle of protection still remains in the tariff, and that a measure of advantage is undoubtedly retained for Canadian manufacturers and producers. This is inevitable under any tariff designed to raise the revenues necessary to the financial needs of the country, and is perhaps essential to the growth and stability of commercial and manufacturing operations in Canada in face of the American method of slaughtering goods in outside markets and the lower freight rates enjoyed by many American exporters as against the charges exacted by the Canadian railways for the carriage of Canadian products. Great distances and a small population compel some of these inequalities, and twenty years of extreme protection necessarily brought into existence many industries which coulij not meet low tariff conditions, and could not be summarily subjected to the free and unobstructed competition of British and foreign manufacturers. Practical statesmen must deal in a practical way with existing conditions, and aside from considerations of prudence and equity, the leaders of the Liberal party were doubly pledged against rash and revolutionary legislation.
But it is vain to argue that the Fielding tariff was not a substantial measure of reform. The special tariff on British goods materially encouraged and cheapened importations from Britain, and many of the duties on farm supplies and household necessaries were lowered, to the advantage alike of the consumers and the revenue. In fact, if the British preference had not been introduced as the essential feature of the tariff, it would probably have been attacked as a. relentless free trade measure, and have evoked the strenuous and enduring hostility of the protectionist classes.
It goes on to say something further in regard, to the views which the English people had and ends with these words which are a quotation from an English economist:
At the present moment it would be a step backward if taken by the mother country; it is a step forward when taken by Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman desire to conclude before six o'clock?
If hon. members are willing to wait,, I shall endeavour to conclude in a few minutes.
Go on while you have steam up.

What was recognized in England as well as in Canada at that time was that the step was in the right direction, but it -was not regarded as the last and only step. It was
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
not so regarded by Sir Wilfrid himself. What were the outstanding .features in the record of the Liberal party while in office? First, substantial reductions in duties in a number off directions and upon a number of occasions; then the introduction of the British preference and an increase in that preference; then a fight for freer trade on the reciprocity platform. While the Liberal party has not stood for free trade it has stood for freer trade; and while free trade is not possible, in view of conditions as they are in Canada at the present time, and is not being advocated, so far as I am aware, by any political party in this country, that is no reason why, as regards the necessities of life, we should not have cheaper food and cheaper clothing and cheaper shelter, if it is possible to have these things, and at the same time get what we need in the way of revenue through such a tariff as it may be expedient to impose.
What was the attitude of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in regard to what had been done under the Fielding tariff? I have here a copy of a speech delivered by Sir Wilfrid at Hamilton on the 27th November, ,1913, nearly seven years ago. At that time the Liberal party was fighting for free food and freer trade, just as to-day it is fighting for the same things. What did Sir Wilfrid say at that time? And if his words had force seven years ago how much greater force have they to-day in view of the * changed conditions which the war has occasioned? These are his words:
I told you at the beginning that new problems are continually arising; there are latent forces which, unnoticed, silent and unforeseen, work out problems which were never dreamed of. This is one of them. In this city of Hamilton, which to-day, as I understand, prides itself on a population of over 100,000, go into the homes of the workingmen and mechanics, of the clerk in the drygoods store and the clerk in the warehouse, even the professional man and the clergyman, and the question which is discussed at this moment is not the price of dreadnoughts ; it is the problem of making ends meet as between expenditure and income. "It is true I might say something about reciprocity," commented Sir Wilfrid, "but I have no recriminations to make. The problem is before us. Let us bury the past and look to the future. There our duty lies. The situation requires action, prompt, unhesitating action. The policy I give you at this moment, the policy I believe every patriot in Canada ought now to support, and the policy I believe it to be the duty of the Government to immediately inaugurate, is a policy of absolutely free food- food free from customs duty. It will be said to me," the Liberal leader continued, reasoning out his proposals: "If you advocate that policy do you not advocate a revision of the tariff to that extent? Certainly I do. But

somebody will tell me that the tariff which is in force to-day is the Fielding- tariff of 1897. -So it is, but the Fielding tariff was made for the needs of that time, not for all eternity. It has been the policy of the Liberal party at all times to stand so far as possible for stability in tariff, but when the needs of the people call for action, action must be taken."
Now, Sir, that was the view which Sir Wilfrid Laurier expressed when leading the Liberal party, namely, that while-there was reason to he proud of the golden era of prosperity, which marked the fifteen years the Liberals were in office there was yet need for action. New occasions bring new duties. 'Changes have come about within the last few years such as the world has never witnessed heretofore, and the need for relieving the high cost of living and for increasing production is greater than ever in the past. And while we as Liberals are proud of the record of Liberalism, going down to defeat fighting for free food and freer trade, we are determined as Liberals to keep up this fight on behalf of the people and to take up the flag where the Old .Chief left it, and see that it is not furled until victory is won.
Let me say just a few words in conclusion. Hon. gentlemen opposite have tried t'o make capital out of the differences of view that have been expressed in reference to details by Liberals here in this House, and at the Liberal convention, but they have overlooked the important fact that there is common ground on which all of us stand. Hon. gentlemen are trying to do the same thing to-day in reference to the platforms of different political parties in this country. I have a copy of the platform of the Farmers' party and a copy of the platform of the Independent Labour party. Hon. gentlemen opposite have drawn attention to differences between the Liberals and the Farmers and the Labour men. Well, Sir, there are differences to which hon. gentlemen can point, but I can tell my hon. friends opposite this, which is a fact of far greater significance, that there is common ground on which the members of those parties can unitedly stand. You will find in the Farmers' platform, in the Labour platform, and in. the Liberal platform, the common demand for a reduction of the duties on the necessaries of life. You will find in all three platforms a demand that the duties should be taken off the instruments of production so that greater production may be possible. These demands, Mr. Speaker, represent the outstanding needs of the country to-day, and on these great fundamental needs we are united.
Let me address a word to my hon. friends in the Farmers party and to my hon. friends of the workingmen's party, and let me address the same word to the people of this country : Take note of the things that you have in common and observe the tactics of the enemy you have also in common. These tactics are wholly apparent. We have seen privilege protected in almost every speech that has been made from the other side in the course of this debate. We have seen hon. gentlemen opposite seek to point to some differences that exist between men of common thought and common feeling in other respects. What do- these tactics signify? They are an endeavour to keep the host in opposition divided. Hon. gentlemen opposite are saying to themselves: "We can hold all the positions of privilege so long as men who are united in thought and feeling on certain common ground can be kept, apart from one another and prevented from uniting in a common effort to- gain a common end." These are the barbed wire entanglements by which the party of privilege would seek to keep separated men of liberal thought and feeling in this country, and to keep them from uniting on the ground which they have in common. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) said, that the purpose of the amendment was to unite these different groups. Let me tell my hon. friend that if that was its purpose, there could not have been a worthier o-ne than to seek to give expression, in one voice, to the sentiments of three great elements. What is the object of hon. gentlemen opposite? It is to keep the progressive hosts who oppose them disunited. Word has gone out from their headquarters urging the necessity of this -action and also the need of filling the war chest with gold. There are announcements already of a fund for propaganda purposes that is to run up into millions of dollars. Mention has been made in the press of such a fund for such purposes and the Government in power purposes to hold on for a couple of years and by so doing give this insidious propaganda ample opportunity to do its work. I would urge all men who think and feel alike on the great questions which affect the well-being of the 'Canadian people, and who deplore conditions for which the Government are responsible, to take note of the tactics of the common enemy. No matter by what name they may call themselves, whether it be Liberal, Grit, Reformer, Liberal-Unionist, Farmer or Labour, if they think and feel alike, as men who are interested in



the welfare of the great mass of men and women in this, country, they should stand together where it is possible for them so to do, and fight to a successful finish the great issues that face them.
My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen-I refer to him again because he has been the chief exponent of the views of the Government in this debate-has given his interpretation of the attitude of gentlemen on this side of the House. In Hansard of May 25, 1920, will ibe seen his characterization of the Opposition.
We are opposed by two wings of wholly opposite views on the tariff, two wings, however, that gather around the motion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. fielding) , two wings that hope to go before the people of this country fighting under two flags and under two leaders, to make the pretence all the better, hut who hope afterwards to coalesce and entwine the two flags into one in an infamous unity, who hope after taking one camp of public opinion behind them and the opposite camp as well, to the utmost of their power to end up by deceiving both, by betraying both, because they must either deceive the one or double deceive the other.
May I say to my hon. friend that there is no deception as to the attitude of hon. gentlemen on this side. We of the Liberal party have our programme, we have right with us and we are prepared to work with the men and women who feel and think as we do. But we are prepared to carry on our work and we will carry it on regardless of the attitude of any others because we are of a party which has a tradition of 100 years to maintain, a tradition of 100 years of advance and progress to greater liberty and freedom. We will strive and seek to make our policies prevail. But may I say to my hon. friend in all kindness: Be cartful, "judge not that ye be not judged." Let me repeat my hon. friend's characterization with its bearing upon the Government of which he is a member as respects the action of the government prior to the last election when he and his party came together with their two flags.

speechtext:
My hon. friends say
hear." X want to deal with some of those points to-night. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), held a brief for the Opposition in criticising the Government's expenditures of the past year. While we have had . general criticism from the opposite side of the House, the member for Antigonish and Guysborough has ventured to go into details and to set out certain specific charges upon which the Opposition wished to stand in its attack upon our financial administration. And the hon. leader of the Opposition this afternoon gave his benediction to the hon. member, and stated that he had set forth the Opposition's criticism of the Government, and commended that criticism to the attention of the House and the country and virtually made it his own. I want to deal briefly with that criticism tonight.
First, the hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough spoke of the increased public debt. They said that the public debt had been increased during the past year at the rate of over $1,000,000 a day, and they described that as wasteful and reckless extravagance. They were quite prepared to allow an increase of the public debt during the war, but they asked: Why increase the public debt after the war? Does not every hon member know, Mr. Speaker, that last year this House voted $350,000,000 for completing the war services, for demobilization and bringing our men back from overseas and returning them to their homes? The increased public debt last year was the further instalment paid by our people for the defence of their country and the work of demobilization. The whole increase of the public debt was for expenditures under the demobilization vote and certain investments the Government made in connection with credits to foreign countries, as I am advised by the Minister of Finance. There was no increase in the public debt in connection with the ordinary expenditure of the country nay, more-the revenues exceeded the ordinary' expenditure by nearly $39,000,000.

Then, the hon. .member's second charge was that the Government had increased ihe expenditure during the fiscal year just ended by more than $100,000,000 over that of the previous year-"yet they talk of economy," he says. Now, I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether the amounts that go to make up that $100,000,000 increase are expenditures to which they are opposed? If so, they are justified in criticising the expenditure, but if not, then I ask is it fair and just to the people of Canada to make any such statement or offer any such criticism, to say nothing of the Government and members on this side of the House? What are the items that make up that $100,000,000? The first is: Increased interest on the public debt because of the war expenditure of Canada, $31,000,000. Do my hon. friends say that that debt should not have been incurred to enable Canada to do her share in the war? Do they say that Canada should not pay the interest on that debt? Do they say that that is not a proper increase in the charges on the country, and that it is not proper to provide increased revenues to meet it?
Let me take the next item: Increase in pensions, $7,717,000. Do hon. members opposite put themselves on record as opposed to that increase in pensions? If they are not opposed to it, then why have they not the manliness to get up and retract the criticisms they have made? My hon. friend opposite laughs, but the women and children who get the benefit of these pensions do not laugh. The next item is $49,000,000, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. That amount is not wholly an increase; in the previous year the expenditure for Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment formed part of the war vote and did not enter into the general current expenditures of the country. Do hon. gentlemen opposite wish to go on record as opposing this item? The next item is Soldiers Land Settlement $2,692,000. Do hon. members opposite say that the Government should not be making these advances and carrying on this work to enable the soldiers to settle on the land? I will give you only one more: Civil Service bonus, $9,497,000-to the civil servants in all sections of Canada to meet the increased cost of living. Mr. Speaker, the five items I have mentioned make up approximately $100,000,000, the increased public expenditure of which my hon. friends have complained. I say to my hon. friends on the other side: Are you opposed to that increase in the public expenditure last year? If you are, then you are perfectly justified in criticising.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friends say
"hear, hear." I say, Mr. Speaker, that the statement that the department was organ. ized for political purposes is absolutely devoid of a shadow of truth. So far as I. am aware there was no country at war the Government of which did not have some kind of an organization or department for the purpose of keeping the people of the country informed as to the war efforts of that Government and of that country, in order to sustain the courage and patriotism of the people and assist in the prosecution of the war.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, perhaps my hon. friends did not need anything to sustain their courage in the war.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to analyse a little bit-
Say it again. Try it again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am afraid that even if I tried it again it would not penetrate the mind of my hon. friend. I want to deal with the items covered by that $200,000. The first, and one of the moist important, was an amount to provide for the cabling to England of news to be published in the Daily Record for our troops overseas. One-eighth of the total expenditure of that department was covered by cable toils in sending news overseas, in order that the boys at the front might have some knowledge of what was going on at home and some tidings concerning their friends in the home-land.
Especially during the election.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must ask any hon. member who has anything to say, or a question to put, to do the House the courtesy of rising and addressing the Chair.
Hear, hear.
Do it like a man.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Is my hon. friend not aware that that same thing was carried out from the first year of the war, the information being furnished by the Department of Militia?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Why the necessity for military experience?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is the settled policy of this Government to give returned soldiers the preference in all important positions. When an appointment of this kind was to be made, we felt, if .there was a soldier who had served overseas qualified for the po.st, he should have it, and it was our duty to search him out and find him. Moreover, we believed that, being a soldier with a military record, he could, render more efficient service and would have a position and standing in the United States which a mere civilian who had not served in the war would not have, and it would he in the interest of Canada to have him there.
The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysboroug'h referring to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment said that a large number of payments had been made to officials which appeared in the Auditor General's Report; as unaccounted for and he cited some twenty or more names with certain amounts set down opposite them and some such words as ."unaccounted for," and he sought to convey to the House and to the country the impression that a large number
of officials of this department of the Government had received moneys for which they had given no account, and that the Government had not endeavoured to secure an accounting from them. What are the facts? These officials, I think, with scarcely an exception, were military officers or officials of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department. They were travelling, many of them coming from the Old Country to Canada, others travelling in Canada. They received their travelling expenses before the end of the fiscal .year; they had not returned so as to render .theil account when the financial year closed, and, therefore, the money was unaccounted for. But since then, just as in all cases, the department has taken the matter up and has had the accounts .adjusted. My hon. friend would have received the information if he had gone to the department and asked for it, or to the Auditor General and made inquiry to find out with reference to these items.
But without any such inquiry he gives this story to the House.
But the big complaint is the $121,000,000 which it is said has disappeared in some unaccountable way. I want to deal with that because it has formed a subject of discussion and debate in this House. Three hon. members of the Opposition, the hon. member foT Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault) and the leader of the Opposition himself (Mr. Mackenzie King), have all put themselves back of the statement that the sum of $121,000,000 has disappeared and i.s not accounted for. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) mentioned this also, but I think it only fair to him to say that he expressly gave the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough as his authority for the statement. Let me quote what the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough said in reference to this matter:
The amount that has disappeared without any account having been given is, roughly speaking, $121,000,000, and the question is, what has become of this $121,000,000? The minister does not know; the deputy does not know; the department does not know; the Auditor General does not know; and Parliament does not know. There is apparently not a scrap of paper in the possession of the Government to show what has become of that $121,000,000.
The hon. member prefaced that statement by reading a certain letter from the Auditor General written in September, 1917, which had no relation whatever to the item under

consideration, having reference to a wholly different transaction-the overseas payments of a previous year. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a deliberate charge that $121,000,000 of this country's money has disappeared and that there is no record of it, that no one knows what has become of it-that it is utterly unaccounted for. You will be surprised, however, to find that this statement that the money has disappeared is not at all borne out by the Auditor General's Report. I will quote the exact words, because it is important that hon. members should see precisely what the item is. It is to be found on ZZ-228. It is headed:
Overseas Department of Militia and Defence.
It is the only item under that head.
What is the report?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The report is for the year ended 31st March, 1919. The item is as follows :
Etapenditure toy the Chief Paymaster on account of pay and other expenses of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, vouchers for which have not been received.
Observe, Mr. Speaker, that the item does not say "unaccounted for." The words are: "vouchers for which have not been received." Why have they not been received? For three reasons which I shall state. An arrangement was made, for reasons which I shall give, that they should not be sent to Canada. Two ships carrying vouchers had been sunk by German submarines and it was deemed in the public interest that these vouchers should be kept in England until the war was over. Further, by an arrangement to which the Auditor General himself was a party, it was agreed that, instead of sending the vouchers over and attempting to audit the accounts in Canada, building up a special audit staff here to handle these particular accounts, the matter should be dealt with overseas by having there, under the minister, an audit branch which would carry out the audit in England. Who was the Paymaster General? Brigadier-General J. G. Ross of Montreal, the head of the accounting firm of P. S. Ross and Son. I appeal through you, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux), who will tell you that there is no more honourable or efficient accountant or auditor in the city of Montreal or in the province of Quebec than Brigadier-General Ross. He was in charge of the pay office and had under him chartered accountants

who checked every item in order to see that not a dollar was paid that was not due, thus protecting the public interest. Furthermore, an audit branch was established overseas under Colonel Dowie, a skilled chartered accountant and auditor, who reported direct to the Deputy Minister. And every night vThen the pay staff left the office, having concluded their work, the audit staff went in and every account was audited. The day's work was audited every night before the staff returned the next day.

May I ask the minister if
the auditors, Brigadier-General Ross and Colonel Dowie, were there as official representatives of the Auditor General of Canada?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, they were not. Brigadier-General Ross was paymaster of the Canadian forces overseas, and in the performance of his duty was responsible for every dollar expended. My hon. friend knows Brigadier-General Ross. Will lie question that gentleman's ability, or his honesty, or his capacity for the performance of those responsible duties? There is no answer. There cam, of course, be none, because Brigadier-General Ross stands at the head of his profession, and the Government could not have chosen a better man for the duties which were discharged by him. I shall explain how the work was done, and every commonsemse man will realize that the Government took every precaution which a Government could take to prevent the loss of a dollar of the people's money and to see that every dollar reached its proper destination and that not a dollar was wasted. In addition to the audit staff under Colonel Dowie, on the recommendation of the Auditor General. Mr. Sutherland-who has since become Auditor General of Canada-was appointed Assistant Auditor General for the express purpose of visiting the Old Country and examining conditions on the ground with a view to seeing that everything was carried out satisfactorily. Mr. Sutherland spent the greater part of the year 1917 in England, and he visited the Old Country again in 1919, doing that very work. He is not an official of the Government, he is an officer of the Parliament of Canada; he is the Auditor General of Canada and is not removable except by an Order of the Senate and the House of Commons. He is therefore absolutely independent of the Government and hon. gentlemen opposite can go to him and ask him how the work was carried out in England under Brig-

adier-General Boss amd Colonel Bowie, and lie will tell them that every precaution was taken to protect the public interest and to see that not a dollar of the people's money was misspent.

Were they not obliged to
make a detailed report somewhat similar to that which is submitted by the Auditor General of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They could not make a
detailed audit without sending the vouchers. They did make a monthly report of the disbursements and I am going to inform the House in a few moments what those disbursements were. They made a monthly report to the Auditor General in order that he could keep track of the whole business from month to month, hut without sending the vouchers there could be no means of checking the details. Let me say, further, that there is another reason why the vouchers could not be sent. Soldiers returning from the front on furlough or in case of disability or discharge desired to settle their accounts in England. How could they settle those accounts if the vouchers were over here? The soldiers often had doubts about payments of which they had forgotten the details, and the only lecords the department had were those signed by the soldiers, and they had to be kept for purposes of administration as well as for the other reasons I have mentioned. What the Auditor General's Report means is exactly what it says, that he has not received these vouchers. Any hon. gentleman can get from the Auditor General a full statement in reference to the matter. The vouchers are now here; they have come over since the war and there are a thousand boxes filled with vouchers. There are over 5,000,000 of these vouchers to be gone through if hon. gentlemen wish to go through them. The Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) told me the other day that in his department they had been cheeking through these vouchers, that they had spent weeks of time and $20,000 in payment of staff and that in the whole time t-hey had only discovered an error of $300. I am going to read a letter from the Auditor General dealing with the matter.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that a very large number of these vouchers had been lost at sea- that they had been torpedoed?
Mr. BjOWELL: No, I did not say so. I said that two vessels carrying vouchers had been lost at sea.

Do I understand that these are duplicate vouchers that are now being
received?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These particular vouchers that have now come over were not lost, of course, The vouchers contained in these thousand boxes were not lost.
Can we he provided with duplicates of these vouchers as well as the vouchers that were lost at sea?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot say that, but if my hon. friend will ask the Auditor General he will inform him; I cannot do so. 1 want to read this letter from the Auditor General dated May 26, 1920, and written to the Minister of Finance in reference to this item:
Sir,-Expenditure by Chief Paymaster, O.M. P.C. in London, $ 121,640,016.62 shown in Auditor General's Report, 1919-page ZZ 228. The bulk of this is composed of pay and allowances of our troops and separation allowances by dependents amounting to over $102,000,000.
The late Mr. Fraser, Auditor General, visited London at the close of 1916 to look into the matter of accounting and audit. On his return he wrote to Sir Thomas White as follows:
"As instructed in the Order in Council of the 16th September, 1916, I made an examination into the affairs of the Overseas Pay Office, in order to ascertain whether it was advisable to establish a branch of the Auditor General's office in London for a more complete and speedy audit of the war accounts.
After a thorough examination of the system in vogue and consultations with the Chief Paymaster, tha* General Auditor and members of the staff as well as with the Minister of War for Overseas, X came to the conclusion that certain changes were necessary to safeguard as far as possible, the expenditure of the public funds. One plan was to have certain changes made in the keeping of the accounts and the checking of the same by the existing pay and audit staff and the other, the organization of a large staff at Ottawa for audit purposes. The first plan seemed to me to be the better one, on the ground that it is better to prevent losses before they are made than to discover them afterwards. I want to feel that the work is done in such a manner that I can accept the same with a certain amount of confidence that the losses are reduced to a minimum. A certain amount of loss is inevitable. I found that the Imperial Government with all its experience and a well organized staff of experts are unable to prevent these losses.
A staff sufficient to make a thorough audit would cost at least $300,000 per annum while the recoveries might not he $5,000. It is useless to find out after a man is dead that he has been overpaid.
The changes that I suggested and that have been agreed upon with the Chief Paymaster and General Auditor are such that if faithfully carried out, ought to produce satisfactory results and 1 propose sending over a representative of this office to see that every reasonable means is taken to secure correctness and to render such assistance as he can to settle such questions as arise from time to time without awaiting for the slow process of submitting them to Ottawa and awaiting replies."

That is what the Auditor General himself says. There are two courses open-to accept the work of the pay and audit staffs over there, subject to certain changes which he said he would direct, or to establish a staff which would cost $300,000. The Auditor General himself recommended that the first course should be pursued because he thought it would save the money of the country.
An horn. MEMBER: Who was the Auditor General then?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That was Mr. Fraser.
This is Mr. Sutherland's letter:
I was sent to London and spent the greater part of 1917 there, and again in 1919 for some months.
The Pay Office and Audit Office were under the direction of two thoroughly experienced men, viz.: Brigadier General J. G. Ross, (P. Ross & Sons, Montreal) and Col. L. A. Dowie, chartered accountant, Canada and London, with a large staff attached to each office.
An individual ledger account was kept for eVery man on the overseas forces so that it can readily be seen how impossible it would have been to carry on an audit here.
You see the present Auditor General says it would have been impossible to carry on the audit here.
It had to be done on the spot and kept up to date. This office was furnished month by month by the Paymaster General with a statement showing the expenditure under various heads, but owing to the ^isk of loss of vou'chers during ocean transport, it was considered advisable to discontinue sending them to Ottawa.
It is not my statement tout the Auditor General's statement is that owing to losses through ocean transportation it was considered desirable to discontinue shipping the vouchers. My hon. friend asks: "Why were the Auditor General's requests in the letters of 1917 not complied with"? Because, in view of this German submarine warfare the vouchers upon which the accuracy and certification of the accounts of the Government of Canada in relation to the overseas forces depended were too precious to be at the disposal of German submarines on the Atlantic. Therefore, they were not sent to Ottawa. Then lie adds:
Two shipments were lost in transit. I understand that all Overseas Military Forces of Canada vouchers and records are now in Canada.
I have just one or two further comments to make. The letter which the -hon. gentleman referred to as being written in 1917 -asking for the vouchers was written while Mr. Sutherland was in England. Mr. Sutherland cannot explain why it was written because he was there at the time as the representative of the Auditor General for the purpose <;f checking these accounts. He was appointed specially as Assistant Auditor General for the purpose of auditing these accounts. I have given to the House the facts in connection with the whole transaction. I have pointed out that the ,$102,000,000 was pay and allowances of the men. These payments extend from the first of April, 1918, to the 31st March, 1919. The transaction did not need an explanation. My hon. friends have only to turn up the Auditor General's report. They will find no item in that report for the pay of the men overseas except this item. Did my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) think that our gallant men went from 1918 to 1919without pay? There is no other item but this to be found covering the .pay of our men overseas. Then I say, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough, the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres, and now the leader of the Opposition, having put themselves behind the statement that the sum of $121,000,000 has disappeared and is unaccounted for-
That is right.

No. I say that is right because the minister has been arguing that the submarine went to the bottom of the sea.
