speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Now that is the position with reference to that item. I make this appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. At a time siueh as this, when the country must impose new obligations, when there must be new burdens of taxation, when my hon. friends find they have made a wholly false charge and false statement, they owe it to themselves, to this House, and to the country to pdblicly retract and withdraw that statement. It reflects on the credit and honour of our overseas military forces, on the whole of the paymasters' branch; it reflects on the credit and honour of the Auditor General who himself made the arrangement; it reflects of course on the administration of the Government of the day, but that is not so important.
More important by far is the fact that it reflects upon the Dominion of Canada. For if $121,000,000 of the country's money has disappeared without any account for it, it suggests gross incompetence, or maladministration, or graft in handling public funds by your overseas military forces. Therefore I say to my hon. friends opposite that they owe it to the House and to the country to make a public retraction and withdrawal of that statement.
They do not retract.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Antigonish and Guysiborough made one more statement to which I desire to draw attention. He took an answer that was given to a question in reference to appointments to the Civil Service since the Armistice was signed, and he says that the answer shows that 27,130 were appointed, and he assumes that of this number 25,000 are still in the public service. The hon. gentleman estimates that these appointees would get an average of $2,000 apiece and in that case, he says, the addition to our public expenditure on that account for the yeaT would be $50,000,000. He asks, "Is it any wonder that the country is going into defbt at the rate of a million a day?" Mr. Speaker, the House and the country will be surprised to learn that the total salaries of the entire Civil Service of Canada, permanent and temporary-i am not now dealing with seasonal employments, that is, men who are employed on ships or otherwise merely for the season, nor am I dealing with the country postmasters paid under different conditions-the total salary bill will not exceed, apart from bonus, $50,000,000. Let me point out the situation : Dealing with the classes that I have mentioned, the approximate number of employees, permanent and temporary, at the date of the signing of the Armistice was 43,000. The approximate number of employees, permanent and temporary, of the same classes, on March 20 of the present year, was 48,000, an increase of 5,000. Now let me tell you how that increase arises. There has 'been an increase of 657 in the Department of Finance caused by the imposition of new forms of taxation. It was absolutely essential that the necessary staff should be appointed in order to administer those laws. There has been an increase of 1,257 in the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and it was absolutely essential that that board should 'be manned to carry on its important work. Does any-

body question that? Then there were 6,296 appointed in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, which is so essential for the re-establishment of our soldiers in civil life; and 275 on the staff of the Board of Pensions Commissioners. Thus there was an aggregate increase in those four departments of 8,485. Those were necessary increases; they were for purposes that arose after the war, not during the war-purposes growing out of the war, for which the staffs had to be created. But the Government has set itself to the task of reducing the staffs that were built up during the war, and let me give you some facts in that connection. Since the Armistice, the Department of Customs has released 160 employees; the Department of Militia and Defence has released 2,627; the Department of Naval Service has released 103; the Post Office Department, 248; and the Printing Bureau-including 40 that went out yesterday-356, or a total of 3,494.
It is much easier to get in new employees than to get them out. But the Government has set itself resolutely to the task of decreasing the staffs in the various branches of the Civil Service to the minimum required for efficiency. One branch in which the Government has acted is the Printing Bureau, and I want to give to the House one or two facts to show what has been accomplished there. We have, as- I mentioned, released) 356 employees from the Printing Bureau. In October, 1919, the payroll was approximately $115,000 a month; in March of this year it had been reduced to $90,000; by June it will be down to $73,000-a total reduction of $42,000 per month. In other words, we will have the payroll on a basis per month that will show a yearly saving of not less than $500,000 for this one branch of the service alone. The re-organization which has been brought about, placing the Printing Bureau on a sound business basis, will enable us to reduce the annual expenditure by $200,000 more, and we estimate that when these savings have all gone into effect the total annual saving in this particular branch of the service will be not less than $700,000. And with what result? To-day we are turning out more printing and better printing, with a smaller staff after effecting that great saving in public expenditure. That is but an illustration of what this Government is doing to put the administrative organization of the country on a sound business basis and to save money for the people.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, when the Government is engaged in this difficult task of protecting

the public interest, what does it meet with from hon. members opposite but captious criticism and false statements as to the facts?
Order.

Order. I ask the hon.
minister to withdraw that statement.
Some- hon. MEMBERS; Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
ance has not given the House an estimate of the amount he will receive from these new forms of taxation, because of the extreme difficulty of forming an accurate estimate. How much we will get from the luxury tax, the sales tax and the other taxes it is difficult to say, but I am quite sure that the Minister of Finance does not expect to get less than a clear $100,000,000 from these new forms of taxation. I believe he expects more. I am going to pat another $100,000,000, therefore, under the heading of income; and that gives us $451,000,000 to meet the balance of the Estimates amounting to $443,000,000. In other words, the Minister of Finance has brought down a Budget by means of which he undertakes to provide through current taxation a sum more than sufficient to discharge all the expenditures he has proposed to the House, apart from this conversion of assets and payment of the maturing liabilities to which I have referred.
Now, let me point out the character of the expenditures included in that $443,000,-
000.	In providing from taxation $443,000,000, what is the hon. minister achieving? He is covering not only all the ordinary expenditure; he is providing the whole cost of completing demobilization, $38,000,000, which in past years was the subject of a special vote; was added to our capital expenditure, and formed part of our war debt. This year the Minister of Finance proposes to meet that out of current taxation. He provides in the Estimates for loans to the Canadian National Railway, $48,600,000, and other capital expenditure, $15,189,000. So, I repeat, the statement submitted to the House shows an honest and courageous effort on the part of the Minister of Finance to secure revenues not only to meet all ordinary expenditures but to meet these other very large expenditures which in the past we have considered as capital expenditures.
One word further Mr. 'Speaker, about our position at the piesent time. We have, as you are aware, not only accomplished this, but our public debt to-day-by way of comparison-is substantially less than the public debt of Great Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand, every country which was engaged in the war except the United States, and she was only a year and a half in the war. When conditions were unsettled in-the early part of last year the Government adopted the courageous policy of asking the people to carry on, and under conditions which looked as if there might fMr. Rowell.!
be a cessation of industry, made provision for credits to enable the country to carry on. And what has been the result? Our foreign trade last year was $166,000,000 *ahead of our foreign trade of the year before. Our total foreign trade reached the enormous sum of $2,351,000,000; in addition, of course, there was the enormous home trade. The Minister of Finance has pointed out that in the five years, ending 31st March, 1915, our excess of imports over exports was $825,000,000. That is to say, the balance of trade was adverse during those five years to the extent of $825,000,000. In the five years ended 31st March, 1920, we wiped out that adverse balance of trade -and have to our credit for the five years a favourable balance of $1,803,000,000. If you compare the two periods, taking the five years before the war, with an adverse balance of $825,000,000, and the five years since, with a favourable balance of $1,803,000,000, you will see that the balance of trade changed during that period a total of $2,628,000,000, or over $500,000,000 a year.
Something has been said about inflation. There has been inflation of credit in all countries engaged in this war. But we have maintained our gold reserve, as the Minister of Finance pointed out, in our banks and the Government at 43 per cent, as compared with Great Britain's 26 per cent, ana the United States' 55 per cent. The Federal Reserve Bank requirement in the United States is 40 per cent, and we have maintained ours during the war at 3 per cent above that requirement. Our bank deposits, as the Minister of Finance intimated, have almost doubled in the last five years. During that period we have added to the bank deposits of Canada a sum almost equal to all the accumulated bank deposits from Confederation up to the beginning of that period. Our debt is funded, -after the liabilities that I have mentioned are disposed of, over a twenty-year period.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) painted a picture the other evening in speaking on this matter. Referring to the statement of the former Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) as to conditions in 1912, he made this statement:
That, Sir, is the story of fifteen years of Liberal fiscal policy as described by my hon. friend:	fifteen years of peace and plenty,
fifteen years of blessed peace, fifteen years of joyous plenty, fifteen years of splendid progress, fifteen years of wonderful prosperity ! Let us frame and glaze this statement; let us post It on the walls of the country; let

us frame and glaze it and put it into every household, and office and factory, so that men may look upon it and say, "Ah, yes, that is the story of the good old days. Pray Heaven that it may come back again,"
I am not disposed to criticise that statement oi the hon. member. That was a great period oi ipeace and progress in Canada's history. But I want to ask >my hon. friend, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and I am sorry he is no-t in his seat, what he would have said if, instead of being a member of the Government during a period oi peaceful progress and uninterrupted development and expansion in Canada, he had been a member oi a Government which at a time of grave national stress carried forward to a victorious conclusion the greatest -war in history; which completed the raising, training, equipping, sending overseas, and finally demobilizing of 600,000 men; which ended the war with our national debt funded over a twenty-year period, with our war securities practically at par, as against the United States substantially below par, and with our national debt much smaller by comparison than that of Great Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand or any other country at war, with the exception of the United States, which had been only a year and a half in the war; which so administered the business and financial affairs of Canada and stimulated the productivity of our people that for the five-year period ending 31st March, 1920, our foreign trade showed a favourable balance of over $1,800,000 as againist an adverse balance of over $800,000,000 in the preceding five years; which practically doubled our bank deposits and brought our borrowing largely within our own borders, so that 'the Canadian people hold practically 75 per cent of our Government securities.
If the hon. member had been a member of the Government that had accomplished this, would lie say: "Let us frame it .and glaze it and hang it up? If my hon. friend had been a member of a government during those years of stress .and had accomplished that result, he would have said: "Nay, blaze it upon the skies so that all men may see." He would pray not that old times might come again, but thank God that in the hour of the nation's need, in the struggle that Canada faced and in the throes through which she was passing, she had a Government with vision, courage and practical ability-vision to see the need, courage to apply the measures necessary to meet the need, and ability to execute those measures,
so that to-day both at home and abroad Canada stands in a higher position than at any previous time in her history.
I had expected to conclude my remarks by this time; but I should like to' say a word or two in connection with our financial proposals and particularly in reference to the address of the ieader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). The hon. member explained to the House in great detail why the Opposition had not submitted the tariff platform adopted last August. He said: " Why, if we had submitted the platform adopted in August, we could not have expected you to accept it." In effect he said "we submitted a proposal which w e thought you might accept." The hon. member is not such an amateur in Parliamentary and constitutional practice as not to know that the Government cannot accept any amendment to the Budget, but he gave another reason, it was the real reason-it was the only thing they could all agree upon. I have before me the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), in which you will remember he practically said that he was in search of a sound and safe tariff policy. He used the words "sound and safe." He said that he could not expect such a policy from the Conservatives. He said that he could not expect it from the farmers; that their policy was neither sound nor safe. This is what he said as reported on page 2584 of Unrevised Hansard:
Where, then, are you going to get it?
That is referring to the "sound and safe" tariff policy.
Shall we get it from the platform of our farmer friends? Sir, I do not think their platform if carried out would give us the sound poliicy which I desire, and I hope to be able to show them-at all events I hope they will find that it is wise to modify some of their views.
The hon. member in moving his amendment was repudiating the Farmers'platform, was moving a vote of want of confidence in the policy of my hon. friends. He said that they did not provide a sound and safe policy. Then my hon. friend came to the platform adopted by the so called Liberal convention of August last, and. he said, referring to the Liberal policy:
I dc not even thiilk we can expect to get a sound and safe tariff policy toy a too rigid adherence to every line and every letter of the Liberal tariff platform.
This amendment is a vote of want of confidence in the platform adopted by the Liberals last August. It is submitted in the present form because it is all they can agree

upon. My surprise is that my hon. friends of the Agrarian Opposition are supporting an amendment the mover of which says, in effect, that it is a vole of want of confidence in their platform. I am even more surprised that my hon. friends in the Liberal Opposition are supporting an amendment the mover of which says that it is a vote of want of confidence in the platform adopted by them last August, because that platform does not provide a sound and safe tariff policy. The hon. member (Mr. Fielding) provides what he considers a sound and safe tariff policy, and in some respects there is no very great objection to it, if we were now revising the whole tariff schedules. The hon. member, when in power, made certain revisions of the tariff with which I will deal in a moment, revisions which I approved and supported, which I still approve and support. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), in speaking on this amendment, said that the reference in the amendment criticising the Government for failure to revise the tariff this session was not fair nor just to the Government. I do not recall his exact words, but that was the substance of them. He said that under the conditions which existed, it was not reasonable to expect that the Government could bring down a revision of the tariff at this time. The reason he gave for supporting the Opposition amendment was that it spoke of a revision downwards, whereas the Government had promised a revision but did not say that it was downwards.
I want to look just for a moment at the tariff situation. My hon. friends on the other side are professing to be the sole representatives of those who are concerned for the welfare of the masses of the people. The leader of the Opposition, dealing with this matter at great length, said that the Government had not lightened at all the burden upon the consumer; that they had not in any way relieved the people of this country from the burden of taxation, nor done anything to diminish the high cost of living. My hon. friend gave as his method to accomplish those particular purposes a reduction in the tariff. I am not going to enter into a discussion to-night as to how far the one affects the other.
I desire to submit to the House certain facts in connection with the matter. When the tariff was revised in 1897 the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), then Minister of Finance, in his Budget Speech estimated that the total reduction in revenue due to the tariff revision would be $700,000. In 1907 he estimated it

at $300,000, but he stated that he was putting on another tax on sugar equal to $300,000 so that the one would offset the other. I am taking the $300,000 however as a reduction. In other words there was a reduction of $1,000,000 in those two revisions of the tariff in 1897 and 1907. In 1911 the hon. member submitted to this House an agreement which, if adopted, would have reduced the tariff taxation by $1,412,000. Now, I am quite prepared to give my hon. friend credit not only for the actual reductions he brought about but for the reductions he proposed and endeavoured to bring about, and the two added together would give us, in tne fifteen years of office of the Liberals, $2,412,000 of reduction in the tariff burden, either accomplished or attempted.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has described the members on this side of the House by various names. We are composed on this side of two groups, Liberal-Unionists and Conservative-Unionists, who are supporting the present Administration. What have the Liberal-Unionists, in co-operation with their Conservative colleagues, done ;n two years? They reduced the tariff burden of taxation last year $17,000,000 and this year $31,000,000, whereas the whole Libeial party, of which I was a member, working together, effected or proposed a reduction of $2,412,000 in fifteen years. In view of this fact, Mr. Speaker, are not the Liberals on this side of the House and the Conservatives doing pretty well? Do they not deserve some credit for the fact that in two years they have brought about a reduction of $48,000,000, twenty times as much as the Liberal party did in fifteen years?
Wonderful.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is wonderful, but my hon. friend does not realize it.
The country does.

We have done this without imperilling any industry in the country and, I believe, to the substantial relief of the consumer.
I turn now to the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year 1918 and I find in connection with the imports entered for consumption the average rates of duty collected. In that report I see the average rate of duty on ,all goods entered for consumption from 1867 down to 1918 and upon inquiry from the Finance Department I find that the average rate of duty last year was 17.61 per cent on all goods entered for consumption. The reduction in duty made this year by the re-

peal of the 7i per cent on the basis of the imports of last year will bring the average rate of duty down to 14.67 per cent, the lowest rate of duty in Canada since the year 1878 when it was a little over 14 per cent. I submit, therefore, that hon. members on this side of the House who believe in a reduction of duties have very strong and sound reasons for supporting the Government and voting against the amendment. I say with every confidence that men can well support a government that has done in two and a half years what I have stated, as opposed to my hon. friend's opposite who in fifteen years accomplished one-twentieth of our achievement. In addition, I believe that the tariff does need a thorough revision that the duties on many articles should be substantially reduced. The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has promised a thorough revision of the tariff, and while hon. members have discussed protection and free trade, the thing which really affects the people of Canada in the last analysis is the tariff schedule. I am not going to enter to-night into a discussion of the relative merits of protection and free trade. Hon. members will see the tariff schedules when the tariff is revised and brought down, and they will see what the policy of the Government is in this matter. If at that time hon. members find that the tariff has not been so revised as to meet the situation existing in Canada as they believe it should be met, then they will be justified in voting against the Government. But not until then will the tariff schedules be fairly before the members of the House.
One word in conclusion. The hon. member referred to the organization of this Government and stated that its mandate had expired. Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand the statement issued by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), with the full support and approval of all his colleagues, at the time the Union Government was formed. That statement sets out quite clearly the objects for which the Government was formed and the task to which it committed itself. I am not going to read the statement to the' House to-night, but I may point out that the first plank, and the first plank only, dealt with the vigorous prosecution of the war, every other plank of the platform deals with problems either growing out of the war or relating to peace, showing that it was the clear intention at the time the Government was formed that while its main and chief duty was to prosecute the war, the other tasks resting upon the Govern-191
ment should not be shirked or ignored, and that the Government must face them and undertake to perform them. Let me say to my hon. friends that the Liberals and the Conservatives on this side of the House will not refer to hon. members opposite, who sought to prevent this Government from being formed and from securing the mandate necessary to prosecute the war, the question of when that mandate should expire.
Are we to infer that the exMinister of Public Works stated the position when he resigned from the Government? '

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Every hon. member of the Government is entitled to take whatever position "he considers to be right, and if he desires to withdraw from the Government he is entitled to do so.
A happy family.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let me say this to my hon. friends. The hon. gentleman knows that the Prime Minister promised that the War-time Elections Act should be for the period of the war only and that a new election law would be passed for times of peace; and this Government could not have been dissolved and a general election held at any time since the Armistice was signed up to this hour, because there is not yet a franchise. law on the statute book under which an election cauld be conducted.
Whose fault?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

What about last year?

We submitted progressive masures to this * House last session and asked the House to adopt them in the interests of the country. Who has opposed those progressive measures in this House? We introduced the Women's Franchise Bill which has doubled the electorate of this country and given the women the franchise on the same basis as the men. The only opposition came from lion, gentlemen opposite. We introduced a Bill .permitting women to sit in this House and the only criticism came from hon. gentlemen opposite. -We have put through a great measure of Civil Service reform. We have introduced many measures dealing with social reconstruction., The hon. leader of the Opposition referred to the resolution of the Liberal convention relating to care for the public health. Were the delegates gathered in that assembly not aware of the fact that upon the initiation of this Government a Department of Public Health was created *at the first session of this Parliament last year and that it is doing magnificent work? This Government has introduced measures providing for technical education, for housing, for temperance and for other advances in the realm of social reconstruction. The only opposition has come from hon. gentlemen opposite. Practically speaking, the progressive 'forces of this country have been on this side of the House. In addition to these measures of social reconstruction, the Government has dealt courageously with the railway situation, they have put an end to' private railway exploitation at the public expense. They are giving Canada a truly national system of railways. Where do hon. gentlemen opposite stand on that question? Real liberalism, the real progressive forces, have been on this side of the House. The reactionary forces have been on the other side of the House. The opposition to the measures that I have mentioned has come from the other side. I exempt the hon. gentlemen who sit at the other end of the Chamber, the Agrarian group. I do not believe that they represent the reactionary elements. I think that in some respects they are a little too radical perhaps, in some not so radical, but they at toast are moving ahead along certain progressive lines which they think are in the public interest or in the interest of the farmers' group.
I do not think we can settle the tariff in this country just according to the likes of the farmers on the one hand or the

manufacturing interests on the other. I do not believe a tariff policy prepared and promoted by the manufacturing interests would be in the public interests of Canada any more than the policy prepared and promoted by the farmers in the interests of a class. I believe it is vastly more important that there should be a good understanding between the people of the East and the West than that there should be any particular rate of tariff. It should be the bounden duty of the Government of this country to so frame the tariff that it will meet the views of reason-
10	p.m. able men both East and West in order that we may present a united front as Canadian people in carrying on our industrial development in competition with the great nation to the south and in the extension of our trade with the other nations of the world. I should like to discuss the other taxation proposals on the Budget but time will not permit. We must if we are to. sustain the financial load that rests upon our shoulders accept the burdens of increased taxation. It may be that there should be some slight amendments to the Budget resolutions but people must be prepared to pay the cost of the war. Some of them have felt the burden very little up to this time and I have not a great deal of sympathy for or patience with any class of men who are able to pay and who object to taxation at the present time. If anybody can devise a better or more equitable basis for raising revenues than the Government has proposed, I would like him to submit it to ihe House and personally I am sure that many on this side would support it.
What we want is a policy fair to all, with special privileges to none; a policy that seeks to unite the Canadian people as a whole, not in sections or in classes, that Canada may achieve in the future a destiny worthy of the glorious traditions of the past and of the honourable name our troops have won for her in that momentous .struggle now so happily ended.

Mr. Speaker, the subject on which I desire at once to speak is indemnities for members. Seven dollars a day is not enough to pay the expense of a poor man at the present time. While it is quite true, Mr. Speaker, that the House is not in session every day, it is equally true that a member's work, like a woman's, is never done; and if he happens to be a married man and is compelled to support two homes on $209 a month, it is quite impossible. I

am well aware that war widows and many .of their dependents have to do with a great deal less; but two blacks never made a white yet, and it is my experience that men who are willing to work for less than a living wage are mighty poor providers for war widows or anybody else.
The Budget makes no provision for increased indemnities either for members or ministers, and that, in my opinion, is a very frank admission of incompetence on the part of members of this House. I had hoped that the right hon. the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden), the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and ,the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) would have got together and discussed this question in a non-political way.
The second subject on which I wish to speak is this: Apparently money is more highly valued and more sacred in the eyes of this Government than human life. I have recently placed in the hands of the Chairman of the Pensions Commissioners specific cases where the whole family of sons have been killed, have been sacrificed in this war. The whole family of sons; sons upon whom had been lavished the savings of a lifetime. The poor mother of those boys applies for a pension, but before .she can get one she has to prove that she is a pauper. Even after the pension of $40 a month is granted, some kind friend gives her work to eke out that pension, and along comes the Government Supervisor and takes the pension away, as by law he is compelled to do. How does this, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen, compare with a man who loaned the Government a thousand dollars? Is he compelled to prove pauperism before he draws his interest? Is it necessary before he draws interest for him to prove that he is not making more than $40 a month? We have been told by the Minister of Finance, and with him I am glad to agree, that it is time we tackled our present problems with the same spirit with which our men tackled the war. At least twice this session I have heard hon. members decry the war spirit, but I am glad to agree with the Minister of Finance that the sooner we get a little of the war spirit into this country and into this House the sooner we will progress. When the Government ran short of fighting men, what did it do? It passed a Military Service Act calling to the colours all ablebodied men between certain ages-whether they wanted to come or not. What recompense does the Government give to the parents of those sons who are lying in 191$
France? It places a tax on luxurious living -luxurious living made possible by the lack of taxation by the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance. It is not necessary for me to labour this point. It is apparent to all that just as in war some men get a lot out of it, others have got it in the neck. What attempt has been made by this Budget to adjust the burden between the two? Apparently none. The man who fought the war at great personal loss comes here to find that he is not even exempt from the special burdens of war taxes. Now to illustrate that-it seems to be very hard to get over-I will tell you a little western story: A bunch of traders were coming down from the North with a very rich pack of furs, when they were beset by Indians and surrounded. Out of their number two young men volunteered to try to break the cordon and bring relief. They wTere successful in getting through to a cavalry post, and they returned and drove off the Indians. But in doing so one of the men who had volunteered lost his life, and both their horses were killed. The rich traders were very delighted to think that their pack had been saved; they gave the returning man a small gratuity-and charged hilm up for both horses. The rich traders of this country are charging up the men who fought with their uniforms-the ones who had the luck to get back-whilst the men who enriched themselves during the war are largely allowed to hang on to their wealth.
With the permission of the House I will read a letter received from a friend of mine on this subject. I may say that I have collected all kinds of evidence of the large fortunes that have been made during the war, but I think sufficient evidence is already before the House without bothering you with any more of it. While an attempt has been made through the business profits tax, and other taxes, to get after this great wealth it is perfectly well-known to the members of this House and the people of this country that some men have made great ' fortunes. The letter in question sets forth:
The impression is gaining ground that a number of corporations and companies are planning to escape their business profits tax through the agency of mergers and by increasing their capitalization, largely through the process of common stock. It is also generally believed that many of them have not paid, and are not paying, as much as they should, for the reason that they are charging up excessive amounts to overhead, depreciation, expenditure, etc. This is defeating the purpose of the tax, and should not be tolerated.
A company paying dividends of 7 per cent now 10 per cent must pay 2>5 per cent in business profits tax, and when the profits ex-

ceed 15 per cent the tax is increased to 50 per cent.
I need not go into the details of that, they are -well known to all the members, but I will take the next clause in the letter:
This means that companies paying big profits on actual capitalization must pay large sums to the Government. This was the purpose of the legislation, and Parliament had this in mind when it passed the Act. A number of big companies, apparently in order to escape these high rates, are issuing bonuses in the form of new stock to shareholders-doubling trebling, quadrupling, and in same cases increasing their capitalization by at least five times. The purpose is to give the shareholders as big a return on their money as they receive through a high rate of profit on the smaller capitalization. It is being arranged so that dividends do not range much higher than 7 per cent on the face of things, and on that basis, the Business Profits Tax is practically escaped, while in reality the dividends are in some eases four and five times the modest earning of seven per cent. In the case of the .	.	.	.	. Paper Company, the
process of reorganization and re-capitalization, means that eagh shareholder is being given five shares under the new capitalization for each one previously held by him, the effect being to raise the actual capitalization from about $5,000,000' to approximately $25,0l00,0,00i. Under the previous capitalization, the business profits tax on earnings over 20 per cent would have netted the Government a very substantial sum. Under the new capitalization 20 per cent earnings will be spread over five times the capitalization, with the result that, while there is actually no more capita] invested than previously the Government will get next to nothing through its Business Profits Tax.
The Business Profits Tax paid by the companies going into the British Empire Steel Corporation Merger should be thoroughly gone into. It looks as though one of the purposes of this merger is to enable the companies entering it to dodge the tax. The big ones such as the Dominion Steel, Nova Scotia Steel and Iron, Canada Steamships, Canada Foundry and Forgings, and others, will exchange their shares [DOT] for 7 per cent preferred, plus a nice bonus in the way of common stock. This new stock will, at the beginning, amount to over ?2f}0,000.0AT), and will be further increased to ISO'O.OOO.OOO. with a further prospect of a capitalization, of $1,00O.'OO0,00'0' by keeping dividends down to 7 per cent and lower, the business profits tax will be dodged. It will he a very serious matter for the country if a number af the largest companies in Canada are allowed to escape in this way. Canada Steamships, Limited, which is supposed to have paid $1,215,000 in taxes on its 191$ business, would thus practically escape altogether. The same thing applies to others. It would be nothing less than a national crime if this were to be allowed. The little fellows are paying their taxes; the big fellows should be made to pay theirs. The searchlight of publicity should he thrown on the whole subject, for Parliament and the country have a right to know the facts.
It looks to me as though the big fellows had made a rich haul and they are now salting it down.

words spoken by the then acting leader of the Government (Sir George Foster):
No nation in the world has ever undertaken, and I do not suppose that any nation in the world ever will or ever can undertake, to make compensation 'for the losses incurred in war; it would he an impossible task.
In reply to those words, Mr. Speaker, 1 would say that the man or the members of a government who tackle a job with the words "can't" and "impossible" in their hearts are licked before they start. The people who sent me from Winnipeg to represent them here on the floor of the House understood quite well that it meant "the last man and the last dollar", if necessary, to clean up this job right; and they are still of the same opinion. I believe that is true of the spirit of our people to-day, and any government that fails to interpret that spirit of "the last man and the last dollar if need be", fails to represent this nation.
It is true that the business war profits tax is retained and with other taxes now imposed will meet our current expenditures. To this extent, at least, I desire to congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, for it is infinitely better than the system of borrowing which we had before. There is an old saying, that he who goes aborrowing goes asorrowing, and I am pretty well satisfied that our people for manj years to come will not forget the borrowings of my hon. friend's predecessor.
But the Budget makes no real attempt to readjust the burdens of the war on a fair and equitable basis. The Government says that it cannot be done, that it is impossible to make such a readjustment. Take, for instance, the business profits, tax. It is no secret that the Government has had trouble in collecting it. Quite naturally the men who have made money dislike to see their profits go into, let us say, railway ventures that, to say the lealt, have not been paying dividends for many years, hut which the Government have paid for at one hundred cents on the dollar. I think if I made any ' money I would hate to hand it over to people who expended it in that way. (In fact, I go further and say that if some of my free-trading English friends did not [DOT] sell to the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) a "pup" when they sold them the Grand Trunk, I do not know what a "pup" is.) There has been trouble in collecting these taxes, for the reason that the people who are paying them are not satisfied that their money is being used to the best advantage. Personally, Mr. Speaker,
I would abolish the war profits tax alto-

gether, and in its stead I would introduce forthwith a Financial Service Act along the lines of the old Military Service Act; in other words, I would conscript millionaires. I would put men who had made $1,000,000 in class A; those iwho had made $500,000 in class B; those who bad*made $100,000 in class C. But 1 would not call these men to the colours as criminals,- far from it; I would mobilize them as the strong, cunning men of the race, men that we can depend on in the country's time of financial need. I would pay them $1.10 a day, with their board and lodgings, and I would keep them on for the continuation of the debt and six months' afterward. I do not want their money so much as their brains, their ability. I am frank to admit, Mr. (Speaker, that they would be a pretty tough army to.handle, but I am satisfied that from amongst their own numbers you would find some one who could handle them, and after they had once caught the spirit of the thing I have not the slightest doubt that they would make good just as their sons and the other young fellows made good overseas.
But you may well ask me: What kind of work would you turn them to when you got them? Roughly, my plan would be to direct them to develop the resources of this country for the nation instead of for themselves. But I do not think it is necessary to go into details at this time; I will wait until after the election. My idea is this: I would call these strong men to the colours and I would say to their leaders: The debt is $2,000,000,000; you have Canada and her resources at your back: Go to it. And I have not the slightest doubt that they would make good.
Now, Sir, it was my purpose to speak at some length on the words uttered by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) in this debate, but my physician has ordered me off this line. I am frank to admit that when those words were uttered they made me angry-righteously angry, [I believe, but apparently that is just as dangerous as any other kind of anger. However, I would say in passing that I hope the hon. member has learned that protectionists can blunder as well as free traders. I must point out to him that many blunders were made in the war. But it is an axiom amongst soldiers that the army that makes the fewest blunders wins the war. Germany made blunders, and even in our own army our poor boys lost their lives through blunders of those in control- but I am not going to make the mistake of
pointing out these blunders to bolster up an argument on free trade. I would point out to the hon. minister that economists and thinking men are of the opinion that the supreme blunder of all was the blunder of starting the war,-and that blunder was committed, not by free trade England but by protectionist Germany.
May I ask what country it was that started the war?
