Mr. Speaker, it is with some diffidence that I rise to speak at this hour of the evening and at this stage in the debate on the very important Budget that has been brought down, f wish to congratulate the former

Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) on the magnificent work he did in connec- . tion with carrying this country through the crisis of war, providing the necessary finances in order that our soldiers might be properly taken care of and that the needs of the country might be properly served.
I congratulate the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) on the Budget which he has brought down. It must have required, a great deal of courage, a great, deal of nerve, on the part of the hon. gentleman to take hold of the duties and responsibilities oif the oftioq of Finance Minister and to deal with conditions as they obtain at present. For years war had done .its work and had had its effect upon the finances of the country, and to come in as a new man, assume the responsibility of administering the finances of the country, and lay down plains by which we might be able to go forward, was a very important and a very trying piece of work to undertake. I. congratulate him upon the degree of success that has attended his efforts in the bringing down of his Budget.
I notice that a certain amount of criticism is levelled at the Government at this time. But it is always the case that a government which has big responsibilities resting upon it, a government which i,s breaking new ground and launching out into new enterprises, meets with much and varied opposition. Naturally there will be opposition from some people, particularly if measures deemed to be necessary call for self-denial on their part.
There are some items in connection with the Budget to which I wish to call attention. First,. I should like to express my recognition of the fact that in his Budget the minister has adopted a method that has been before the people as a proper *method for raising money for administering the affairs of the country. I refer to the introduction of the principle of direct taxation. I believe that direct taxation is the proper way to raise revenues for the conduct of the business of the country. There was a time when money was raised by indirect taxation; when a large part of the finances of the country was secured in this way,-secured by methods which placed the burden of responsibility as indirectly as possible on the people. But the time came in the history of this country when it wa,s necessary that the people should be taken into the fullest confidence of the Government in connection with the admin-
[Mr. Henders.J
istration of its affairs. This was brought about particularly by the increased financial responsibilities and obligations resting upon us in connection with the war. As I say, I have always believed that direct taxation is the proper way to raise revenue.
I wish to express my approval of some of the methods that are laid down in the Budget for the securing of mofiey by direct taxation. First I would direct attention to the luxury tax. I have heard criticism of that tax. Some hon. members have expressed the view that the minimum amount taxable on luxuries was too low; that the taxation should be on higher priced articles. I am not of that opinion. I believe that a sufficient number of useful and. essential articles are free from taxation; that the burden of taxation will not touch the people until they have reached the point where they are able to bear it. The responsibility increases as the resources of the people increase and they are able to bear responsibility. I have no criticism to offer with regard to the levying of that tax, and I believe it will prove a splendid source of securing revenue. If I were to offer a suggestion or criticism at all, it would be with regard to the method adopted in raising that money. Some incline to the belief that, instead of taxing, say, a pair of boots costing over nine dollars on the full value of the article, it would have been better if the tax had been levied upon the excess of the purchase price over nine dollars, and that the tax instead of being 10 per cent should be 20 per cent. I am not quite so sure but, perhaps there is some merit in that suggestion. It would not allow the tax to fall quite so heavily on the one who would have to pay it, and as the article was considered to be a greater luxury and the price increased, the increase of taxation would be so much heavier and, therefore, the burden would fall on those who were better able to bear it. The same criticism -would apply to all similar lines of taxation, namely that the tax, instead of being on the full value, should be on the excess beyond a certain amount fixed as the minimum where the taxation should begin.
I am in perfect accord with the stamp tax. No one will suffer seriously from it, and a certain amount of revenue will be readily collected.
The sales tax is another direct method of taxation with which I find myself in perfect agreement, and I believe that good will come from the securing of money to

the fullest possible extent from that line.
It could better be operated as a straight, turnover tax payable by each class of the business community and not to be passed on from the manufacturer to the wholesaler and then to the retailer.
I come to the income tax which I' consider the most important and most reasonable method of taxation, in the form of a direct tax of any found in connection with the Budget. I believe the income tax is a reasonable and fair way of raising revenue; that it is a method that we should use to the fullest possible extent. As regards the amount of money to be raised by the income tax, I am inclined to think that the tax might well be increased at a greater rate after you reach an income of $10,000, and that the ratio of increase should be greater all the way up to $500,-
000.	A man who has an income of $10,000 could reasonably pay 10 per cent; a man who has an income of $15,000 might reasonably pay a little more than 10 per cent, and he would not suffer seriously from that increased taxation. We could continue along that line, increasing the ratio of taxation between incomes of $10,000 and $500,-
000.	In that way a large amount of money would be secured, and the people who would be making that contribution would not suffer seriously as regards enjoying the comforts and necessaries of life.
I should like to call attention to another feature of the Budget proposals which commends itself to my judgment. I refer to the removal of the 7i per cent war fax. It has been charged against the Government that they have made this a rich man's Budget; that the rich are having the best of it and that the poor naan is being burdened. I do not think so; I believe in the removal of the 7^ per cent war tax, because by the removal of that tax, $7.50 is taken off every $100 worth of goods a man buys, so that rich and poor alike receive benefit thereby.
I wish also to call attention to the fact that it has been charged against the Government that, by removing that 7J per cent war tax, they are simply bringing us back to conditions as they were before the war and, therefore, the Government deserves no great credit for removing that tax. That is a very unfair and unjust criticism. It was found necessary, during the stress of the war, to levy a 7J per cent war tax in order to carry on the Government of the country * and meet the conditions through which we were passing. An expenditure amounting to $1,000,000 a day has to be provided for. It could therefore be argued that this tax
should on that account ibe retained. The Government has decided otherwise. This is now taken off the people, which means a reduction in the prices of the necessaries of life of over $30,000,000, a direct contribution to the people in connection with their living expenses.
I wish now to refer to the promise made by the former Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that there would be a revision of the tariff last year. With the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) I find myself in perfect agreement on that point. If I remember rightly, that hon. gentleman's comment was that conditions were such in connection with the former Minister of Finance that he found it necessary through illness to abandon his post, to leave the Government and to go into other lines of business. This change made it necessary for the [Government to secure another man to take the position. It was further felt that of conditions in connection with raising the war loan, it was necessary for the time being to abandon the promise made by the former Minister of Finance. There is no one in this House who is more sorry than I am that that condition of affairs has come about. I had staked a good deal on the promise of the former Minister of Finance, and I had taken the position with the people out in our western country that that pledge given by the former Minister -of Finance at that time was part of the contract which led me to accept the Budget. That promise was an important factor in leading me so to decide. It was, therefore, a disappointment to me that that arrangement was not carried out. But the Minister of Finance ('Sir Henry Drayton) comes to us this year with a pledge that the arrangement which was made last year will be carried out this year. I am not among those who are prepared to receive no explanation for a miscarriage of any promise that is made; I am not among those who are prepared to say that, because it was found necessary last year on account of the circumstances to which I have referred, to abandon the promise, therefore, I will not accept in good faith the promise that is made again. I believe the promise of the Minister of Finance is made in good faith; I am going to receive it in good faith; I am going to act on it in good faith; I am going to tell the people all the facts that have transpired, just as I told them last year; I am going to tell them , that this pledge will be carried out; That there will be a revision of the tariff and that before that revision

takes place-inferences will be held throughout the country and the people will be invited to appear, and present the facts of the case as they see them before the men engaged in the work of gathering the evidence, before the revision in connection with the tariff takes place.
I believe it is necessary on the people's account that this opportunity be given to study the tariff. We do not understand1 the tariff, and I believe that many of us here do not understand it as thoroughly as we should. We do not understand the conditions in -connection with it, and I -have no doubt that these conferences that will be held in different places throughout the country will bring out evidence of incalculable value- in regard to the merits or otherwise of the claims of the different parties who are demanding consideration, and will show clearly the grounds on which they base their claims for that consideration. This information will be valuable, and it will also be a great source of education, which is what we need. What do we find in connection with this promise of a revision of the tariff? Do we find opposition to it? Yes, Mr. Speaker. We find opposition from two sources, and I want to call particular attention to that fact because it has been -said by -hon. members opposite time and again that this is the Government of the predatory interests, the Government of the privileged classes. So far as that allegation is concerned, may I ask if the reduction of per cent of the duty was an example of protection for the privileged classes? Now, who are the people that are opposing the proposal to have conferences to study this question? Where is the opposition -coming from? I find1 that the manufacturers' associations have passed resolutions condemning the action of the Government in proposing a revision of the tariff and condemning the calling of conferences to study the subject. They say they want a revision of the tariff, but whom do they want to revise it? They want to have a board of men appointed to which they can be sure that only certain classes of people will be eligible for appointment, people who perhaps are standing close to their own interests and who will see things from their own point of view. My view, Mr. Speaker, is that the 'Government of the country is responsible to the people for the administration of public affairs, and on its shoulders must rest the responsibility for providing arrangements to take care of the business of the country. I say, therefore, that you cannot take from the Government and put upon the shoulders of any separate (Mr. Henders.]
board the responsibility which properly belongs to the -Government. The Government must undertake the work that lies before it. They must see that an opportunity is given for collecting all necessary information, and with that information before them the responsibility will then rest upon them to bring down their tariff policy, the wisdom or unwisdom of -which the people may judge of at the proper time. I am strongly in favour of a revision, an-d I trust that there will be as little delay as possible on the part of the Minister of Finance in completing the arrangement he has already started for the Carrying out of this part of his programme. I make an appeal now, as I did a year ago, to the people in the West, that whenever these conferences are held those who are studying the question -be met in good faith. Last summer, Mr. -Speaker, I encountered opposition to this proposal -for a revision of the tariff, and that opposition came from sources which I had not expected. It came from those who I thought would fully endorse it. They sai-d: "We do not want a tariff investigation for the study of this question; we have all the information we need. We- know all about the matter; we understand it thoroughly. What we want is that the Government shall act and act as we want them to act." Mr. Speaker, I have no use for that kind of argument. None of us know too much about the tariff; none of us know too much about the fiscal policy of the country; and none of us can afford to ignore any opportunity that is offered us for better informing ourselves along these lines. I shall make the appeal, when I go to the West, that this tariff commission, when it appears there, shall be met by the representatives of all classes and that all the facts that are available and that can throw any light on the subject be placed before the commission.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I find it necessary to state my position to-night on the tariff question. It has 'been suggested by some that I have changed the views which I have hitherto held on this question and which I expressed on former occasions. Allow me to -say that this is not correct, the statement is entirely -beside the mark; my views on the tariff have not changed except perhaps on two points, in regard to which they have undergone some modification. A fuller study of the -question places me, I think, -beside the leader o-f the Farmers' party (Mr. Crerar) in one respect. A more detailed study of the whole subject has led me to the belief that we are not in a position at the preeent time to enjoy the

privileges of free trade. If we were establishing a new civilization and we had one simple community, I could very well understand that we could introduce the principles of free trade. But we are not introducing a new civilization. We are living in a civilization which is hoary with years, and we are surrounded by methods of taxation that introduce a principle that is the opposite of free trade; and while we have these conditions to contend with we must govern ourselves accordingly. We must make circumstances the best that can possibly obtain for all the people in the country. We must have a tariff of some kind. Some people say that we have a tariff for protection purposes, while others assert that we have a tariff for revenue. I can make no distinction between the two. If you have a tariff up	to five per
cent you may call it a tariff	for
revenue, but the fact remains that it is, up to five per cent, a protection also. If it is a tariff far revenue, it is also protection against the people who desire to come from other countries into this country to trade, and it is ten per cent of protection to the interests of the manufacturer in itlhis country. No matter how high or how low you make it, call it by what name you will, 'a tariff means protection. If it is only one per cent it is so much, if it is forty per cent it is so much more, but it is protection in dither case.
Do you call it protection in the case of tea?

I am speaking of industries that are indigenous to this country and are supported by it, I am not referring to articles that are not manufactured or do not grow in this country; that is an entirely different thing. We tax them directly for the purpose of raising revenue. Where shall we draw the line? I find a person who says: "I do^ not 'believe in a tariff for protection, but I do believe in a tariff for revenue." I have tried to discover where the line of demarcation is drawn between these two points.
In looking over the Budgets of the past I found one instance in the course of the last few years where a distinction Was made and where one had the courage to state what was a tariff for revenue and what was a tariff for protection. The future fiscal policy of the country was under discussion in 1906 and 1907. There was a certain arrangement made for gathering information as the basis upon which the tariff policy should be framed. When the Budget was before Parliament for discussion opposition was directed against the policy of the Government that was then in power. They had reduced the tariff on agricultural implements to 17J per cent. A resolution was introduced by those who were in opposition at that time demanding .that the Government bring down the tariff on agricultural implements to ten per cent. The advocates of a tariff for revenue only said: We believe thait a tariff of 17J per cent is only a tariff for revenue and not a tariff for protection. If it be true that 17J per cent was at that time considerd a tariff for revenue then our present tariff is below a tariff (or revenue. What argument then can be offered by the Opposition in support of the ameridment offered by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's?
In regard to my attitude in supporting the proposals of the Budget I will state my position in a few words. I have watched the discussion with a great deal of interest and I have paid close attention to the amendment introduced by my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's. After going carefully through that amendment I found that it was beset with a great deal that was vague and indefinite. It did not appear to me to be blear cut and specific. It appealed to me very much along the line of the speech we listened to this afternoon from the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) who gloried in the fact that they had not a clear-cut specific policy. It was a policy that embraced everybody and it reminded me of the man who would be all things to all men, if by any means he might "gain some." Studying this amendment in the light of past history I find thait the man who moved the amendment, land those who surrounded him at the time that he and his friends were in power, made strong protestations, before they had achieved power as to what 'would be their policy if they were returned. They went up and down the country de-dlaring substantially for a definite policy. There was no mistaking their position at that time. Everybody understood what they meant. But when they came to practise what they had been preaching there was a wonderful disparity between their preaching and their practice. I find also that the Government which was in power
11	p.m. before these hon. gentlemen assumed office was a Government that was accused of being a Government of special interests and special privileges, just as these hon, gentlemen opposite are talking about the Government of the present day being a Government of special


interests and special privileges. Who are the men who are coming to this city day-after day beseeching members of this Government in regard to the tariff under discussion? Men who are going away disappointed with conditions as they find them in connection iwilth this Budget. Men who are looked upon by the Opposition as being the foster parents of this Government are the men who are in this position. The men who- are writing bitter things against this Government are the men who were looked upon as the sponsors for it.
When the Government of the late Sir John Macdonald went into power they went in with a clear-cut protective policy. Influence was brought to bear along certain lines with the object of securing Changes in that policy and we find that certain changes were made. I followed the history of that Government down through the years and I found that in the year before they went out of power they made radical changes in their policy. They reduced very materially the protaitive tariff which was then in operation. Then, another party came into power on a free trade policy practically, and we find on reading over the record that the Finance Minister of that Government announces "No radical change this year in /the fiscal policy." Year after year this is the announcement. Finally there are some little changes made and then it goes on again from year to year the same old story of no change. How about the Union Government? In the first year that the Union Government was in power a change in the tariff policy in the form of a reduction off $17,000,000, and that after tflie second year they come down again with a reduction of $30,000,000.
I was reminded-as I studied this over in my own mind-of a passage in the Scriptures, where a certain man called his two sons. He said to one son, "Go, work to-day* in my vineyard"; and the son replied, "I go, Sir", but went not. And he said to the second son, likewise, and the son said, "I will not go", but afterwards repented and went. The question was asked which of these did the will of his father, and the answer was in favour of the latter. I am in the position of making a similar choice, and I am inclined to give my approval to the man who at first refused but finally went and did as he was requested. I find myself in this position to-night: after weighing all the evidence that is before me I am going to trust the man who has prepared the fiscal policy that has given to us a reduction of over $30,000,000, and who- says: 
I am going to study the question and come down with a fiscal policy that will be the fiscal policy of this Government when it makes its appeals to the people. I am going to give that man and that Government a fair chance, and will reach my conclusions as to my future course after they have declared themselves.

Mr. Speaker, the Budget delivered recently by the Minister of Finance has given rise to a debate which, though it little resembles in tone and in substance the debates of previous years on this vital question, will nevertheless in my opinion arouse far more deeply than in the past the interest of the people of Canada. We cannot, close our eyes- to the- fact that if within the walls of this Parliament there seems to be, in some quarters at least, a tendency to approach this question with the set opinion of pre-war days, there is outside pf this House a public opinion more critical, more alert, more resolute, and more determined than ever to see to it that the abuses which have crept in to our fiscal system shall no longer be tolerated in this country. Little can we wonder, Sir, at this change of attitude, at this new spirit-which can so easily be detected and still more easily be explained -which has permeated, gradually but surely, throughout the country, with greater force since the advent of peace. As I was listening to the Minister of Finance unfolding to us what we already too well knew- the ghastly story of our financial situation; as I read on the one hand the appalling figure of the national debt of two and a half billions of dollars; and as I saw on the Other hand notwithstanding that tremendous burden which we have to carry and to bear-a burden partly hut not wholly due to the war-the unmistakable evidence of waste and extravagance in the expenditure of our public money, I came, Sir, to realize more fully that whatever may be the other causes, the real explanation for the grievances and the discontent of the people at the present day, can be traced directly to the Government and to their lack of foresight and of courage in not leading the way, or even entering into the new stage of social growth. To me it appears of far greater importance in this debate that we should note and study the feelings of unrest so prevalent amongst our people, and try to remedy a situation truly alarming in the present juncture, than that we should indulge ourselves, for parly purposes, in the luxury of discussing the historical

merits or demerits of free trade or protection. For my part, Sir,-as between the extreme views of those who belong to the one school of thonght and of those who belong to the other, I stand by the policy of the party to which I belong, a policy which has for its immediate object, as I understand it, to maintain our custom duties for revenue purposes only and not for giving to any class of our population an unjust preference, privilege or protection detrimental to the great mass of our people. In a word, Sir the aim of Liberalism to-day is what it has always been in the past; not to destroy, but to reconstruct and to develop.
I know full well, Mr. Speaker, that this fiscal policy of the Liberal policy has been persistently assailed in the past by the Tory high protectionists in this country. Did we not hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Sir George Foster) quite recently in this debate-by a change of tactics as sudden as it was surprising,-pretend to see no difference between its scope and object and that of the policy to which he seems to still adhere with the same confidence and with the same enthusiasm with which he so often in the past gave testimony in this House? But, .Sir, whatever the opinions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this point may be, we who belong to the Liberal party, looking back to the fifteen years, of its adminitration, can find remarkable grounds for gratification at the thought of its splendid record and achievements. By whatever name you may call the fiscal system that was in vogue between 1896 and 1911, what we do know is that never before were Canadians so prosperous, so happy and so contented as during that brief but all too short period of Liberal administration. Such, Sir, was the success of that .administration that when in its last year of office-forging ahead wisely but resolutely in the path it had traced for itself-it introduced and announced its policy of reciprocity, those who are sitting to your right could find no other weapon with which to .attack their opponents than to shout on every housetop what was in facta tribute to their opponents, "Let well enough alone". Brave indeed would be the public man who would to-day step on a public platform, and, facing a Canadian audience representative of all classes in the community, calmly repeat as a remedy for our present day troubles this old worn-out doctrine. "Let well enough alone". Were a Cabinet Minister to try this ordeal, when we are witnessing at the present time such
an unnatural and unprecedented ferment spreading throughout the country, he would soon realize what he now feigns to ignore, the full sense and full feeling of indignation and alarm throughout the country provoked and accentuated by the folly, the ignorance, the lack of policy and the sad mismanagement of this Government.
Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing a remarkable change in this country. Canadians have come to learn, to better compare and to digest what passes before their eyes. They know, Sir, what they want. No mere promises will again satisfy them, or divert them from their course. Let us look, Sir, at the case of the farmer. He still remembers his unsuccessful pilgrimage to Ottawa He is still resentful of the cold reception that was then given him by the members of this Government. Can we restore his confidence, so badly shattered by the unfortunate events to which I have just alluded?
Let us look at some features of his programme. The farmer comes forward once more with a just and reasonable plea that if there is any sincerity in the appeal of this Administration for " production and still more production " as a cure for many of our present day troubles, the Government should immediately facilitate thr work of our farming population by removing the duties on farm implements, thus cheapening the cost of the instruments of production and eliminating the chief obstacle to the successful achievement of their labour. Sir, that is a request which amounts to a sane policy, and which should be adopted by this House-a policy which is embodied in the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and which, I may venture to say, is endorsed by the unanimous voice of Liberalism in this country.
But what does the Government do? Their attitude dn this respect resembles their conduct on other questions of public policy. They hesitate, they linger, and finally they drift into the easier course of evading a decision and doing nothing. In 1911 they promised a tariff commission-nothing came of it; in 1919 there was to be an investigation preliminary to a tariff revision; this year a new Minister of Finance comes forward and promises to redeem the broken pledge of his predecessor. Strange would be this attitude were we not familiar with its true underlying causes. The weak protest of a small group whose interests seem to be merged with the fate of this .Government, clinging desperately to a privilege which they feel is slipping from their

nngere, is sufficient to paralyze the efforts of this Government and to prevent justice being done to the great bulk of our population. It is said, Sir, that great men do not always know their well-wishes. Better for our Cabinet ministers would it be could we but rescue them from their friends!
Sir, there is another phase of this situation closely and intimately connected with the question raised1 by this amendment. We believe that substantial reductions in the tariff along the lines suggested by the hon. member for i .Shelburne and Queen's would contribute to solve, without ham or injury to any legitimate business in this country, the two most pressing economic problems of the hour: In the first place, diminish the. high cost of living; in the second, place, encourage the vigorous development of our national resources,-essential not only to procure us revenue, but essential also for the progress and prosperity of this country. Needless for us sitting here as representatives of the people to idly lament over the people's sufferings. A greater effort is expected from us than a casual glance at some newspaper which will inform us, day in and day out, that the high cost of living is still persisting in its ascending course. We may not please the present rulers of Canada, but we would surely be rendering a service to the cause of government could we but suggest a probable method of removing the cause of the present troubles and discontent amongst our people, which no honest and sane man would care to dispute or to deny. It is in this spirit that I have approached the perusal of this amendment; it is in this .spirit that I intend to give it my hearty support.
I summarize my views, Mr. Speaker in one phrase: Greater production would mean more prosperity for the producer, greater relief to the consumer, and by tending to raise the purchasing power of the dollar proportionately to the reduction of the prices of commodities would eliminate the dangerous necessity of indefinitely increasing the wages without corresponding benefits to the wage earner. But, as usual, we are doomed to disappointment. The Government, after having taken the initiative in this campaign of production, fails to support it in the only practical way in which it could be supported. Instead of a policy founded on common sense, they prefer to lavish the people's money on commissions;-commissions for the regulation of prices which do no regulating-com-
[Mr. Pa..and !
missions for stimulating of production which fail to do any stimulating.
Not only does this Government fail to do its duty, not only does it fail to relieve the consumer by reducing the high cost of living, but it has the temerity to introduce a Budget which by the form of taxation proposed will leave unmolested the war profiteer to better crush the man whose only crime is to have preferred to remain honest rather than to become rich. This Budget is a direct challenge to the public opinion of Canada. But what cares this Government? It does not rest on public opinion; it knows and feels that it stands on private humour, that the foundation of its administration is on a quidksand.
What a pitiful position for a Government to be in! We heard the other day the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) make a vain attempt to save the sinking ship, to restore order in his own .household, to desperately appeal to his supporters to remain steadfast as the members of a rapidly vanishing crew. Sir, I would pay this tribute to my hon. friend, that usually when he enters into a debate he is well armed with every sort of argument that would tend to strengthen his case. But there is a limitation to the resources of man, and when the hon. minister suddenly realized that his mission was to defend the record of this Government, and that he held in his hand but the slim material upon which to build his case-the promise of a tariff revision at some future date- he quickly sidestepped before such an arduous task, to enter into the easier course of finding fault with those who in this House disagreed with him. He attacked the Farmers' party; he did not spare the Liberal party. The former he reproached for their free trade principles; the latter he chastised because 'he seems to have found in the speeches of some of their leaders a tendency towards moderate protection. But free trade-moderate protection, will never satisfy the hon. Minister of the Interior. It was the voice of a staunch Tory, somewhat indignant at the thought that there may be some men in this country who fail to see the wisdom of maintaining intact the high protectionist policy of his party.

Might I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?
Order.

There lies the line of demarcation between the Government and those who oppose them. We see more clearly the true position of parties in this

country. May it help to bind more closely the forces which by the very nature of their programmes should be united and not divided. This Government, Mr. Speaker, is growing weaker and weaker. The popular torrent is gaining upon it every hour. Its fate is definitely sealed. From every nook and corner of the land is heard the wide clamour for a general election. To this chorus is added quite recently a new voice by no less a body than the Great War Veterans of Canada.
We are witnessing, Sir, a strenuous tug-of-war between those who, representing the last vestige of autocratic rule in this country, blind to the popular will, will not disgorge until (they are dislodged, and those .who, still mindful of a successful war for freedom, demand the restoration of the fight to a free election, indispensable to the renewal of our work of peace.
To make this country safe foT democracy, Mr. Speaker, we can do no better than to turn towards Liberalism, to find in the glorious pages of its history the principles of sane and sound government. They have never failed in the past; they will not fail in the present instance to restore to the people their freedom, so badly shattered during recent years.

Mr. Speaker, any member who rises at this hour, after two weeks of debate of the tariff question, surely has assurance. But I feel that the occasion must not be allowed to pass without my saying at least a few words, and I shall endeavour to be brief.
The first Budget of our new Finance Minister is certainly breaking new ground, not only in Canada but perhaps in the world of finance. The method adopted has been discussed in recent times, but I know no case in which similar taxes have been imposed, save, perhaps, in France, where they are now considering a Budget which proposes a tax of one per cent on turnover and ten per cent upon luxuries. Possibly one of the things we have now to consider is whether a sales tax or tax on turnover is the better. Possibly the Finance Min-inister is not wedded to this particular method; he is willing to consider, I imagine, the adoption of that method which will get the money with the least expense to trade and the least expense to the Government*
At the bottom of any consideration of taxation proposals lies, of course, the present outlook in business. That is far from satisfactory, in spite of the figures which have
been quoted again and again in this debate. An examination of the amounts or quantities of goods or commodities that we produced during the past year indicates a disappointing result, although the money values have increased. That certainly is small ground for satisfaction. Again, our money is at a discount in the greatest market which we have-that is, where our greatest buying is done-and that also is unsatisfactory. Another cause for dissatisfaction at he present time is the fact that the market in which we do most of our selling is not readily reached by our buyers. Our importations from England have not balanced with our exports to that country, and, in consequence, have muddied the situation.
On the other hand, there are certain grounds for satisfaction, or at least for hope that we will deal with the situation to our satisfaction. There was throughout .the war an immense use of credit, mainly by the Government. As one English author says, perhaps as a result of that use of credit, we are inoculated against a panic or crisis at this time. Indeed, looking back over the history of other wars we see that usually from two to eight years elapsed before the crisis came. Probably .the shortest period was the crisis of 1857, following the Crimean War. I believe that in about six years the crisis followed the Napoleonic wars, and after the Civil War in the United States the panic did not arrive until 1872 or 1873. From that, perhaps, it would be a reasonable deduction .that we have before us a few years in which to readjust our finances.
(Now, that these finances are not satisfactory we all admit. We have even, this year, not balanced our expenditures with our taxation, and it is questionable whether we shall do so next year. More taxation was needed during the war. The great cause of our troubles knday is that inadequate taxation was then imposed. This was not peculiar to Canada; it was the case throughout the world, because I think we were all optimists; we were always hoping that the war would end within six months or a year. It was hard to adapt our taxation and our expenditures to a continuing state of war. That consideration stands, and .the man who to-day comes forwards to criticise the financing of the five years of war must remember that he is looking at it with the wisdom of hindsight and that the man who was actually dealing with it had only human foresight to guide him. Nevertheless, there were men who during the war dwelt upon

the necessity for greater taxation than we had, and I do believe that the Government which preceded this Union Government was slack in not adopting other methods of taxation before they did.
At present we need, first of all, to balance our expenditure with our taxation. This Budget promises a prospect of so doing. Next, however, we need a surplus. I have not been in the House during the whole of the debate, but I have heard no one yet mention the necessity for providing a sinking fund in the very near future. II had hoped, indeed, that the Finance Minister would be able to tell us how soon he expects to have any considerable surplus and how he proposes to. use that surplus. It is plain that if a change in values takes place we have a very considerable inflation of currency and that that surplus may be needed first of all to remove that inflation; next we must undoubtedly establish sinking funds for the redemption of our debt. How soon will that be reached? Will we reach that before we run into the storms which certainly will follow the vast waste of five years of world war? It is necessary that we should; otherwise we shall run into difficulties thereafter.
'Something has been said about the necessity for reduction of expenditures, and upon that I 'wanted to speak this evening; I doubt whether I would have risen at all but for that. II wish especially to deal with the project which has been recommended to the British Government by the Select Committee on National Expenditure of 1917 with regard to a Committee on Estimates. That great man, Gladstone, said that it was very difficult for a minister to control the expenditure of his department at any time. I know that our Finance Minister has found it very difficult to	get
the reductions in 'Estimates that he has got this year. There are four points at which financial control may apply. Two of these are departmental with us, the officer having the expenditure in hand and the departmental auditor. Then the matter comes to the Minister of Finance and finally it must come to Parliament. I take it that in the Cabinet, the ministers stand1 more upon an equality than ministers do under the English system, where the Treasury has a predominant voice in all these matters. That being so, our Minister of Finance cannot have full control, and he needs some means beyond what our present system gives him. No man has sat in this House through four sessions-and most of those around1 me have been here at least
[Mr. Davis. 1
as long as that-without- being impressed with the futility of the proceeding of passing Estimates. If an hon. member were a company director and authorising the expenditure of sums in connection with his company with no more knowledge of the requirements of the service than he has when passing Estimates1, he should be committed to a penitentiary and probably he would be. The real reason why that is the case is that at the present time Parliament lacks the machinery for getting that information, and the proposition of a committee on estimates would provide Parliament with that machinery hy which it could ha informed. When the estimates were once submitted to and passed that committee and came before the House, the House could vote upon them with some measure of knowledge and assurance. It does not so vote now. The British House endeavoured1 to apply the idea of a committee of estimates in the year 1912. This was just a House committee without any machinery, and they found it would take them about thirty or forty years to get around the departments, and therefore, at the beginning of the war it was laid aside. But when the matter was examined by the Hon. Herbert Samuel's committee, a machinery was devised consisting of an Examiner of Estimates, having an office of practically equal rank with the Auditor General and a staff which could go into the various departments under the direction of the committee in the recess and gather the information which the committee would require to act upon. At this time our lack of such machinery is a defect in our system, and if we had such machinery, it would get us the reduction in expenditure we all know is necessary. For instance, a few weeks ago a statement was issued that there were 70,000 names on Canada's list of employees, and when you look over i't you find 6,000 employees or thereabouts still in the Militia Department and thousands in the Department of Soldiers' Givil Ke-establish-ment. These departments have not been greatly cut down since the war, and it is very difficult for the minister or for the permanent officials to make the necessary reduction; but I take it that if that duty were laid upon Parliament, it would be done.
I wish to make a remark or two more directly in connection with the Budget, and I shall have finished. The present reduction in prices is rather coincident with this new taxation than an effect of it. The

reduction bad begun before the taxation was imposed, and possibly it would have proceeded without our taxation. There is no doubt that a fall in prices to-day is the most desirable thing that could happen to allay unrest. If prices go down, wages will not follow them for some time, and this will do more than any Other thing could to bring us out into more peaceful times.
Let me depart for a moment from my line of thought and refer to this matter lest I should later forget it. It seems t-o me that the Government at present should watch with a very jealous eye the many mergers and new issues of capital which are now occupying the financial world. After five years of war, disturbed business conditions such .as we have had and enormous profits, it seems to me that an attempt . is being made to capitalize the situation which attempt it is the duty of the Government to prevent big finance from putting across. These companies have been paying large dividends; the change in the value of money has greatly increased the apparent value of the properties, and it is undoubtedly a tempting time for the launching of such enterprises. If we cannot deal with this matter, we are going to leave one of the greatest causes of unrest ndt dealt with. There is no doubt that the ordinary mam is quite willing to see capital get a fair return in the shape of dividends, but what is continually disturbing the workingman, the farmer, the community generally, is to see unearned amounts, hidden assets, converted into visible and*real assets, and melons cut. A company is after all a creation of the legislature and it can be dealt with. There is no doubt whatever of omr power to take hold of the question, and it is one of the great things that is now facing us. The limited liability company has a history in England-(and there it had its origin)-of only about 95 years. It was in 1825 that the Bubble Act was repealed in Great Britain and the incorporation of a limited liability company-there were chartered companies before-then first became possible. We have not learned how to control the device and we must learn how to control it if we are going to have any degree of satisfaction in our handling of big finance.
Last year I found it necessary to vote against the Government on its Budget because no new taxation had been imposed, no new areas of taxation had been opened, and regard was not had to the demands of the West in the reductions that were made.
This year, because the Government has entered upon a course of opening up new areas of taxation in which we need experience and organization, out elf which we learn something with every application, and because a real effort has been made-when we are increasing our taxation by 25 per cent in one year, I think that is a very real effort-it seems wise to me to support the Government. I have said that at this point because I have one or two other things tot say in regard to much of the debate to which I have listened during the past two weeks. It has been comparatively easy ito accept the Budget; it has been relatively difficult to accept the arguments in support of the Budget. The fact of the matter is that when we argue this question of protection and free trade, surely the stalest and most unprofitable question which this House ever deals with, never is even one instance exhausted; it is largely a case of "after this" and "therefore on account olf this" when protection is alleged to have been the cause of prosperity. Let us examine for just a moment what occurred in Germany which, perhaps, is the great and classic example of what is claimed to be the great success of protection in our time. In 1834, the German Zollverein was formed; free trade was introduced into an area which before had been cut up by conflicting tariffs. In 1879, the Germans .adopted a protection policy. But Germany's industrial success had begun before the adoption of her protective policy. Something which I have never heard referred to in this debate, and which I am sure had a very large share in the shifting of trade from England to Germany, is concerned with the currency. When England adopted free trade in 1846 she was the only country in the world that had a gold currency. Germany adapted a gold currency basing it upon, the indemnity which she re-[DOT] ceived from France in 1874. England had been for many years a manufacturing country and was a large buyer of raw materials and foodstuffs, and down to 1874, and even a little later-the Latin union was not dissolved until 1876-the best use the seller of these commodities could make of his money was to spend it in the .English market. England was already a wealthy country. She had plenty of money and where money is plentiful goods are dear. Money was scarce in Germany and goods and services were cheap, and when the money was freely transmutalble from English into German currency the seller of these goods took his money to Germany and bought cheaper

goods. The result was that Germany's increase in trade began before her protection came into force. More than that, it was just about 1870 that the iron ores of Germany were made accessible to the iron trade. Her iron ores are largely phosphorous, and it was not until the Gilchrist-Thomas process of smelting was adopted that she was able to use her ores and build up her iron trade. I do not propose to follow the matter through all the ramifications of finance and science. Germany had just won three great wars, and in such circumstances it is impossible to hold a people down. Psychology, science, finance and political economy came to her aid at that time and her industrial prosperity began. So far as England is concerned, it certainly seems to me that when we survey Europe, with every protective country on its last legs trembling even yet on the verge of bankruptcy as a result of the war, and find England their support and the hope of civilized Europe, England being a free trade country, there is some reason to doubt whether protection has all the virtues that have been ascribed to it by some members on this side. Nevertheless, I must say this, that when our forefathers founded this Dominion of Canada, which otherwise might have been four separate communities, there was probably, in the then state of political and economic knowledge, some excuse for the application of protection to build up the consciousness of mutual interest. It at least was an obvious way and it would probably have taken longer under free trade to do the same thing. But even if that were so, it is no justification for the continuation of the process, after the lines have been laid down upon which we now have trade east and west and have a community who have fought through this war in such a manner as to consolidate the country to a greater extent than had been possible by reason of the economic efforts of the last fifty years.

What about the United
States?
In what respect?
As an example of protection.

I want to iray a word or two with reference to the Canadian Northern Railway, which we now own, and. to point out- to the House something with regard to the extravagance
wasteful, wanton, wilful extravagance- shown by that company before the line was turned ova'- to the Government of Canada. We are responsible for that extravagance. We permitted the Canadian Northern Company to go on in their mad way until they reached a position where we were obliged to take over the line. These people came to Parliament year after year for the purpose of obtaining money. We handed this money over to them and seemed to be entirely unregardful as to whaJt they did with it. Before the Canadian Northern was merged into the Canadian National Railway 'System the Company obtained a charter from Parliament to build a tunnel through Mount Royal, and I understand the cost of that was $11,000,000. We permitted that to be done, Mr. Speaker, we gave the company this power, and we allowed them to pierce this mountain, costing the people of Canada $11,000,000, when that work could have been obviated by forcing the Canadian Pacific, or the Grand- Trunk Railway 'Company, to allow the Canadian Northern to negotiate the mountain by going about a mile or a mile and a half outside of their present line. Now in order to pierce the mountain the company were obliged to undermine valuable property in the city of Montreal, and as a result of the construction of this funnel the buildings along the streets-shops, houses and so forth-fell into ruins, and the com-

pany were obliged at the cost of very large sums of money to settle with the owners. But the point I want to make particularly is that we allowed this company to do1 iwhat they liked with the money we gave them. We had no>
supervision over it, we allowed them to build a station for their Transcontinental railway on Lagauohetiere street about a hundred yards from the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk stations. I say that the Government-not particularly the present Government, but the Government of yesterday, and perhaps, the Government of the day before-will be held to account by the people for the manner in which they allowed the Canadian Northern Railway Company and Mackenzie and Mann to deal with these railways that we have been obliged to take over.
The immigration problem is of great importance to this country at the present moment. Without a proper immigration policy this country is bound to go into bankruptcy, for we must have immigrants if we ar.e to live financially. At the present time we have a population of about 8,000,000 and a national debt of $2,000,000,000 and our annual expense is something like $400,000,000. It does not require much of a mathematician to discover that if 8,000,000 people bear that debt, 16,000 would have to bear only one-half, and if we had a population of 32,000,000 people they would have to bear only one-quarter of that debt. We must have a proper immigration policy, and I submit that the present Government is not adopting a policy calculated to attract proper immigrants. We have placed all kinds -of stumbling blocks in the way of prospective immigrants. Whatever may he said IMr. Jacobs.]
of Sir Clifford Sifton-and I am not here to be his protagonist-I want to say that the immigration policy he adopted was the policy for this country, and since his time we have had no Minister of Immigration who came near to him in the wide vision he had in regard to a national policy in that regard. At present we raise every kind of objection to immigrants; we encourage only a certain class; they must come from a certain district; they must be farmers and domestics. That is not the right policy. To-day a man may be an agriculturist; tomorrow he may be a shop-keeper. To-day a woman is a domestic servant; to-morrow she may 'become the wife of a profiteer. There is no guarantee that the people we bring in are going to remain in the same avocation, for this is a land of opportunity and those who come to this country naturally expect to improve their lot, otherwise they would not leave their native land.
The unfortunate part of the whole thing is that we are aping the United 'States in the matter of an immigration policy. But the conditions in the two countries are not comparable. They have 110,000,000 people and can pick and choose their immigrants; but we are not in that position, and yet we blindly follow the regulations of the United States in respect to immigrants. If to-day the United States pass an immigration law, to-morrow it is put on our statute books. They take the snuff to-day, and we do the sneezing to-morrow. So long as we follow that policy, just so long will we be a land without people.
When immigrants arrive on our shores what do we offer them? At this late hour I am not going into the question of our naturalization law. But suppose a man comes from that hated tyrannical country, Germany; he wants to forget the life he led there. 'He has read about this great land of opportunity. What does he find? On his arrival he has to wait ten years from the date of the signing of the Peace Treaty in 1919 before he can become a fully enfranchised Canadian citizen. And before that is possible he must obtain from Germany the consent of that Government that he may shed his allegiance to the Fatherland and become a British citizen; if he does not obtain that consent he remains for all time an alien in this country and can never aspire to the rights of British citizenship. Why does he come here? He can go to the United States where no questions are asked, and where after five years, if he has been a good citizen, he can become a fully naturalized American citizen

and hold his naturalization against the world. In the United States they put -no obstacle in his way, certainly nothing like we have here under the proposed Franchise Act. We have that Act, we have the Naturalization Act, -and we have the Immigration Act-all tending to keep the new citizen an alien as long as possible. So long as that alien -can go across the border and obtain all the rights and privileges of citizenship it is not likely that we shall ever increase our population by immigration.
