I would like to refer for a moment to the election in East Elgin. The House will remember that last year a Bill was passed declaring that by-elections must take place within six months after the seat is declared vacant. When 'I introduced my original Bill II had it at sixty days, but when the Bill went into Committee it was urged by the Solicitor General, the present Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) that in the Hudson Bay region and in other remote districts it would be almost impossible to have an election within sixty days, for various geopraph-ical reasons, particularly in winter. The member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) pointed out clearly that in his division, if, God forbid, there should be a by-election, it would be absolutely impossible to get the writs out .and have everything done within sixty days, so we finally reluctantly agreed to fix the period at six months. Well, the Government are taking every day of that six .months in connection with the East Elgin by-election. Is that the spirit in /which the matter was discussed at the time? I say that the Government is acting in bad faith in not bringing on that election within a reasonable time. During this entire session there will be no representative from East Elgin, and that division is to be left unrepresented .purely to satisfy the whim or caprice of something ulterior of the Government. These are matters which I leave to the Government to think about, and I feel confident that, when the gravity of the situation with regard to the election is brought before the Government, particularly when it was

promised that that election would be brought on within a reasonable time, they will act at once.
I feel that I have taken up too much of the time of the House. I did not rise to make any set speech; any views that I had at the time the Budget was brought down were so thoroughly discussed previously by hon. members on this side of the House and by Government members, that when I came to speak I was in the position of my good friend the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), who said that there was nothing left to glean. But my hon. friend found that his gleaning was pretty effective as he spent two hours in discussing matters which he found were of interest. If the President of the Council had to do some gleaning wjien he rose to speak, wha: shall be said of me when I have to speak after the President of the Council ha3 spoken? He has covered the ground thoroughly from his point of view, and I must congratulate him on the speech he made. It was a vigorous fighting speech, and I must say this for the President of the Council, that he evidently forgot that the war was over; this was a speech which he evidently had in stock, and he wanted to get rid of it before the taxation proposals went into effect, fearing that if he had to pay a 10 per cent tax on that speech, he might have to carry it in stock and not be able to dispose of it before it became shelf-worn.
Mr. WILLIAM S. LOGGIE (Northumberland!, N.B.): Mr. Speaker, before I enter upon a discussion of the matter before the House, might I be permitted to extend a word of welcome to the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) who has returned to this House, I hope, so thoroughly restored to health that he may be able to continue in the good work in which he is engaged? May I also express a word of congratulation to the Speaker of the House and to the Deputy Speaker of the House, that they are the first two gentlemen to occupy the Chair in this wonderful chamber of this magnificent building.
Mr. Speaker, as I wander through these spacious halls-marble halls, imay I say?- I am reminded of the conflagration that took place so short a time age and of the wonderful deliverance some members had on that occasion. It is fitting that I should congratulate the people of Canada for giving the lawmakers, of this country, not only the present lawmakers but the lawmakers for generations to come, .such a beautiful chamber to occupy.
May I have this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry
Drayton) on the Budget that he has presented 'to the House? It is the first Budget that he has delivered as a member of the House of Commons, and it certainly is one of the best that I have ever heard.
Let me refer for just a, moment or two to a statement he made. He told us that for 'the past year he has a surplus of $39,000,000, and in that regard he has done very well. But he told us also that he will require altogether 'about $541,000,000 for the coming year. That, of course, takes up some treasury bills to the extent of $74,000,000, which, I think, mature during the present year. We find from his statement that he expects to receive from the customs $167,000,000 for the current year. But last year, that is the fiscal year ended March 31, 1920, he received from the customs no less a sum than $187,520,613. Those figures clearly isfhow that, over and above any .amount that is added to the customs tax, he is reducing the customs tax during the coming year by an amount of upward of 20 million. And yet the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) told us this afternoon that the Government had not taken any duties off the necessaries of life. He also said that the Government have taken no steps to .make it possible to relieve the cost of living, and further, that the Government were protecting the profiteers instead of the consuming public. If L were to use unparliamentary language, I could, peihaps, say something that I ouglht not to say, but I will say in the meantime that those statements iare inaccurate. If we have taken off $20,000,000 more than we are putting on through the customs, then surely rwe have reduced the duties. I may be asked, what we are reducing them on. We are certainly reducing them on the necessaries of life. Let .me point to one item of the necessaries of life. For a number of years we have had a war tax o>f 7i per cent on raw cotton, and I am sure that every hon. .gentleman present will admit that cotton textiles are a necessary of life. Do hon. members know how much duty the consuming public paid into the treasury during the past fiscal year on raw cotton? Nearly $3,000,000. Yet, as was pointed out by the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), during the fifteen years of the Liberal regime a reduction of only about $2,400,000 was made in the way of tarff. taxes. A reduction of some $125,866 has been made in the duty on nails, which are a necessary of life. If you go right through the schedule, you will find that we have reduced the duties on the necessaries of life and, to that extent, have reduced the cost

of living. If that toe true, is it statesmanlike for the leader of the Opposition to say that this Government have not taken any duties off the necessaries of life?
Then he goes onto say that iwe have protected the "profiteers and ignored the consuming public, tout he gives no proof in substantiation of that statement. It is a mere allegation, and so far as I can see it is not in accordance with the facts. The hon. member further says that we tax the middle and poorer classes. Well, of course, it is a matter of dispute as to who are the middle and poorer classes who will pay this tax, but I venture to say that all the people in Canada will share in the benefit that will be derived from the net reduction of $20,000,000. Then the leader of the Opposition says that we are safeguarding the rich and their friends. I do not know what ground he had for that statement, but I can see not the slightest shadow of actual fact in it. *
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me point out what a constructive tariff policy is. The Minister of Finance tells the people of Canada that he intends' to have a thorough revision of the tariff; and, more than that, he tells them on what toasis that revision and investigation will toe made. It is to that point that I wish to direct attention particularly, because if the Minister of Finance carries out his proposal on the basis which he has stated, then I say that the effect will not be such as hasi been suggested by the leader of the Opposition. I say that the policy of the Minister -will tend to reduce the duty on the necessaries of life and will be a step in the direction of relieving the cost of living. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it will not protect the profiteers instead of the consumers, nor will it unduly tax the middle and poorer classes any more than those who are better able to bear taxation. Indeed, Sir, there is every indication that those best able to bear taxation will be asked to shoulder the brunt of it. Now, the first plank in the minister's platform-and this will surely bear out my statements-is an undertaking to prevent the abuse of the tariff for the exploitation of the consumer. I would ask the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) whether he does not approve of that plank. That hon. gentleman would protect infant industries, tout I am sure he will agree that it is an eminently wise provision of this plank that the consuming public are not to bei exploited'. The first plank of the minister's platform therefore announces the fact that the consumer will be taken care of. The second plank is to stabilize legitimate industries and encour-
age the establishment of new industries essential to the proper economic development of the nation. Perhaps some hon. gentleman will contend that these cannot go together. My view is different; I think they can and ought to go together. As to details of the way in which the matter is to toe carried out I shall have a word or two to say later on.
The next plank is to develop to the fullest extent our natural resources. I am sure there is not much opposition to that on either side of the [House. On the question of developing our natural resources I think we are all at one. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), in order to do that, wants to have the duty taken off agricultural implements. He asks us to take the duty off the instruments of production, but he says not a word about taking the duty off farm products. I cannot see the consistency in this.
May I tell my hon. friend that the first plank in the platform of the Dominion Council of Agriculture is absolute freedom of all food?

I am very glad to take this opportunity to state that I cannot entertain any such proposal for one moment, and I will give my reasons. There are very many manufactured food products in this country, and if you let goods of that kind in free you will destroy those industries. I challenged the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MdMaster) last year to go to Montreal and tell the Clark Company there that he would let Kansas City and Chicago send in canned goods here free. I contend, Sir, that you connot let these goods in free without destroying the industries.
What about fish?

conditions are abnormal, and the prices of textiles in the United States and in the United Kingdom are practically as high as they are here.
Let me illustrate that in another way.
I was in Winnipeg a few days ago and I went into a knitting factory there, and I was surprised to see them packing up knitted goods to go to New Zealand, goods that were sold at the same price as they were sold to Canadian consumers, or to the Canadian trade. Now, if it he true that that knitting company sold those goods to go to New Zealand, did they not sell them at the world's market value? At any rate they sold them on the basis of the price they could get them for in England, and surely that demonstrates the fact for which I have been contending. Whether they sold them cheaper I do not know-all I know is that the buyers, as business men, were purchasing them to the best advantage, and the goods were going from Winnipeg to New Zealand.
Now this proposal of the Minister of Finance-and it is to my mind the most important fact-stabilizes the general tariff and places 'businesses on a firm foundation. In that policy you have the interest of the consumer, and the industrial life of the country looked after. If you can frame a tariff based on these two principles then I think you can have a stable tariff. You will not get the revenue that is necessary from a stable tariff, but the minister has very wisely proposed a new plan for that purpose; let me tell you, I think it is a very important plan. Before I make any observations as to that let me read what I said last year in that regard, and the extract shall only be a very brief one. My words on the occasion referred to were as follows:
If we frame a tariff and reduce the cost of living' and we are short $50,000,000, how are we to get the money? If you refer to the imports in 1918 you will find that we imported Into Canada about $860,000,0D0 worth of goods, and if we framed an adequate tariff on the basis I have indicated,-and by adequate I mean in the interests of manufacturers and consumers alike-
Mr. Speaker, you will admit, I am sure, that I have not changed my mind this year in regard to the matter; I am arguing to-night exactly the principle I argued last year-
I would add a surtax of, say, 2 per cent on the $80 0vO'O'0,0 00-, and would get $16,000,000 thereby. But I would still be short $34,000,000, and to raise that balance I would; do this. I And by the Canada Year Book of 1918 that we 
manufactured $1,381,547,225 worth of products.
I would put an excise duty of 2 per cent on $1,700,000,000 of Canadian manufactures and obtain $34,000,OOO, and that together with the $16,000,000,000, would give me my $50,000,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have very much pleasure in congratulating the Government upon having adopted a policy that will enable them to get the money they need without interfering unduly with the industrial life of the country. That is to say, they get a portion of the money from the manufacturers and the importer of like commodities must pay that additional tax. It is a fair and businesslike proposition. If our values fall and if our imports decline our tariff may remain stable and you can change the surtax and the excise tax to meet the circumstances in which you find yourself. If you have too much money you can decrease these taxes, and if you have not enough you can increase them without interfering with, and upsetting, the business of the country. I think the minister was wise in not putting any tax on food products. You wil remember, Mr. Speaker, that in the new taxes that we are imposing-the excise tax and the surtax- food products are not included, and yet the leader of the Opposition contends that the Government is taking no steps to make it possible to relieve 'the cost of living. Why, we are raising $90,000,000 of extra revenue, and we are not getting a dollar of it out of the food products. I must say, therefore, that the leader of the Opposition was not at all accurate in his statement. The hon. member did not say upon what his statement was based; he merely made the allegation, and allegations without proof are, of course, not very reliable and do not carry very much weight.
iSome bon. gentlemen thought taxation should be applied to exports. Would it be fair to the manufacturer of this country to pay an export tax when he had to compete with the manufacturer in another country? I think the minister was cautious and wise, and acted the part of a statesman, in not making exports subjects to taxation. ,1 did not suggest these additional exceptions last year, Vhich I think are an improvement-at any rate for the present. The Minister of Finance is imposing a straight tax of one per cent on imports, and proposes to collect an additional one per cent from wholesalers. Personally I would have preferred that a rate of two per cent be levied upon imports, and leave the wholesaler alone; hut the minister has thought it wise to do as stated, and after

all there will not be very much difference. Then again, the ,minister is collecting one per cent from domestic makers, plus one per cent again from the wholesalers. Personally I would have preferred collecting two per cent from the manufacturers. However, I understand there were difficulties in the way, and I can conceive that such is the case. Let me illustrate what I mean; it will only take me a moment. This is my objection to placing the 2 per cent on the manufacturer:	Supposing I
manufacture automobiles, of course I do not make all the component parts that enter into the complete machine and I have to purchase from my friend here rubber tires, and from another manufacturer wheels; those wheels and tires are subject to the excise tax, and when I build them into my automobile the Government will collect another 2 per cent on the finished product. However, I think this anomaly might be rectified in the revision of the tariff, and I am sure the Minister of Finance will consider the matter. I would suggest as a means of overcoming my objection that the manufacturer of the wheels should get his tax .receipt from the Inland Revenue people, and the manufacturer of the tires should do the same, and when the automobile was completed the tax so paid on the parts could Ibe deducted from the excise on the assembled machine. Possibly other commodities would be affected in the same manner. But these are only suggestions, and it gives me a good deal of pleasure to support the proposals made by the Minister of Finance in such a businesslike manner. And I venture the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that when the people understand the financial condition of the country, they will welcome a stable customs tariff on business principles, and will be perfectly willing to bear the burden of these special post-war taxes. Again I say I most heartily approve of the tariff proposals; in my opinion none better could 'be devised.
Now a word or two on the amendment. I submit that to carry out the proposals it contained would be to precipitate this country into chaos. For the present we do not know what commodities we are to reduce the taxation on. If we reduce the duties on grey cotton, white cotton or any other cotton, I do not think the people of this country will be able to buy those commodities any cheaper than they can be purchased under present conditions. If the amendment suggested our taking ten cents off the tea duty, I would say that would be
a step towards reducing the cost of living; but nothing of the kind is suggested. The amendment asks for relief to the consumers and producers, without giving to the people anything tangible whereby that result will be brought about.
Then the amendment proposes to make substantial reductions on the burdens of customs taxation. The Government is doing that. I have already explained that a net reduction of $20,000,000 has 'been made. In effect the amendment asks us to take a leap in the dark,-to take so much off prints, so much off woollen goods, so much off knitted goods-goods, as I mentioned a few moments ago, that we are producing in Canada about as cheap as they are produced in England.
The amendment also proposes to reduce the cost of the instruments of production. Yes, it will reduce the cost of those instruments, I presume, that are used on the farms. But what about the instruments of production for making prints, cottons, knitted goods? The amendment ignores those instruments; they are to be left undei the same duty as they bear at present.
I see my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) right opposite, who spoke the other night in this debate, but this amendment does not contain any of his ideas regarding free trade, so he must be running counter to what the amendment proposes; and the same with respect to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster), and my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). If the latter were here I would draw his attention to the fact that last year he told hon. gentlemen opposite:
I would as soon look to this side of the Housethat is to your right, Sir.
-for a reduction in tariff as to your left, Mr. Speaker.
I am really sorry that my hon. friend, whom I esteem very much, should go back on that declaration, because under the Government's proposals he will get a real reduction on the necessaries of life,-the very thing he is asking for we are giving to him. What he is voting for is a leap in the dark. I am disappointed,-that is ail I can say in regard to my hon. friend's attitude to-day.
Then again the amendment does not contain a word of how the loss of revenue is to be made up if the proposed reductions in duties are put into effect. In a word, the amendment lacks any practical basis on which the suggested reductions can be

made,-it lacks the earmarks of the declared policy of 'the Liberal party. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) made that so clear to-night that I do not think I need enlarge upon it. This amendment, it seems to me, would tend to the destruction of Canadian industry, in that it asks for an immediate reduction under present abnormal conditions without any investigation to determine the practicability of such reduction, so it would be a leap into the unknown future.
To-day the cost of living is not very different here from what it is in the United Kingdom or in the United States, and with textiles in Canada practically as cheap as in those two countries, any reduction in duty would not lower the cost of living. If that be so, then what duties are we to lower in order to reduce the cost of living?
I want to say just a word about the tariff plank in the platform of the Liberal party. The preamble is apparently the same as that set out in the platform of United Farmers. But to me the funny part of it is that a great party should itemize certain articles and ask that they be put on the free list when they are already on the free list. Mr. Speaker, listen: I want to tell you a secret. The Liberal party have asked that nets and net twines be put on the free list, whereas they have been on the free list ever since Confederation. Why do they ask that goods which have been on the free list for a long time be put on the free list? Do you not think Mr. Speaker, that such a course would have a tendency to deceive the reading public? Would the people not conclude that nets and net twines are now on the dutiable list? Would they not conclude that lumber, rough and planed on one side, is also on the dutiable list; that gasolene is now dutiable? Whereas all the items I have mentioned are on the free list? Yet that is part of a plank in the Liberal platform.
Now, the next thing they ask is that the principal articles of food be made free. Evidently the member for Brome (Mr. Me-Master) has been educated since this time last year, because in his amendment of last year he asked that all food products be made free; now the demand is that the principal food products be made free.
We wanted to protect the public from lobsters.

Allow me to say to the
hon. member that that will not be a very easy matter. If you get a lobster after you you have to look out. In my judgment it is. not practicable in Canada to make all 
the principal food products free. Of course I am referring not to the food products that are now free, but simply to those that are on the dutiable list. I say that it is not practicable to make them all free, because if you did you would destroy a domestic industry.
Now, they ask also that mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and agricultural implements be made free. On what basis are they to be made free? Why do you ask that saw-mill machinery be made free while other machinery shall be dutiable? No basis is submitted, so far as I can see. No provision is made for the continued output of domestic-made machinery; no provision for loss of revenue incurred through abolishing duties; no suggestion for the imposition of duties on the basis of revenue. Perhaps hon. gentlemen are quite right in that, because a tariff for revenue is not practicable at the present time, although hon. gentlemen have argued in favour of it. This platform does not recognize the gigantic annual revenue that is required, nor does it suggest how we should overtake it if it were reduced as is set forth in this platform.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just a word about our friends on the other side at the end of the Chamber. They ask for free agricultural implements; they do not ask that natural products be made free. I have been in conversation with hon. gentlemen from the West who are farmers and they have indicated to me that they do not care whether or not the duty is taken off farm products. But strange to say I have never heard them argue in the House that it would be all right to put all natural products of the farm on the free list. The consuming public of Canada paid into the treasury during the past year on meat products alone duties amounting to $716,271.11; yet hon. gentlemen in their discussions would certainly lead me to believe that farm products were free. I know that wheat and wheat flour are free, but because these products are free and they must look to the world for a market, they think that everything else .should be free and that they should buy wherever they can buy the cheapest. If we are to succeed in this country-and I am sure that it is our destiny to be a great country-first of all we ought to manufacture most of the goods that we consume. No country situated as we are adjacent to the United States can be a great country unless it manufactures most of the commodities which it consumes. The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), speaking the other day, said that he saw

no great advantage in our people manufacturing cotton textiles; that we should rather devote our efforts to the production of farm products. I do not want to minimize the importance of farm production, but we cannot all be farmers. If we are to be a successful country, we must pay due attention to our industrial life as well as to our agricultural life. In our legislation respecting the farming interests we must not run counter to the interests of our industries. To my mind the Minister of Finance has set out to take care of these two interests, the consumer, and our industrial life. I cannot see how a saner, a wiser or more courageous proposal could be put before Canada to-day, when we have to obtain a revenue of $500,000,000 annually. We cannot get it through the customs; we must stabilize the tariff and then raise what we are short by an excise and super tax.

would not stand for. In his speech last Thursday he made this further statement:
As I say, the headquarters of the Independent Labour Party associated with the United Farmers of Ontario, are in the One Big Union hall.
That is another statement that cannot be borne out by the facts nor proved by any court or investigating committee in this land. The One Big Union hall in Cobalt was never used by the Independent Labour party or the Farmers, and I as the member for that riding never made use of the One Big Union hall. The hon. member in his speech goes on to say:
At the present time a suit is pending in the Ontario courts for possession of that particular property. The parties to that suit are, on the one hand, H. J. Everett, an officer of the Independent Labour party, and1, on the other hand, an executive officer of the International Union of see the awful futility of all that sacrifice.
It is true that the president of the local branch of the Independent Labour party in Cobalt is a party to that suit, but is it because he is a One Big Union man? I desire to ask the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) if he has anything to show that H. J. Everett ever belonged to the One Big Union. I am free to state the reason why he is a party to that suit. It is because he was a trustee of the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers, and he devoted his time and energy to a purpose the very contrary of that which my hon. friend from Algoma would wish to lead the (House to believe he did.
The hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson), in the course of his speech, used this language:
If all the sacrifice of that awful war is for no other purpose than to bring about the condition suggested, then I say that it is in the Providence of God that those boys were taken to their rest before they were forced to live to see the awful futility of all that sacrifice.
I wish to state most emphatically, Mr. Speaker, that I iam one of those Canadian and British subjects that revere the memory of the men who now sleep amidst the weeds and poppies of France and Flanders, and so long as reason remains on her throne 1 will do all I can for the man who went Over There and who was told by the flag-flappers and the so-called patriots of the country that nothing would be too good for them when they returned. I honestly assert that I revere the memory of my hon. friend's son, and I will go further and say that perhaps it is a blessing, so far as that young man is concerned, who sacrificed his life in the cause of democracy, that

he died Over There rather than see his illustrious father trying to saddle an autocracy on this country.
So far as the Budget is concerned, Mr. Speaker, there is no course left me by the rules of the House other than to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
Oh, oh.

If my hon. friends opposite are so anxious to go home iall they have to do is to call a general election to-morrow and they wilj. stay home for a good while. I was not anxious to bring this matter up but it 'is altogether unjust on the Government's part to use their strength, their power and their weight to force this House to sit all night in order to dispose of the Budget debate. I say that it is unjust, and if the people of this country knew what is going on here they would certainly give no credit to the Government for what they are doing.
I do not think I would be fulfilling my duty if I did not join with hon. members who have already offered their congratulations to the Minister of Finance. I disagree with many statements he made, but for several things that he did he is deserving of congratulation, and I take this opportunity of thanking him publicly for the way in which he has treated me in connection with a certain matter which I had at heart and which I was afraid might be brought into the Budget-I mean the tobacco question. It has been rumoured for the past few months that there was to be a change in the duties imposed on raw leaf tobacco, and 'although the Minister of Finance could not commit himself, although he could not tell me as to whether he would or would not make any change in those duties, on the divers occasions on which I had the privilege of meeting him he alwtays received me with am open mind, -and with a great deal of good-will and sincerity, and allowed me to take up a considerable part of his time in the discussion of this question. For that reason I consider he merits my public congratulations, and these I am glad to tender him.
While on this subject let me say that I hope that the duties on tobacco will not be disturbed for some years to come, because this industry is one of the most flourishing we have in Canada. Last year we produced in the neighbourhood of twenty-five million pounds of tobacco which, selling in the neighbourhood of thirty or thirty-five cents, has produced for the people of this country $8,000,000. On the other hand, we are importing a like amount of tobacco from the United States; in other words we are only producing about one-half of what we consume. Under these circumstances, if we take into consideration the fact that it is essential for this country to import as little as possible from the United States-*-especially at this juncture when our dollar is only worth from eighty-five to ninety



cents in the adjoining republic-I think the Government should seize every possible opportunity to aid our people in producing all that they can of articles that are being imported from the United States, in order to reduce importations from that country.
Coming more directly to the subject under discussion, namely the Budget, I read with a great deal of care and attention the speech which was delivered lately by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England, and this is the way in which he opened his remarks:
It is recognized on all hands that the present financial year is one of capital importance in the history of Europe, and not alone for those nations which emerged victorious from the late world-wide struggle. Eighteen months have elapsed since the preliminaries of peace were signed with Germany, and though peace follows with limping footsteps the time has come when each of us should set his house in order and, not content merely with facing our immediate necessities, should lay broad and deep the foundations of future credit and prosperity.
Sir, such were the words that were uttered by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England, and I think they constitute a guiding principle not only for the United Kingdom but for Canada as well. These words of the great English statesman are worthy of our solemn attention. Let us now see how they apply to Canada. The Chancellor of the Exchequer says that the time has come when each of us should set his house in order.
Does this Budget provide for that emergency? Certainly to set our house in order when the national debt is over $2,250,000,000, our expenditures, to say the least, should be met by our revenue. Has this been accomplished? I must say that from my point of view it unfortunately has not. Beading the Budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance one would be inclined to think that we were meeting our expenditures by our revenues. This is how the minister expresses it:
With the total revenue of $388,000,000, and an ordinary expenditure of $349,0'00,0>00, it will be seen that during the fiscal year 19191920', the Government, after meeting all ordinary expenditure, including an increased amount for interest account and pensions over the previous year totalling nearly $'39,0,00,,000 has a surplus of approximately $ S<9',0 OiO.'O'O'O' over ordinary expenditure to apply to capital expenditure.
As I have said, on the face of it it would seem as though, leaving aside for the moment the enormous debt created by the war, and taking ordinary expenditures only, this country's finances were in a prosperous condition; but I am sorry to say that the facte are in direct opposition to the state-

ment made by the hon. minister. Before going further, I wish to eay, in order to avoid any misunderstanding, that I do not for a moment question the truthfulness of the statement made by him in so far as that statement is derived from the books of hie department. But those books do not tell the whole truth. Technically they do; practically they do not, as I will demonstrate in a moment. The Minister of Finance says that we have a surplus of $39,003,000 over ordinary expenditures. On the contrary, I contend that we have an enormous deficit on both ordinary and extraordinary expenditure. I eay further that the financial statement this year is the most discouraging that has ever been submitted either during or before the war.
A few days ago the hon. member for 'Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) brought out the fact which, so far, to my knowledge, has not been controverted by the Government, that our revenue is composed of two parts, and that if we take the whole of our revenue we should compare it with the whole of our expenditure. In other worde, we have our ordinary revenue, and we have our extraordinary revenue, or the revenue which ie derived from the iwar taxes. The extraordinary revenue in this case, according to . the figures given by the hon. member, was $ 11-8.000,000 for last year. Consequently if we subtract this amount, our ordinary revenue, instead of being $388,000,000, becomes $270,000,003, so that instead of having a surplus of $39,000,000 we have a deficit of $79,000,000.
I will now make a comparison between the expenditure'and revenue for this year and the expenditure and revenue for past years. I have prepared a statement which is based upon the Budget speeches made during the last five years. Those items, Sir, tend to prove that not only are we not meeting our expenditures, but that we have this year at least a deficit; and if we take the accounts as submitted by the Minister of Finance we might find that we have had a deficit in each of the past years. For instance, he has told us that $337,000,000 was lost by the fact that the country could not get anything from the items composing that sum. These items in past years served to demonstrate that we had a surplus; but now that they are stricken off they serve to demonstrate that instead of having a surplus each year we had a deficit.
It had been my intention, Sir, to speak at greater length, but at this time of the night I do not think it would be reasonable for me to proceed further. The Government should by all means try to meet the country's expenditure .by its revenue, and in order to do that its first duty, in my estimation, would be to see that no public service be subsidized. I mean that no public service should have its deficit made good from the Treasury. In England, where there was a deficit in the operation of the postal service, the postal rates have been increased. In Canada the postal service has also shown a deficit, but the service in connection with which there has been the greatest deficit is the railways, and I submit that in order to make good this deficit the Government should increase the rates. Each public service should pay its own expenses, and until we make up our minds that this shall be done I do not think that we can achieve any practical results.

Mr. Speaker, I may say in that connection that I was told that I came on next; I have had the place for some little time. I certainly do not want to interfere with anybody else.
I was about to remark that it was not my intention and it is certainly not my intention now, to discuss the Budget in detail, the time being two-thirty in the morning. But I have a few observations to make in connection with two of the main features of the Budget.
In connection with the direct taxes that have been imposed by the Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) I may say that I have no quarrdl with the Government in regard to the principle of direct taxation; I think that the idea is all right. Taxation along this line should have been imposed long before this. It is not with the general policy in this matter, however, that the chief difficulties may arise; any criticism in connection with these taxes would rather be in respect to the carrying out of the idea and the collection of the tax in a satisfactory manner. These taxes have been named "luxury taxes." It seems to me that that is a wrong name. Either changes will have to be made in the taxes, or some other name will have to be applied to them. The ques-. tion of boots and clothing has been discussed; I am, in the main, in conformity with those who have criticized the minimum taxable on these goods. But I would like to add another to this list; there is a matter of furs. Out in the West particularly, and perhaps in the northern part of the West, the wearing of furs is not a luxury; it is the next thing to a necessity. I think I am correct in saying that the minimum amount upon which the tax is collected in connection with fur garments is $100. It is absolutely impossible to get any kind of fur garment that is wearable for that sum or even

considerably more. I assume that this matter will be discussed in detail when we get into committee; doubtless the minister will see his way clear to make some variations in connection with some of these matters.
It has also been drawn to my attention that this tax bears very heavily on some particular lines and will have the effect of putting out of business some people who are engaged in perfectly legitimate businesses. I shall not go into the details at this time.
There are also in connection with this taxation onerous conditions. I would refer the Government to the case of canoes which are required by prospectors, miners, trappers, traders and so on. As I recall it, the tax must he paid when the canoe is purchased, and on proper representations being made that this article is to be used for trading or other purposes of a similar nature, the tax may be refunded. I would simply point out to the Finance Minister that when a trapper or prospector gets a canoe he usually wishes to take it a long way from the place of purchase. It is notorious that questions of refund are slow in being dealt with, and if a man purchases a canoe in this -way it is not likely that he will'be able to get a refund of the tax until perhaps a number of months afterwards. This works upon the purchaser an unnecessary hardship and I suggest that arrangements be made by which the purchaser may hand in to the merchant at the time of purchase the declaration referred to, in order that he may take the canoe away and have the whole transaction closed.
But I take it that the chief difficulty in connection with a tax of this kind is in its collection. As in the case of the income tax I am afraid that the collection of this tax will be unduly expensive. A telegram from the Retail Merchants Association of Canada has been handed to me since I sat dowm here this evening. It is despatched from Vancouver, and reads in part as follows:
Proposed luxury taxes meeting with intense antagonism from public and will result in many proposed taxes not being collected unless Government employ host of inspectors and collectors entirely out of proportion to amount collectable. Retail trade unanimously of opinion only logical way to collect such tax is through manufacturer or importer.
Without entering upon any further discussion of this matter, I wotfld be inclined to agree with the terms of that telegram.. I sincerely hope that when the matter is taken up in committee some variation will be made to meet the difficulty. I may say 
that I personally know that these taxes are not in all cases being collected. Not very long ago I had a conversation in the city of Winnipeg with a merchant whom I know well,-he does not live there. He told me -by the way, this was some days after the proposals of the Finance Minister had been brought down-that he had paid no attention up to that time to the directions contained in the Budget, had collected no taxes, and did not know when he was going to start. I am afraid that this situation is altogether too common throughout the country and that there is going to be great difficulty in collecting these taxes under the plan as proposed. I trust that some more efficient scheme will be worked out under which they can be looked after with the least possible trouble and expense.
The main feature, however, of the Budget proposals so far as I am concerned is the question of the tariff. Unfortunately I was absent from the House at the time of the delivery of the Budget Speech. I was on business in the West, public business, as a matter of fact,-and did not hear the speech delivered, nor did I have an opportunity of listening to a number of others which were delivered shortly after. But I have read some of these, and from what I have read and from what I have heard since my return I have come to the conclusion that the one outstanding feature in connection with these tariff proposals is that the Government is committed to a policy of protection. It may be called by various names, but it would appear to be what has hitherto been known as the National Policy. I gather this more, perhaps, from statements made by members on this side and from press comments than from any statement made in the Budget Speech itself. The speeches of hon. members on this side would appear to convey conclusively to my mind that that is the stand which the Government takes and which members on this side wish them to take. As to newspaper comments, I simply refer you to the following -which appeared in the Ottawa Journal shortly after the Budget Speech was delivered:	It said that the Unionist
tariff policy as shown in the Budget
-is the Ola N.P. brought up to date and camouflaged a little to break the news gently in certain quarters.
The disguise is not very apparent to me, the policy sems to have been quite openly stated. I wish to state frankly and fairly to the House that I am not in favour of this policy; I have opposed it on numerous

occasions hitherto, and I see no good reason for changing my attitude at this particular time.
On the other hand, I am not a supporter of a strictly free-trade policy. I do not think there is any issue at the present time between extreme protection and absolute free trade. Some time ago, in a debate on the railway question, I had the temerity to state that I did not think the matter of public ownership was an issue at all, notwithstanding the fact that very learned speeches were being delivered pro and con. A similar situation exists now. We speak of protection and of free trade; but the issue at the present time is between those who believe in what may be called adequate protection or reasonably high protection and those who believe in a tariff mainly for revenue. I differ from the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Hen-ders) in'his designation of what protection really means. There is a vast difference between a tariff for revenue with incidental protection and a protective policy which is mainly intended for protective purposes and which may or may not result in revenue for the country. I do not think there ,are in this House any hon. members who are in favour of the kind of protection which has beep described as being as high as Hainan's gallows, or if there are any, there are very few; nor have I heard anybody come out and out absolutely in favour of a free-trade policy. Therefore, I take it that when hon. gentlemen refer to free trade, they are referring to that term in its popular meaning or usage which covers a tariff for revenue purposes with, perhaps, occasional incidental protection. Ais has been pointed -out by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis), the issues in connection with matters of this kind have been somewhat mixed. I have listened carefully to some speeches, and I find the effect of tariff, prohibition, slow work, lack of proper machinery and various other things have all been confused. The hon. member for Neepawa traced out the situation as regards Germany and pointed out just wherein protection affected the situation and wherein the situation was affected by other things. I had intended to discuss that question, but I will not do so as it has already been dealt with effectively by that hon. member.
One hon. member, in speaking the other day, pointed out that England had a policy which was bringing about her decadence, and from which serious results were likely
to follow, and he said that the last thing that Canada should do would be emulate that policy. Before concluding his speech, if I recollect correctly, he produced a list of about four pages of articles in which he showed that Great Britain had imposed a considerable tariff, and then intimated that that country was not such a free-trade country as we had been led to believe.
Another matter in which some confusion existed was with regard to the situation in England in connection with steel. An hon. member, in' discussing the question of production of steel in Great Britain, the falling off that has taken place there and the question of whether Great Britain would ever again be able to compete with the United States and other countries, stated to me that one of the reasons why steel production in Great Britain was not on the same plane it had been formerly was on account of what is generally known as " slow work;" that the workmen did not produce as well nowadays as they did in previous times, and in that connection he referred to an' incident regarding a certain piano firm which did business in London and which was compelled to quit because it was not able to manufacture at a profit. He intimated that this firm had stated, in an announcement which was made when they decided to go out of business, that whereas before the war started it used to take five men a certain length of time to manufacture one piano, it now took twenty-three men to do in the same time the same quantity of work; or in other words, it cost more now to polish	a piano
than it did to manufacture a whole piano several years ago. Soane people in relating that incident would give us to understand that this piano firm went out of business and that the steel situation was bad, simply because of the trade policy of the country-which would be most erroneous.
I might discuss the question of mergers, balance of trade and so on; but at this time I shall refrain from doing so. What stares us in the face at the present time is the question-what is to be the trade policy of Canada from now on? This is a period of reconstruction; we are at present confronted with new conditions, and the question that we must face is, as I said, whether we are to continue the old policy under these new conditions, or find a new policy which will be more appropriate to present conditions. Whatever may be said in favour of policies that existed in times past, what we need at the present time is

a policy of development along natural lines where the maximum revenue will result with the minimum of burden on the shoulders of the poorer classes. In this connection we, of course, must take into consideration the experience of other countries. It is in order for us to adopt those schemes which we think have been beneficial to other countries and have worked out well and to avoid the mistakes that other countries have committed. To adopt the policy of the United States holus-bolus, because the United States appears to have prospered, or on the other hand to adopt the policy of Great Britain, because a certain amount of prosperity has resulted therefrom, or to refuse to adopt the policy of Great Britain because some hon. gentlemen have said that conditions in that country are not as good as they were some time ago, is not reasonable. The fact that Great Britain has a free trade policy may or may not mean anything in particular to us. The fact of the matter is that conditions in Canada are so entirely different from conditions in England that, while Great Britain might prosper under one policy, Canada might be more prosperous under another policy. At the present time the main industry in Great Britain-how that came about I shall not discuss-is that of manufacturing, whereas in Canada the basic industry is undoubtedly that of agriculture. The situations are entirely different. In the United States great industries have been built up. It may be that the protective ^policy of the United States has had a good deal to do with the building up of those industries, although I am not so sure about that. It is quite possible that those or even greater industries might have resulted had the policy been different. At any rate it is unquestioned that in connection with the greatest industry in the United States, namely, that of steel, during a considerable period of time, owing to the protective policy, consumers of steel had to pay almost twice as much they otherwise would have had to do. This was the period of in the system in the United States, so that the railways cost a great deal more than they otherwise would have done, and it may be that we now sec a reflection of this in recent developments railway construction in the United States, It is a very complex situation and I only wish to reiterate that we cannot credit the progress that the United States has made to their tariff. There are various other considerations to be taken into account. I have not the paper with me, but I read in the 
Saturday Evening Post of a few weeks ago an editorial in which the writer expressed the opinion that it was questionable whether the policy pursued by the United States in the past had been in the best interests of that country. He raised the question concerning the situation of the agricultural class and the opinion was expressed that the farming community had undoubtedly suffered as a result of the tariff policy in that country. The policy for Canada is to make the most of the natural advantages which we have. A father raising a family does not now do what I am told was done in days gone by. He does not allocate one member of the family to the ministry, another to law and another to the military profession and train them up for these vocations irrespective of their particular adaptability to the .work which they will have to perform. The responsible father who has a family to look after now uses his utmost endeavours to ascertain for what particular occupation each child is peculiarly adapted, and he trains his children along the lines in which they give evidence of adaptability. If this policy is pursued there will be experts in the country, and that is what we desire; and the same kind of policy that is adopted by an intelligent father with reference to the education of his children should be followed in the development of the country. Agriculture being the basic industry of the country, the industry which we are in the best position to prosecute, the industry in connection with which we are in advance o-f every other country, or at .any rate, of most other countries, qualitatively and in extent; the western plains of Canada being the future granary of the world if a proper policy is pursued; it would seem to me that the line of action this House should take would be to do everything possible to take the utmost advantage of that and allied industries in connection with the development of the natural resources of the country. The farmer asks no help in this connection, but it is only fair and reasonable that no handicap should be placed in his way to hamper his operations. He does not ask for protection, but on the other hand it is unfair that other industries should be protected to his disadvantage. I fail to see the logic of the situation. Items of food, the necessities of life, should be on the free list, or be so dealt with as to have a minimum of tariff against them. In this respect I desire to draw the attention of the House to some of our natural resources, especially minerals. Next perhaps to the farming industry, mining is the most

important of the natural industries of the country. A short time ago I had on the Order Paper a resolution to which I intended to speak, but I did not get the opportunity to do so and I withdrew it, and that is one of the chief reasons why I am taking up some time to-night. That resolution was as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is in the interests of Canada in connection with the development of its natural resources that all machinery required to mine, recover and market the mineral resources of Canada (including oil and gas) shall be placed on the Free List in the Customs Tariff.
I .am of the opinion that it would be the part of wisdom fo.r the House to pass a resolution of that kind and for the tariff to he modelled along those lines. At the present time a great many instruments used in mining are on the free list; but, in the first place, some of the instruments in the tariff schedules are not free, and secondly,
I would point out that there have been developments within recent times evolving new implements whidh are not provided for by these tariff items. I do not propose to go into the details; I will simply say that one imporant mineral that does not seem to have been properly taken into account in these tariff schedules- is oil. It is questionable whether machinery that is- indispensable to the discovery and development of oil can be brought in under the schedules as they at present stand, and an amendment in this connection sihbuld undoubtedly be made. That, however, is a matter that can be taken up in committee.
Something has been said m regard to the political aspect of the situation in connection with the tariff. Now, when I say that I am opposed to the policy that has been put forward by the Government, which means that I shall perforce vote for the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), I must state that I shall t-ake this step simply on the merits of the case, and because I think that the amendment is- along the correct lines which Canada should follow at the present time. As to whether it will be put into operation by one party or the other is a matter that does not concern me now. The fact that -a certain party was in power for a member of years and did not carry out all its tariff pledges is not a sufficient reason why I should vote against principles which I have held for some time, and support a tariff policy entirely at variance with my ideas. .1 am free to confess that I was not satisfiied with what had been
done under the Laurier regime in regard to relieving the tariff burden, and I might state that had it not been for the reciprocity policy introduced in 1911 I am satisfied that I would not have supported that Government at that time. I might discuss this question at further length, but time forbids.
There is, however, a question which I desire to take up and which is indirectly connected with the Budget, and that is the question of the development of our natural resources; and I wish particularly to refer the transfer to the Prairie Provinces of their natural resources. I had intended to discuss this- matter in another way but I -have not hitherto had an opportunity to do so, nor is it likely that I shall otherwise have that opportunity. There can hardly be too much stress placed upon the importance of developing the natural resources of the country. The results of su-ch development are numerous. One of them is the creation of wealth. We have heard a great deal about the illimitable resources of Canada .and of what use they will be in paying off our national debt. But if they are left in their present state they will be of no advantage to us. Only by full development can they be of advantage to the country directly or indirectly. I am thoroughly convinced that we have great and almost-boundless resources, although as a matter of fact they have never been carefully surveyed. That as my impression, and I regret that time does not allow me to give an account of some of these to the House. But the point remains that unless a policy is adopted which will result in the development of these resources we might as well not have them at all. In the second place this development will provide raw materials as the basis for industry. Such development will help to -adjust exchanges and if these resources which exist in the western provinces are developed and industries spring up as a result thereof, we will have a situation in the west similar to that which exists in the east.
My point in connection with this is that the Government does not appear to have any policy regarding the development of these important resources. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) introduced a resolution in which he called upon the Government to formulate a definite policy in regard to these resources.
A necessary prerequisite, in my opinion, to the formulation of a -sound policy of development is the settlement of the ulti-

mate control of the natural resources of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. An anomalous situation exists at the present time with reference to these resources. The situation is such that development is being retarded. The question is up in the air. The provinces will not do very much in connection with these resources because they do not control them and the Dominion does not take such steps as we think advisable because it is in the realm of probability that the resources will ultimately be transferred to the provinces.
I have been endeavouring to find out where the Government stands in this, connection. Before the election of 1911 the present right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), made the promise that these resources should be transferred to the provinces. I did not hear the promise made myself but I. take the word' of the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) who stated in the House a few weeks ago that such a promise had been made. The transfer of the resources to these provinces was definitely promised in the manifesto issued by the party of which the present Prime Minister was then the head. In the House some time ago I asked some questions in regard to this matter and these are the questions and answers:
Mr. Campbell:
1.	Was any definite promise ever made by the Government or any member thereof to transfer the natural resources of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to these provinces?
2.	If so, was any condition attached to such promise which would affect other provinces by way of re-adjustment of subsidies or otherwise?
3.	Is the Government of the opinion that the other provinces have any interest or equity in the resources of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba?
4.	If such promise was made is it the intention of the Government to carry out the terms thereof? If so, when?
5.	If not, does the Government not think that it would be in the public interest to make a definite statement to this effect and thus put an end to the uncertainty which at present exists?
6.	Is the proper development of the natural resources of these provinces not being seriously handicapped and retarded by delay and uncertainty in this connection?
Sir George Poster:

The necessity of fair terms and the interests of other provinces arises from the fact that when the provinces in question wrere created in 190>5 a special subsidy in lieu of those resources was granted them.

Referring to the last question I can hardly understand the 'Government making an answer of that kind as it seems to be palpable to any man studying the question that the situation must result in the retardation of the development of these resources. The difficulties in the way created by this situation have prevented development in certain important instances.
This question was discussed thoroughly at several meetings of western members on this side of the House and a committee was named to draft a report. That report, which was submitted to these Western members and adopted, unanimously, has been placed before the Government. It is as follows:
Ottawa, April 30, 1920.
Report of Special Committee on Natural Resources.
In the opinion of your Committee the question of the development of Canada's natural resources is one of the most important before the country at the present time. The financial condition of Canada makes a definite policy in this respect of immediate concern.
A necessary prerequisite to any satisfactory national policy herein is the definite settlement of the question of the ultimate control of the natural resources of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
The Government has recently announced that it is, and has been, its policy since the Government was formed to transfer to these Prairie Provinces their natural resources, on such terms as will be equitable to the other Provinces, and is apparently deferring action in this connection until such time as representatives of all the Provinces shall meet together and agree on a scheme or basis of transfer.
Such agreement is no nearer being reached than it was eight years ago, nor does there appear to be any likelihood of a settlement of the question being arrived at in this way in the future, near or remote.
The question is solely one between the Western Provinces and the Dominion. The Dominion Government is possessed of all the data in connection therewith and is in the position, and is the proper party to work out and1 present to the Western Provinces for acceptance an equitable scheme or proposal for the transfer to these Provinces of natural resources of said Provinces according to the promise made to them by the Prime Minister.
Therefore, your Committee recommend that representations be made to the Government that it is imperative in the interests of the country as a whole, and particularly with reference to the development of its natural resources, that the question of the ultimate control of the natural resources of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba be settled immediately, and that the Government take the necessary steps forthwith to have this done.
Respectfully submitted.

' As I said before there is no string to the promise of the Prime Minister as far as I ean learn or to the pledge contained in the platform of the party of which he is the leader. If there were any conditions attached it is up to the Prime Minister to state definitely what they were. If conditions have arisen since that promise was made which prevent him from carrying out the promise, or if conditions have arisen which make it advisable that these resources should not be transferred, it is in order for the Prime Minister to make a statement and then we will know what the situation is and shall be governed accordingly.
The question cannot be settled until it is settled right. It may be a debatable question as to whether these resources should be handed over to the provinces or not but certainly there is no question as to the desirability of having the matter settled definitely and having it' settled
3 a.m. right away. There has undoubtedly been serious loss caused by the delay. Whether they shall be handed over to the provinces or not now, the transfer must ultimately take place in order to put these provinces on the same basis as the other provinces of the Dominion. Therefore, if eventually, why not now?
It has been argued that there is a legal reason why these resources must be handed over. It is that the British North America Act did not contemplate such a thing as. a landless province. It is contemplated by the British North America Act that all the provinces shall be on an equal footing. Such is not the case in this resipect. There is a national reason why these resources should be handed over because it is in the interest of Canada as a whole that this matter should be removed from further discussion. The question has certainly been complicated by bringing the other provinces into the discussion. My contention is that the other provinces have no right to a say in reference to the disposal of these resources than the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have to a say in the disposal of the resources owned and controlled by any other province. A mistake was made by calling the other provinces in for consultation in the first instance. The Government should take the matter in hand forthwith and submit a proposal to the western provinces which the Government itself believes to be a satisfactory and reasonable one and in accord with promises made.
If it is not accepted it means that the resources will stay where they are and this Government can then formulate a policy in regard to their development. I had contemplated dealing with one or two other questions of interest to the Western country at this particular time, particularly the Hudson Bay railway, but as I may have an opportunity to do so- again, and as the hour is very late, I shall defer any further discussion until another time.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this hour of the morning to occupy very much time, but I feel that I would not be doing .my duty to my constituents or to myself if I did not put myself on record in connection with the Budget.
In the first place I wish to' congratulate the Minister of Finance upon at least making an effort by direct taxation for the purpose of paying our way, instead of going on increasing our enormous national piebt. The Minister of Finance being a man for whom I have a great regard, I am sorry he was not been better advised as to how he should have placed that direct taxation. Had he followed the platform of the National Progressive party he would have adopted measures which would have secured a further considerable sum, and at the same time would have given relief to the great masses of the people, both urban and rural, at present oppressed by the high cost of living. For there is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that if the tariff were reduced to a much lower level than it is to-day on many articles it would not only reduce the cost of living, tout would bring in a great deal more revenue-that is revenue to the Government and not to the manufacturers.
A few minutes ago the member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) spoke of some protection which the fanners were being benefited by. I am not sure of the figures which he quoted, but as far as I could gather the hon. member meant to say that some $700,000 of revenue had been received in connection with this article produced by the farmers. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is not pro^ tection for the farmer in any shape or form. It is protection for the packer. In proof of that I may say that the farmer sells his meat on. the open market, and if this money is collected from cured meats shipped into Canada it goes to prove-knowing as I do that our cattle and hogs in the West are very often shipped to the American markets-that the American packer is buying the Canadian product, curing it, and shipping it back into Canada again which.

after paying the duty, appears to me, is not very creditable to our Canadian packers. However, I will let it go at that. The member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) said that the present Budget is the greatest combination of free trade and protection that he has ever known. The protection is there all right, but up to the present I have been unable to discover just where the free trade part of it comes In. In so far as I can see the protected interests are not interfered with in any way by the Budget.
I feel that the best thianks of the Progressive party are due to hon. gentlemen on the Government as well as on the Opposition benches for the attention given to our group, as the attacks in which they have indulged, unwarranted as they are, will have the effect of focusing public thought on the policy and platform of the Progressive party on which the broad light of day is always welcome. I particularly wish to thank the hon. member from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) for the new name, "Levites" which he has applied to us. The Levites, Mr. Speaker, as no doubt you are aware, were the spiritual advisers and leaders of the children of Israel when they were going through their period of re-establishment and reconstruction-in other words they were the "little leaven which leaveneth the whole lump," and I congratulate the hon. member upon his keen foresight in recognizing the same distinctions, comparisons and functions for this small but growing group. But, Mr. Speaker, I would rather, very much rather, be a Levite than a parasite, for the name parasite is the most fitting I can think of for those who draw their profits from the consuming public of this country under the shelter of a protective tariff.
I do not consider it wise to go into the different phases of the Budget, as they have been dealt with from almost every angle, but 1 would say that during 1a recent trip West I found continual adverse criticism with respect to it and I have received a large number of letters and telegrams along the same line.
I deplore the attacks made on the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), notably those made by the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), the member for St. John (Mr. Elkin), the member for Algoma Eiast (Mr. Nicholson), and the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). Apropos of that I wish to read a short editorial from the Winnipeg Tribune of May 29, and in passing let me point out that this paper

is owned and operated by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) whom I congratulate upon the fairness ot the article, and I cannot help but think that this expresses the feeling of many- -in fact a large majority-of those sitting ;n the Government side. The article in question is headed, "Unfair Talk," and reads as follows :
Charging that Hon. T. A. Crerar, leader of the Farmers' Party, is "associated with the Bolshevik party"-as a press heading puts it- or characterizing the farmers as a dangerous class, politically, is just common, ordinary rot.
Ton; Crerar has been able to hold) his head up among the people of Western Canada for many years. And there is no sign that he is other than a good Canadian, and worthy of the highest respect. Mr. Crerar takes his stand, out in the open, on certain fair political ground. He invites attack, and he may be open to attack, but away with the petty, personal stuff. It is cheap and unworthy in a discussion of the great principles which should enter into the government of the nation. Let us have fair play and the elimination of all pettiness of spirit.
This goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that the people who really know the hon. member for Marquette, and are honest about it, will not stand for the tactics adopted by the members whom I have mentioned, to say nothing of the cheap, petty spirit which they have displayed, and to which, Mr. Speaker, only the rules of the House prevent me from giving its proper name.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to diverge a little from this much-hashed subject, and to say that in some measure I agree with the Hon. Minister of Finance, and I admire the spirit of optimism which he displayed when he said that he does not believe that the job ahead -of this country is a bigger job than Canada can look after. I certainly agree with him in that, but T believe we will have to change our method of procedure, and instead of developing our unnatural resources-as we have been trying to do for the last forty years-we should give a little attention to our natural resources. Mr. Speaker, it is now a few days more than thirty years since I landed in Canada. At that time Canada had, roughly speaking, a population of five millions of people. I was an optimistic young man in those days, Mr. Speaker, and had great visions of Canada's future. In thirty years' time the natural increase should have brought ou rpopulation to at least eight millions. During that time we had three millions added by immigration.
Yet, Sir, we find to-daj'- that our population is still in the neighbourhood of eight millions. Surely this is proof positive that something is radically wrong. And my theory is

that when a wrong is proven to exist, we are not doing our duty if we do not try to set it right.
In the Northwest-and I have particularly in mind that part of Saskatchewan which I have the honour to represent, and which I might say in passing is one of the largest constituencies in the Dominion, and in which during my 30 years farming there I have not seen- one crop failure-there is room for millions-in the northern portion of my riding, there are vast stretches of unoccupied lands, almost unexplored lands, which await the railway and the settler- I put the railway first, because we have already extended settlement from the present railways as far as it is possible to operate. Many farmers are hauling their wheat 30 and 40 miles, from north of Prince Albert, and the same may be said with regard to Melfort and Tisdale; in fact, wheat is coming to Tisdale from a distance of 50 miles. Another thing that the people of my constituency ask for is the completion of the Hudson Bay Railway.
It is well known that there are great stretches of land fit for grazing and there is plenty of hay for stock extending for 150 miles north of Prince Albert. I am so confident of the possibilities of this northern country that I have persuaded the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to attach a fully qualified man to the Indian Treaty party which is going north from Prince Albert in a few days, so that he may report on the agricultural and other natural resources now lying dormant there.
In conjunction with this, I believe we should institute a sound immigration policy, making a speciality of the immigrant who is willing to settle on the land, knowing that the development of the mines, forests ' and fisheries will naturally follow. And I may say that we have all of these natural resources in the territory which I have described. But to enable these natural industries to prosper, it is essential that if they cannot be given encouragement, they at least should not be penalized by having a heavy customs tariff on their instruments of production. That is where the platform of the National Progressive party would come in with advantage, and I have no hesitation in recommending it to the attention of this House as something which much better suits the needs of Canada to-day than either the present budget or the amendment. However, Mr. Speaker, as the rules of the House prevent a further amendment, which this party would gladly have offered along the lines. I have mentioned, I find myself
in the position of having to choose between two evils, and as I believe that the sentiment of the people, both urban and rural, whom I represent coincide with my own views I shall vote for the amendment.

It is my misfortune, Mr. Speaker, owing to a sore throat and other disabilities, thait I have been unable to take any part in this debate until this late hour, and therefore I do not wish to unduly delay the House as I know hon. members are all anxious to vote and get home. But the fact remains that this is the most important Budget that has been brought to the attention of this House since 1879, and as we have reversed all our previous ideas and preconceived notions of how taxes are to be imposed, I do not think that a little further discussion on this question will be lost to the House or to the country.
It is extremely fortunate that ever since Confederation one of our great parties has been opposed to the policy of developing our natural resources, and has been inclined to favour free trade, and on almost every occasion on which it has appealed to the country it has done so in a spirit of antagonism to our manufacturing interests. But the question now before the House is not a question of protection versus free trade, because the Government of the day has virtually conceded every tax that would be necessary if we had free trade in this country and I have not noticed very much objection taken to them by either of the two parties on the opposite side of the House, while on this side I have heard speeches tending towards the view that after we have had an investigation of our tariff by a commission of necessity the tariff must be reduoed.
The hon. minister (Mr. Rowell) who spoke this afternoon informed the House that the tariff had been reduced to 14 per cent. In that connection I want to remind hon. members that when a merchant imports goods into this country he is allowed to deduct 5 per cent from the value of his invoice, and that -advantage reduces the protection of our manufacturers generally to something like 9 per cent,, which is lower than the protection in force in any other country.
Now, while that may seem very nice to some people, a very large body of public opinion in Canada do not look favourably upon any such proposition. There is a remnant of one of our great historic parties, which to my mind constitutes fully sixty or

seventy per cent of our voters, composed of National Policy. men. And the National Policy is just as different from the policy that has been advanced by this Budget g.s day is from night.
