As a Liberal-Conservative who has sat at the feet of Liberal-Conservative leaders from Sir John downwards, I can only say that I was very much surprised that the views of that party have not been put before the House, and that is the reason I desire to-night to re-state the tariff principles of the Liberal-Conservative party. That question will certainly be fought out at the polls,-the Liberal-Conservative party will be united, and before another year will be prepared to meet all corners and to reaffirm its old policy, which I now wish to read to the House.
The National Policy is not a policy of high protection; nor is it a policy of free trade. It is a policy which is directed towards collecting by means of a t-ariff, the revenue needed to meet the national obligations and utilizing that tariff to foster native industries. Let me read the resolution that Sir John A. Macdonald in 1876 moved in this House:
That this House regrets that the financial policy submitted by the Government increases the burden of taxation on the people .without any compensating advantages to Canadian industries ; and further, that the House is of the opinion that the deficiency in the revenue should be met by a diminution of expenditure, aided by such adjustment of the tariff as will benefit and, foster the agricultural, mining and manufacturing interests of the Dominion.
If I were moving a resolution in opposition to the Budget now before the House I could not better express the sentiments of the Liberal-Conservatives. The fact of the matter is that the Government did not bring its proposals to make.such a drastic change in the fiscal policy of this country before its supporters in caucus or otherwise. It brought those proposals before the House, and I for one was not consulted in the matter whatever. It is true that a certain element in the community seems to have risen in its wrath and said, "Let us tax somebody." We have been runfling to programmes and to crusades against this body and that; first the liquor sellers, then the race-horse men, and now the manufacturers aie the unfortunates at whom everybody is aiming a blow. I regret that very much, because this country can never become great unless our industries are balanced and we have more team play. Our last trade statement will show that our manufactured exports ran over $500,000,000 as compared with about $250,000,000 of agri-

cultural products. Agriculture although important is not everything.
It has been said in order to pay for this war we must produce. Suppose we all started to produce agricultural products, where would we sell them? Europe is getting back on its feet again. France is not going to take very many of our agricultural products this year. Great Britain has increased her agricultural production to such an extent that she now produces over fifty per cent of what she requires for her own use, whereas before the war the figure was only something like thirteen per cent. The United States has also increased her production-and the farmers of our West are clamoring for greater markets. To'my mind the only way that we can get greater markets is by fostering our manufacturing industries so that we will consume in our own country what we ourselves grow. We must look forward to >a greater population, a greater manufacturing population. Most unfortunate for us has it been that one of the great parties has constantly opposed the manufacuring interests. Some hon, members may deny that, but the fact is that a threat made by one of the parties has been hanging over the manufacturing interests of this country since Confederation and has prevented millions of people from coming into Canada and helping to build up our industries. The time will come soon, in a few months, when this question will be settled, I hope finally, at the polls. They had that same row in the United States. The question was fought out finally there in 1897 and nobody of any standing in the United States will now preach the policy of free trade, even with Canada.
I have heard a lot of free trade talk in this House. A number of members are in favour of free trade. I said to myself why do hon. members not- go and preach free trade in the United States? Thefact-is that the United States has not shown any evidence that she desires free trade with us. It is a question of wasting your sweetness on the desert air. If you do not get free trade in everything with the United States, then what do you have? You have what Sir John A. Macdonald characterized as "Jug-handled" free trade; they have your markets free, and you cannot get into their markets. Why, hon. gentlemen opposite of the agrarian group know very well that we granted free wheat and flour to the United States in order to receive reciprocal advantages only a few years ago, and the moment our grain started to flow into the United States, what happened? They placed an embargo on

our wheat, and I should not be surprised if they did the same thing again this year. What is the use of talking folly and nonsense. The great economist, Mill, states that in a case of that kind there must be countervailing duties. He says:
"The only mode In which a, country can save itself from being a loser by the revenue duties imposed by other countries on its commodities is to impose corresponding revenue on theirs."
That, .Sir, is the National Policy. Sir, I am a stout enough Canadian to say I am not going to pay ' for police protection, light and sidewalks to give a free market to the Americans of over $800,000 a year.
May I ask . my hon. friend where we would sell our Western cattle if it were not for the American market?

My hon. friend may think that he must sell his Western cattle in their market, but his greatest danger to-day is from the market of the Argentine Republic, and so with the Americans. If my hon. friend goes to any grocer in Ottawa he will find that grocer's windows filled with pressed beef from the Argentine Republic, sold in opposition to his beef.
Will my hon. friend answer the question?

You should be able to sell your beef to good Canadian working men; that is what you should do. That is the proper policy and the one that should prevail in this country.
Now, I want to say a word about cotton. Hon. gentlemen do not know that when the American States seceded from Great Britain such a thing as. cotton growing was unknown in the United States. At the time of the Federal settlement when Hamilton and Washington were discussing things, the chief products for export of the United States were indigo and rice. From Wilmington and other places in the United States petitions came to the first .Congress setting forth that the people could not sell indigo or rice in the markets of the world owing to the competition of India. The cotton goods that were used in the United States were then made from cotton grown in India-and that threat still hangs over the United States. Well, what happened? The United States Government, under Hamilton, placed .a duty of two cents a pound on raw cotton, and from that day to this there has been a duty on cotton entering the United States. They do not even now go around asking that the duty be taken off.
And what happened then? The Government provided the people of the United States with seed for cotton and to-day the bulk of the cotton of the world is grown in the United States. That is how they fostered agriculture. There are men to-day in this House who know very well that prior to 1878 the principal exports of this country were potash and wood products, lumber, etc. There was no such thing as export of grain, -nothing to speak ,of, at any rate. The farmers were not growing grain because the Americans were exploiting the lumber in the province of Ontario. American companies were operating here. They brought in their own horses, harness, sleighs, oats, flour,-everything that they consumed in their camps. They brought them in from Michigan and other adjoining states, and the Canadian who was trying to grow wheat Gloats or hay on his farm in Ontario could not.sell a pound of it to the Americans. ThSy were exploiting this country just as they would exploit it to-morrow, if you give free trade. But it is not the American with whom you will -have to compete in our factories here in the near future; it is the Japanese. I believe that to-morrow fifty per cent of the jobbing houses in Canada will have a Japanese salesman in their office trying to sell them goods which ought to be manufactured here. And with Japanese labour at 20 to 30 cents a day, how are we going to manufacture in that case?
But, reverting back to the question of the tariff, the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald put a duty on wheat, and immediately there was established in this* country the wheat industry, which runs parallel to the cotton industry in the United States and is our principal industry. Hon. gentlemen who arrived in this country only a few years ago did not know that; did not look into the history of things and consequently then-views on this question are distorted. I say without hesitation that if you throw open the market for wheat, in a few years your market for wheat will be taken away from you just as your market for cattle would be. Millions of dollars' worth of meat products are brought into this country-
Is the hon. member ready to answer the question, that I put to him? Where would we sell our cattle if it were not for the United States market?
The market for the surplus meat of Canada is Great Britain.
For cattle?

Everybody knows that the United States produce enough cattle and meat for themselves. The statistics show that. All that the hon. gentleman and his friends get so far as market is concerned is what we call a " slush " market. They " slush " into the American West a certain amount of grain and cattle and the United States automatically slushes that same amount into the markets of Europe from the East. There is no real demand in the United States for these products. They just milk the Canadian. There is not a pound of meat produced in this country that could not be sold abroad, given the proper conditions and markets. Why is it that we buy so many millions of dollars' worth of hog products in the States? Why is it that last year we purchased over a million dollars' worth of oats in the States? They grow lots of oats in the West. These are facts that you can verify by reading the blue books. Nearly a million dollars' worth of plums were bought by Canadians in the United States last year-and the Lord knows that Ontario and British Columbia are good plum-producing countries. Why, our markets are wide open to these people, and our greatest danger to-day is not our war debt, but the debt we are running up with the United States, which now amounts to a billion dollars, on our trade balance. Some hon. members speak about wishing to go to work and pay off the war debt immediately. In Great Britain, the Napoleonic war debt is not paid off yet, and it will not be paid off for four hundred years. If the Government would not pay attention to people who are giving them wrong advice, the proper policy for them to pursue would be to fund the war debt and to set about reducing taxation instead of increasing it.
The National Policy is so different from this Budget policy that I cannot understand how any man who has made any study of political economy could get- the two mixed. The National Policy was a policy of " indirect " taxation. If a man in Canada ten years or twenty years ago offered to put direct taxation on the people of this country, he would be taken out and hanged, or else he would be sent to an asylum and bis wife would be given a divorce. No political party would dare to go to the country with a policy of direct taxation.

They are getting
braver now.
.

I do not know about that. My opinion is that when hon. gentlemen go to the country and hear what the people have to say about the taxation proposals and all the free-trade discussion that is carried on in this House, there will be one grand scramble; they will be " going to the country," like the lobster about which we heard this afternoon, going to war backwards.
Dissolve Parliament tomorrow and let us have an opportunity.

If Parliament were dissolved to-morrow, hon. gentlemen on that side of the House would not have ten followers, because they have not taken a stand against taxation and the country is getting tired of this yelling for taxation and the slogan:	" Tax my neighbour, tax
everybody."

What about the
Progressives?

I should be glad if the
hon. gentleman would let me alone for a moment. I think I have answered him very satisfactorily. The farmers do not bother me and I represent a riding that has more farmers in it than the hon. member has in his riding. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not dare to oppose taxation, why? Because their policy is free trade, and if they give free trade, they must put on just such direct taxes as are proposed in this Budget. I am giving the old-time Conservative answers to all those proposals. I do not believe in direct taxation-
Hear, hear.

I believe in lower indirect taxation; I do not believe in direct taxation. This country will rise in its wrath, and it will smite in a few months everybody who proposes to impose direct taxation, and for this reason. Direct taxation is not at all necessary. The Government assume that there is going to be a demand for a big amount of money yet on war account, and, therefore, we must of necessity have heavy taxation. A luxury tax may be all right, because nearly every nation has to-day a luxury tax, but I think we were very ill-advised in putting a luxury tax on what I might call a key industry. One of our key industries is fur; millions of dollars worth of fur are produced in Canada, and we should not tax furs out of business. The country never (was as prosperous as- it has been for the last few months, and who has been making it prosperous? The manu-

facturers by their work and the industrial workers in the factories. Everybody is getting down to a position where he wants to do what everybody wants us to do, namely, " produce." If we are going to succeed, we must produce and sell more than we buy. Hon. gentlemen opposite want us to throw our barriers down and buy everything from the United States; Japan or Germany; hut to-day we are nearly $1,000,000,000 in debt to the United States, and that is the reason why the exchange is so bad. How are you going to remedy the situation? If an hon. gentleman from the West wants to buy a cook stove, and, in particular, an American cook stove, he may get it a few cents cheaper, but the people of this country will be paying for that cook stove for years to come on bonds and things we sell to the United States. That is not a fair deal for Canada, and I do not see why I should be asked to open the markets of my country and hand them all over to the United States free of duty while we are taxed to death in this country. That, however, is what hon. gentlemen opposite wish to do. The Americans are not so gracious to us; and if hon. gentlemen opposite want to give open markets to the United States, let them preach that doctrine in the United States and they will get a very warm welcome; they will be chased out of that country, because the United States have not one man of standing who will rise in his place in one of their representative bodies and propose free trade with Canada. The great danger of all this agitation for free trade is that it is sectional. Anybody who studies the history of the United States knows that the question of free trade and tariff was fought out there in the Civil War. This was due to the agitations of the planters in the South who all wanted free trade, whereas the northern manufacturers took the other side; they wanted' tariffs. The ultimate result of the whole business was this, that the country landed in civil'war because both sides of Mason and Dixon's line were stirred up over every political issue that could, be stirred up, until finally they flew at each others' throats. If you look over the West you will find, that on the issue of free trade versus .protection the next time possibly Saskatchewan may bring back a majortiy here of free traders, but none of the other western provinces will do so. An hon. gentleman who spoke to-night said that Winnipeg was manufacturing for New Zealand, and so might every city in the West do if we
had a proper system of protection. Why, this country has not begun to protect her industries as it should1. We have not given any protection to the glass industry in connection with which we might have thousands of workers in this country. We have ample natural gas in Saskatchewan, and we have good sand there to make plate glass and window glass. The West imports millions of dollars' worth of window glass, although all the elements, necessary to make the glass are to be found in that part of the country. As regards crockery and china-ware, kaolin, feldspar and all the other elements requisite for making crockery, just as the crockery is made in the United States, are to be found in the West; but instead of making that crockery in the West, we have been importing it from Japan and China to the tune of millions of dollars a year. Every year there come through British Columbia trainload after trainload of Japanese and Indian silk, going where to be spun? Not in Canada, but in the United States. That is an industry which we might foster, because we have ample power for the looms in this country. We could have thousands of silk spinners in Canada if we chose, because our power is cheaper than it will ever be in the United States, and the great secret of developing industries, in the future is cheap power. We could put electrical power on the spindles at the price of one dollar a ton for coal, and how can the United States or any other country compete with us as regards power?
The question of tin plate has been discussed in this House. At one time, away back in the early nineties, 'the United States manufactured only a few tons of tin plate; but McKinley put a tariff on tin plate and since then nearly 75 per cent of the tin plate of the world is manufactured in the United States. If you look up the statistics, you will find that inside of three years after the United States protected tin plate and went largely into its manufacture the Welsh price of $4 a hundred pounds was cut to $2 in the American markets. A few days ago II quoted from the Iron Age, and (I pointed1 out that, the United .States Steel Corporation and other companies were selling goods there cheaper than in England or they sell them abroad. Is that a sign that protection is a failure or increased prices?
We have passed through this war, and I give all hon. gentlemen opposite and hon. gentlemen on this side credit for desiring in their heart of hearts to see this country succeed. I am not one of those .people who ascribe wrong motives to anybody in that

regard; I never offered a word of criticism to hon. gentlemen as to their motives, and I do not desire to do so. But we are going into the future, and there are two. roads for us to follow. One road is to smash and ruin and to be, as we were before the war, lame ducks in the face of the world. There is another line of policy for us to pursue, and that is a line that is going to build this country up with population and to make it the seat of the great Anglo-Saxon people of the future of whom we form part, because this must be the cradle of the future expansion of Great Britain. We are the premier colony, and for those reasons we must try to do our best.	-
Now, what are the elements that make for success in a country? First of all, a country to be great must have resources, and there is in the world no other country that has greater resources than we have. The only thing Canada requires to round this country out is tropical fruits and foods that are necessary to round out our ration, as it were. Many people have tire idea that the United States contains all those tropical fruits and things. They say, look at sugar. Why, the United! States has only a few townships down in Louisiana that grow sugar that will crystallize. All the tropical fruits that come here, the oranges and bananas, the oils and the co-coanuts, come from the British West Indies, with very few exceptions by way of the United States. We are this week in conference with representatives of the British West Indies, and in this connection I may point out a remarkable fact. In 1910 the United States made a treaty of reciprocity with Porto Bico, and at that date, if my memory does not fail me-and it seldom does- the foreign trade of Porto Rico was $7,000,000 a year. Last year-Porto Rico now being a part of United States territory-its foreign trade was over $75,000,000. If we entered into some reciprocal arrangement with the British West Indies I have no doubt that this country and the West Indies would benefit to the tune of at least $200,000,000 a year. Jamaica is far richer than Porto Rico and so is British Guiana, and we could carry on a mutually beneficial trade with those colonies direct. The tropical resources are all that we need so far as material things are concerned.
Our next need is an intelligent population and I am satisfied that we have such a population. We may quarrel somewhat over our political views, but after all is said and done, I think we are all desirous of seeing the country succeed, no matter what 
our political or economic views may be. There is no doubt that we have an intelligent population, for the war has proved that fact beyond the slightest doubt. When it came to doing anything of importance in the wat the Canadians, either mechanically or from the point of view of courage and endurance, were the equal of any other race in the world. No one will deny that. Now, having these elements, the next thing -we need in order to develop a great country is to have a wise and paternal government.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members may see something humourous in that statement, but let me say that you cannot have a government run by Bolshevists and Internationalists in any country. Do you want to be Internationalists ?
No.

Then accept my view.
When I say paternal I mean national. It must be paternal, because the hand of the Government must assist every interest that stands in need of assistance. Hon.. gentlemen forget that when the Western farmers were in trouble this Government went freely to their assistance with seed. It also rendered aid to the inhabitants of the chief city of Nova Scotia in its hour of trial. The Government, I say, must be national and mhst do everything in its power to build up all the industries of the country and see that everything is kept on an even keel and given fair play. If time allowed me I could tell the House what I consider that the Government should do. In the first place, I think the Government should impose a tariff such as would encourage industry. All this row for free trade has prevented any new industries from being established in this country for the last fifteen years. You cannot point to one single industry established here even by reason of the Avar. Why, the industry established for the making of shells,.owing to the political agitation for free trade that was carried on in' this country, was compelled to take its machinery out of Canada; and it Avould be a brave man indeed who would start a new industry here. Furthermore, I want to tell hon. gentlemen that there is not a large industrial concern in Canada to-day that has made any money within the last ten years that is not building factories in the United States. Take Hamilton, and you will find that one of the largest concerns there, that made millions out of the manufacture of shells, when it wanted to start up a new factory, did not build it in Hamilton hut

put up a great plant at Albany, under protection, in order to carry on a business that should be conducted in Canada. Then there is the manufacture of motor tractors.
Those are luxuries.

Does the hon. gentleman say that traction engines are luxuries? They may be luxuries around the North Pole and in the Peace River country, but I can inform the hon. gentleman tha/t traction engines are highly essential industrial machines. However, what I have stated is a fact and instead of these industries being solidified in Canada, and instead of a dozen new industries being started here to keep Canadian people working in the factories, those who would undertake to establish industries are driven out of the country. Members supporting the Government have been charged with taking Government contracts. Well, Mr. Speaker, members of the House have a perfect right to take Government contracts for the companies they represent if they desire to do so, and if you go back over the history of the Liberal party you will find out where such contracts used to go. I could take the hon. member for Victoria to Rosedale in Toronto and show him a fine lot of beautiful homes in one of the loveliest places in the whole of Canada or, for that matter, in America. There are beautiful homes there, and the hon. gentleman will find that sixty per cent of the owners are Liberal manufacturers. They knew very well that under the hon. gentleman who was leading the Liberal party they could get into any line of business they wanted to develop and even start new industries and they would get ample protection. They were sure of the Liberal-Conservative protection.

No.
Mr. .CURRIE: I could name a dozen industries which the Liberal party started in this country and which are flourishing.
No.

There is no use in protesting against that statement. I have been in politics too long not to know what has happened. Now, the policy hon. gentlemen are taking now is to Oppose the manufacturers, and I am glad that they are showing their colours. We have never failed to meet them on that issue and they have never failed to go down to defeat; and when they come along at the next election with their anti-manu'facturer policy we shall leave them in a worse position than they were in in 1911. I was criticising the Government, 194
Mr. Speaker, and it does a government good once in a while to be criticised a little.
Hear, hear.

I must say, however, that I never heard hon. gentlemen on the other side criticise their party. There were just three solitary bolters on the reciprocity pact and that is all the sentiment they could show. Now, I disapprove of these taxes because they are in opposition to the old National Policy. In the first place, the luxury tax tends to make a class distinction. It divides the country into two groups. It distinguishes the man who can afford to wear a $50 suit from the man who can wear only a $35 .suit.
Or none at all.
I am afraid that the hon. gentleman, politically speaking, will not have any suit at all after the next election. It also divides the ladies into two classes.
Oh, oh.
It divides them into the class that can wear silk stockings and the class that can not.
Order.

But hon members opposite have cried for this tax. Their newspapers from one end of the country to the other clamoured for the luxury tax, and it seemed that every one wanted to tax every one else and every one else's wife and relations.
Oh yes ! they want a tax on every one else; they want to tax their wives' relations and everybody but themselves. They have declared themselves to be the great party of taxateers. They want to conscript wealth. They want to take a certain amount of the money that everybody in this country has. They are an aggregation-I would not like to say-of socialists but their press is largely dominated by socialistic editors.
Oh, oh.

Yes, I know what I am talking about. We had the leader of the Opposition talking about the depopulation of the country. If the honorable gentleman will go to the Library he can look up the literature of the Fabian Society of Great Britain. That is a socialistic society. And he will find pamplet after pamphlet about rural depopulation. That is one of the things that the socialists are preaching in order to subvert the loyalty of the farmers of Great Britain. They are preaching depopulation. They are doing the same here. The other is reforestation. You will get



socialistic pamphlets edited by Bernard Shaw and Sidney Webb on reforestation and rural depopulation. These are the topics they spring upon the farmers of Great Britain, and their followers are preaching the same doctrine to our own farmers. What is the result? The result is that some of the farmers are seeing red.
Oh, oh.

Yes, that is quite right. They are preaching subversive doctrines of that kind, and there is no anewer from the other point of view the public will respond. They will respond to the socialistic preaching. It was the preaching of subversive doctrines that brought about the French Revolution.
Oh, no.

Yes. I am quite willing that hon. gentlemen opposite shall be tax-ateers but I want them to remember one thing and that is that in so far as people of the Anglo Saxon breed are concerned they do not take kindly to taxes and they have not done so from the days of John Hampden. Charles the First found that they did not like taxes. There was a tea party at Boston because they did not like taxes. Yet, if you are going to have free trade, you must have these taxes. I have listened patiently to find out from the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who is the boss free trader here-
Hear, hear.

1 have been listening
patiently to hear how he was going to make up the revenue. An hon. gentleman who rises in his seat to criticise anything should be prepared to criticise constructively and to say what we are going to do. But, he has not shown yet how we are going to raise the revenue. And we do need revenue. Another idea that seems to have come from these hon. gentlemen and which they have been preaching from one end of the country to the other is that of a tax on sales. I am sorry to see that some of my hon. friends from the west are going in for the sales tax. I believe in Adam Smith the same as do hon. gentlemen who are free traders. Adam Smith never was a free trader. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster) never believed in his Adam Smith or he never would have brought this question up before the House. It shows his ignorance. I am going to ask the hon. member for Brome to tell us if Adam Smith has ever favoured a tax on sales. I will wait for his answer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Brome has already spoken.

The hon. member for
Brome is so fond of bluffing and talking about free trade I want to show that he does not know anything about it.
Order, order.

Now I will read Adam Smith on this very tax on sales question. I think it will show that I am right in the position I have taken: Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations, says:
Ifi consequence of the notion that duties upon consumable goods were taxed upon the profits of merchants, those duties have, in some countries, been repeated upon every successive sale of the goods. If the profits of the merchant importer or merchant manufacturer were taxed, equality seemed to require that those of all the middle buyers . who intervened between either of them and the consumer should likewise be taxed.
That is what we are doing.
The famous aleavala of Spain seems to have been established upon this principle. It was at first a tax of ten per cent, afterwards of fourteen per cent, and is at present of only six per cent upon the sale of every sort of property, whether movable or immovable, and it is repeated every time the property is sold.
Surely that is the tax we have here.
The levying of this tax requires a multitude of revenue officers sufficient to guard the transportation of goods, not only from one province to another, but from one shop to another. It subjects not only the dealers in some sorts of goods, but those in all sorts, every farmer, every manufacturer, every merchant and shopkeeper, to the continual visits and examination of the tax-gathei-ers. Through the greater part of a country in which a tax of this kind is established nothing can be produced for distant sale.
What is going to happen to the farmers in the West? -
The produce of every part of the country must be proportioned to the consumption of the neighbourhood. It is to the aleavala, accordingly, that Ustaritz imputes the ruin of the manufactures of Spain. He might have imputed to it likewise the declension of agriculture, it being imposed not. only upon manufactures, but upon the rude produce of the land.
Now, if hon. gentlemen who are such great students of economy have read their Adam Smith as some perhaps have-the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who is not in the House is a great authority on Adam Smith-they would have seen this reference. I think that possibly Adam Smith is right there. I believe this form of taxation is wrong. There is no other country that has adopted this method of taxation. It remains for us to stand out prominently as the country that has adopted- it.

The one great thing we need if we are going to reduce our per capita debt Is population. The easiest way h>
reduce our per capita debt is to double our population [DOT]which will produce for us. If we are going to get population we must make this a cheap country to live in and call a halt on direct taxation.
Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

Exactly, that is true. Well, then, who pays the duty? It is not pleasant to have to pay a duty to get in here, and that is what will happen if you impose a countervailing tariff. How are you going to develop or build up this country if you adopt free trade? Are you going to open your markets and let the American farmer walk over and exploit you whenever he wants to? I am a good Canadian, and' I believe in a national policy, and for that reason 1 do not approve of anything of the kind.
(Now, I have to offer some criticism to the Government. II pointed out to them the difficulties with regard to this new tariff. This is a new imposition of taxes of which I do not approve. I do not wish to object to it now, however, for this reason: I think it will do this country good to have a few months of this free trade tariff. I think, then, that from one end of the country to the other they will be so sick of trying to collect this taxation, of trying to finance this country directly out of their pockets, that they will be quite willing to take sides with the good, old Liberal-Conservative party, and wipe out all the people who want free trade and who want to turn us over to 1941
the Americans. The hon. member for Victoria, Alberta, will get a run for his money up in his riding-do not forget that.
I always did.
Yes, and you came through the last time, did you not?
Yes, I did.
Because the hon. member is such a good' fellow. I never heard, him open his mouth before in this House to interrupt.
ll would like to ask the hon. member a question.
Another county heard from.
We are hoping to hear from the county of Simcoe. The hon. member says he has no faith in the new tariff. Will he vote against the Budget?

I said that I had no faith in a free trade budget, and that this is a free trade budget-I have no hesitation in saying that. The Government have stolen the clothes of hon. gentlemen opposite-that is the trouble. That is why they were stunned for two or three days after the Budget came down. They were so stunned that they did not know which way to turn. What will happen will be this: These taxes will go to the country and the question that will confront hon. gentlemen will be to put up an argument to show how the money can be raised under free trade except in! this way The country will ibe so sick and tired of ali this taxation that they will be glad to vote into power the party that goes in for low indirect taxes, the party of the National Policy.	.
Why do you not go to the country?

Go; to the country ! If we went to the country the hon. gentleman would never see the inside of this House again. He knows that he got into Parliament at the last election by subterfuge, and we will see that he does not get in by subterfuge again.
Order.
That is true, he stole the riding.
I did not do any such thing.
Any man that comes into this House on an anti-British cry is not fit to be answered.
Ran like a hare.
Yes, he ran like a hare, and hunted with the hounds.
'Somebody else did that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. (It is quite in ordler for hon. 'members to ask questions with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor, but I must ask those who desire to do so to do the House the courtesy of rising and addressing the Chair.
There is no necessity to intervene, Mr. Speaker. As far as answering hon. gentlemen opposite is concerned, 'I am quite capable of doing that.
He is the man.
My hon. friend (Mr. Ped-low) desires an answer. He has asked me if I would not oppose the Budget.
Will you go to the country?
With respect to the hon. member who is interrupting, I know what is wrong with him. I do not need to tell him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I understand the hon. member for Simcoe correctly, he is proceeding to answer a question which has been asked by the hon. member for South Renfrew.	[DOT]

After that I am sure he will allow the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) to put his question.
Mr. '.CURRIE: I have already said the hon. gentleman from Lunenburg is not quite himself, and consequently the best thing for him is not to ask any more questions.
I will ask the hon. gentleman if he is willing to go to the country and prove whether I am right or whether he is right.
Go to the country?

Yes.
Mr- CURRIE: Wild horses could not drag the hon gentleman to the country. This is the best job he ever had. We are accustomed to that kind of talk. The hon. member is new to this House, but I have been here a few years, and while I have often heard clamours to go to the country I never yet saw an Opposition or a Government that wanted to do so very gladly. Now, returning to my hon. friend from South Renfrew, I said I would answer his question. Yes, I will support the Budget most gladly; I want the hon. gentleman and his friends to have a taste of a free trade Budget of their own medicine.
Yet you have no faith in it.

I have no faith in it? I have faith that it will act like medicine- sdmilia simitibus curantur. That is the reason I intend to vote against the amendment of the hon. .member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding). It is very nicely drawn in order to try to put a little salt on the tail of the agrarian bird. My hon. friend drafted it before he had heard the Budget and then-old parliamentarian that he is-he was very intent on his speech. I watched him memorizing his speech almost, instead of listening to the Budget. Had he listened closely to the Budget I do not think he would have spoken as he did. He could have put up a much better criticism had he done so. As far as his proposals are concerned they are nothing but camouflage. It is a great platform which they produced last year. I Temeahber sitting in the chamber when the late hon. member for Brant, Mr. Paterson, in 1911, got up to speak on the reciprocity question. He put his hand down into the tail of a long, black coat, and produced a document, and said solemnly: "I have here before me the platform of the Liberal party of 1895. I was in Toronto this week and went into a store and found this platform that the Liberal party had in 1895." That was it, 1894 or 1895. Somebody asked him, " Did you find it in a pawn shop?", and the House roared'. Evidently the platform that the Liberal party promulgated last summer has been relegated to the pawn shop and a new platform has been produced now. It is no't quite so drastic as the free trade platform of last year. That would not be acceptable, especially in Quebec which my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) knows very well. You could not get him to adopt free trade as they have it in England, even if you tried. Now I said that I intended to vote against the amendment because I think that it is pure camouflage, it does not strike at the questions or the issue straight. It has made no objection to these taxes which to my mind are obnoxious. As a red hot Liberal-Conservative they are obnoxious to me. Of course the country must have its dose-it is getting it and will get it-and for that reason I am going to vote against the amendment and vote for the Government s Budget. I think every Liberal-Conservative here will do the same thing, and we will try it out. We will try it out on the dog, and see what the people think of this direct tax free trade tax policy. I am satisfied that in the next session of Parliament, when it

meets next fall, there will be some new light on all these questions, and there will be a new alignment. Hon. members, whether they follow the Liberal-Conservative party or not, because of its political leanings towards protection, will have some new light. I have followed this National Policy question.
I have heard it discussed by Sir John Macdonald, by Tilley, by Edward Blake, and by Sir Richard Cartwright, who was perhaps the ablest critic of that policy my hon. friends opposite ever had, and I was never otherwise than convinced that the National Policy was the proper policy for Canada. To-night I proclaim that same old policy- not the "National Policy made up to date," but the old National Policy that I read to the House to-night which discloses the best way in which we can carry on the business of this country. If you want the people of a country to be happy and contented, you must not grind their noses off with taxes.
I had a call from several soldiers the other day in the city of Toronto. They called me up by phone and they said, " Colonel-
Colonel!

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. They called me up on the 'phone and said:	" They are charging us
35 cents luxury tax on a string of ribbons on which we hang the medals that we won in the war." That is a fact, and that is one of the things we will have to remedy. There must be some adjustments made when these resolutions are discussed in committee. The proposals so far are too drastic, and we must modify them. But if I had my way and were playing politics, I would say:	"Make it a little bit
stronger, and let the Grits and Free Traders have a taste of their own medicine." Then you would see everyone of them squirm. I know many of them are good men, engaged in manufacturing and other interests, and yet some of them will speak on the platform in favour of free trade and practice protection to beat the band. And I am sorry to say that some of our Conservative friends will advocate protection to " beat the band," and then practice free trade when they want to get something into the country a little cheaper. The only effective way is to face this thing squarely. So far as I am personally concerned, I do not pledge myself to follow this policy further than the next session of this House, for the simple reason that I am opposed to it in principle. And the only reason that I shall vote for it now is that I want to see hon. gentlemen opposite get a dose of their own medicine.
Mr. P. R. DuTREMBLAY (Laurier-Outremont):	Mr. Speaker, at this late
hour of the night-

It is morning.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	-well, at this
early hour of the morning I do not propose to make any lengthy address on the Budget and the amendment before the House, but there have been many manifestations of objections on the part of the people of the city of Montreal whom I have the honour to represent, and therefore I feel that at this juncture it is my duty to offer certain criticisms and objections to the proposals of the Government.
The eloquent speeches delivered by hon. members on this side of the House has proven beyond doubt, I believe, that the proposed taxes will not decrease the high cost of living. On the contrary, I believe that they will increase that already high cost, and at the same time will act as a deterrent on our trade and commerce. One of the principal reasons for the high cost of living to-day is that we have less production than formerly. There is an old English saying that if you put more taxation on dogs there will be fewer dogs. And if you put more taxation on industry, there will be less industry, and consequently, less production. That, I believe, will be the effect of this one per cent Sales Tax and the ten per cent Luxury Tax-they will be detrimental to the consumer and will discourage production, and it seems to me that the Government should have devised some other means of taxation to fill the gap between expenditure and revenue.
Recently the manufacturers and retailers of Montreal met and expressed their dissatisfaction with the taxes proposed by the resolutions of the Finance Minister. A report of that meeting which I have before me states:-
Much criticism was expressed of the new Budget proposals at a meeting of representative members- of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the one per cent sales tax being particularly objected to as likely to repeat itself until it became a burden to the consumer.
This one per cent tax is only apparent, and in practice it will undoubtedly work a hardship on the consumer. In my opinion the Government should make the manufacturer pay this tax. In many cases the manufacturer sells his goods to a jobber or a wholesaler, who in turn sells them to retailers, with the result that the one per cent will be paid two or three times on the same goods, and of course eventually the

consumer will have to bear the burden, which in some cases will be aggravated by the luxury tax of ten per cent.
To-day there is a general clamour throughout the country against the minimum values above which this luxury tax becomes operative. At a meeting of those interested in the clothing trade held in this city on the 25th of May a resolution was passed urging that the minimums be raised, and I presume the hon. Minister of Finance has received a copy of the resolution. In the United States most of these articles that we consider as necessaries of life are exempted from such taxation. I have in my hand a list published by the Toronto Star Weekly, I believe most hon. members have received a copy enumerating a large number of articles which in the United States are exempted from any luxury tax.
I hope that when these proposals are taken up in Committee the Government will see that these minimum amounts are raised so as to protect the public. I may point out that in the United States the tax on luxuries is paid not on the whole amount of the purchase but only on the amount in excess of the minimum. But under the present proposals of the Finance Minister if you buy a pair of shoes at $16 you have to pay the tax not merely on the amount in excess of $9, but on the whole purchase price of the shoes, that is, $1.60. Surely that does not meet the purpose of the taxation as stated by the Minister of Finance, who states that it is a tax on luxury only. I say again that I hope this matter will be adjusted in Committee so that the middle classes and the poorer classes in this country may be protected.
I should like to say a word with regard to the income tax. I know that members on both sides have advocated still further increases in the income tax. At the last session the Government saw fit to bring in further income tax legislation putting our system on the same level as that of the United States. Our income tax law was already a very drastic measure, for this country has not the means, as has the United States, to recover the money in all cases. The raising of the rate on certain amounts to five per cent may bring in a few million dollars more, but the effect on the country will be detrimental, because there will be a tendency on the part of investors not to put their capital into enterprises in this country. It is true that we need capital for the develpoment of our industries and our different enterprises, and this in-

creased income tax will have an influence upon their decision to invest their money here. I warn the Government that they should stop moving in that direction, if they desire not to interfere with future investment of capital in this country.
It has been shown that we must economize in order to meet our expenditures. The argument of hon. members on the other side in support of the imposition of these taxes is that revenue is needed. I have no doubt that their principal aim and intention was to get revenue and not to increase the already high cost of living, but this legislation, while not decreasing the cost of living, may injure trade and commerce and decrease production. It may be said that it was necessary to impose these taxes in order to get the $70,000,000 that was needed to meet our expenditure. But it would have been easy for the Government to cut down expenditures in the different departments by at least $25,000,000. I am confident that if all the ministers got together they could cut down expenditures to that extent and save that amount to the ratepayers of the country. Then, there is the Department of Railways, where there is a deficit of $48,000,000, and the Post Office Department, where there is also a deficit. It seems to me that these departments should be so administered as to pay for their own operation. Why charge to the ratepayers of the country the cost of operation and the amount of deficits resulting from the operation of the National Railways? Why not charge such rates on these railways as will make them pay their own way? Wiry not have those who use the railway pay for the service which they get? The same applies to the Post Office. In this way the Government could get another $50,000,000, and this, with the $25,000,000 that I have mentioned, would make up the $75,000,000 that is required for this year.
The speech of the Minister of Finance, as I said a moment ago, was more a general taxation of all persons and things in the country than a statement of fiscal policy. Actually, business men in Canada do not know what kind of a tariff will come into effect next year, and that condition of affairs is harmful for trade and commerce and it is harmful for manufacturers in this country to be in such a position. It is all very well for the Government to say: We will appoint a commission; but this commission should have been appointed immediately after the war. Two years ago I believe the Government were asked by the Opposition to appoint such a commission;

but this year I hope this commission will be appointed; that it will be independent of party politics; that it will be permanent, and that it will be composed of business men of different classes of our community and representing different provinces of the Dominion. I hope they will go throughout the country, studying the needs of every manufacturer and making comparisons with similar industries in the United States and in England. There is no doubt that today certain Canadian industries have too much protection while others do not have enough. I hope all these matters will bp adjusted, and at the same time the needs of the other classes of the community will be taken into consideration.
After the war the people of this country expected that the Government would put into effect some kind of programme of reconstruction, and the fact is that the Government said that they were remaining in power for the purpose of reconstructing this country. So far I have not seen any reconstruction programme, but I hope in this reconstruction they will not forget the important industry of shipbuilding that was started during the war. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that in this country we have a new industry of shipbuilding comprising different shipyards that employ more than 25,000 men, with an additional 25,000 or more other men w'ho are employed in manufacturing articles that are essential in shipbuilding. We are to-day in a position in Canada to obtain from France and Spain many contracts for building ships at a good profit, and people from these countries are coming to this country asking the owners of shipyards to accept contracts for ships. As a matter of fact, the world is short of ships at the present time; the shipyards of England have contracts for building shlips sufficient to keep them busiy for more ,than five years, and the same condition exists in the United States. During the war the Government, under the present Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), took some steps toward creating this industry, and to-day we have a large number of skilled men able to create a permanent shipbuilding industry. A few days ago I had occasion to meet some gentlemen who are building ships, and they see in the near future the possibility of employing in this industry on a permanent basis more than 60,000 workmen and if you consider that there is an average of five persons in a family, that means about 300,000 people. There is a new industry that we must not let go. The programme of the Government is nearly completed; and if the Government do not
protect this new industry and see that it develops, the result will be that in the end it will disappear. A large amount oi capital is invested in this enterprise, and I wish to draw particular attention to this industry of shipbuilding which is of national importance to Canada The last question that I wish to bring before the House at this early hour of the morning is one that is near my heart, namely the German indemnity. It has been hard, I must say, for the last couple of years, to find out from the Government much information regarding this important question. In Canada we have made very important financial sacrifices in order to help England in this war, and according to the memorandum sent by the Government to Sir George Perley, the representative of Canada in England, the amount claimed by Canada is about $1,800,000,000. But according to the understanding between the Allies and Germany, the only indemnity to which the Allies would be entitled would be for damages which have been incurred on account of the violations of the laws of war. If we examine the memorandum prepared by the Government and sent to our representative in England, we find that Germany would be entitled to pays us only about $31,000,000. If that be true, such an amount would be a joke. According to the understanding arrived at between the Allies, France is to receive 55 per cent of the indemnity that they will be able to get from Germany; England is to receive 25 per cent, and the balance will be divided between the other nations that took part ton the side of the Allies in this war. The aid that we gave in this war was given especially and solely to England, and that was the understanding on which this country went into the war. The principle that was put forward was that when England was at war Canada was at war. This principle, which was enunciated by my late chief Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was .accepted by the right honourable the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), and we went into the war to assist Great Britain, making sacrifices that brought us very nearly to the verge of bankruptcy. It is not necessary, Mr. Speaker, that I bhould state the immense, the appalling liabilities which this country has incurred by reason of its participtation in the war. The interest on our debt and pension amounts to about $160,000,000, which is about half of the entire debt which we had before the war, and this tremendous burden will have to be borne not only by ourselves but by our

children and our children's' children. We spent these vast sums of money and contributed our best manhood for the purpose of assisting Great Britain. But Mr. Speaker, it is not of the sacrifice of life that I am now speaking. That phase of the subject I shall not touch upon now. Let me say, however, that the monetary aid which we contributed! to Great Britain was given on an understanding from the Prime Minister that Germany would pay this country an indemnity that would cover every cent we expended and on that assurance Canada was prepared to spend its last dollar. Now, is England in a position to pay this country this sum of one billion and three quarters? A conversation is reported in the press in which Mr. C. W. Hingham, a member of the Imperial Government, is credited with the statement that England is not much worse off now than she was before the war and that her trade is very prosperous, the people in that country being able to go back to work in the factories. He goes on to state that an era of prosperity has now dawned in that country such as has neveT before been known in its history, and that the London market will once more be the gold market of the world. I believe that statement, Mr. Speaker, and I am glad that England has been able to recoup her losses and that her commercial possibilities are now so promising. By the treaty signed at Versailles Great Britain has received many advantages. Everyone is aware of the enormous sums which have been spent by the English treasury to maintain the British fleet so that it might compete not only with Germany but with all the other nations of the world, but these vast sums which she has had to pay in the past will be offset in the future to a great extent by the advantages which will accrue to Great Britain as a result of the settlement. Today England, through her ships, is still Mistress of the Seas and is in a better position, from the maritime standpoint, than any other nation of the world, as this member of the Imperial Government stated a few days ago.

Hear, hear.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that this statement is applauded so hartily by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, for it shows the loyalty which everyone of us feels towards Great Britain. Now, Sir, shall we not undeT these circumstances turn to Great Britain and ask her to pay to this country, if the German indemnity is not forthcoming, the sum of

one and three quarter billion dollars which we spent during the war? If the hon. Minister really had this matter at heart and, as he should do, gave to it his best consideration morning and night, we would probably obtain a great part of this sum from the British Government. But so far as we have been able to judge of the enterprise of this Government, they do not seem to give the question any consideration at all. It would be a matter of great importance to Canada, Mr. Speaker, if this amount were paid by Great Britain. We would wipe out our immense indebtedness and be in the position in which we were before the war; and it is but due to this country that something should be done to bring about this condition.
The amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is clear and precise, and I shall be pleased to support it when the time cemes.

Hear, hear.
Mir. DuTREMBLAY:	Some -hon. members -are applauding that statement. Well, I hope they will see their way clear to vote with us on the -amendment. In so doing they would, I can assure them, receive the heartfelt gratitude of the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite, Mr. Speaker, know very well that there is a general demand throughout the country that the high cost of living should be decreased, and they are well aware that the Budget as introduced by the Minister of Finance has nothing in the- way of relief to offer the -suffering -consumers-.
The Budget has been brought down by the Finance Minister, but we- know very well that he is not responsible -for the present financial position. I wish- to join with other hon. members in congratulating the Minister of Finance upon the manner in which he presented the Budget. He must be given credit for performing a hard task in bringing this Budget before the House. No doubt he bad considerable difficulty in bringing the different elements of the Council to an agreement upon this question. But it -must be remembered that this Budget does- not in any way lighten the burden of the high cost of living. Hon. members on the other side of the House know that there is a clamour from ocean to ocean against the high cost of living. We are here as the representatives of the people and we have to face the responsibility of dealing with the demand that the people have put before this Parliament. We must, by some kind

of legislation, act or deed', do something to diminish the high oast of Jiving. The amendment of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) meets the demand of the people of this country. I am glad that it comes from the 'Liberal party, which, with its splendid traditions, can be depended upon, when it again comes into power, to render justice to all the people of this country. When that time comes we will have a return of that .prosperity which the country enjoyed when the Liberal party was in power.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following this debate as it has proceeded day after day, I have been very much struck by the fact that there exists, in this House such a great variety of opinion on such an important and oft-debated subject as " The Tariff."
One would naturally expect that on a question such as this, one that has been to the fore almost constantly during the last forty years, there would be laid down certain distinct lines or principles, and that hon. members would have by this time .made up their minds where they stand on those principles. Such does not seem to be the case, however, and there seems to be as much variety of opinion as there -are members who speak on this subject.
First, we have the spectacle of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding), an avowed' free trader, making a protectionist speech and submitting an amendment, which demands a lowering of the tariff. Then we hear the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) making a .protectionist speech, insisting that his opponents have always been and are now inconsistent. He declares that he is and always was a protectionist, but insistently declares that he is a moderate protectionist. He places much stress on that word' '' moderate," and would have the country believe that at this time he is particularly moderate. He, however, is unfortunate in .qualifying the word " moderate " by saying that by moderate protection he means " such as we have bad in this country since 1867, which ranges anywhere from 15 per cent to 45 per cent (.page 2618). " Moderate protection with favour to none and justice to all" (page 2607)-is another rather paradoxical way in which he sets forth his position on this very important subject.
Again, we hear the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), who has always been an ardent protectionist, laying particular
stress on the " moderateness " of his views. He argues valiantly for protection, mercilessly denounces free trade, and1 then points with pride and words of commendation to the action of the present Administration in reducing the tariff on many goods to the point where protection is almost eliminated and placing many other articles on the free list. (Pages 2780, 2781 1
It was surely a noteworthy acrobatic feat to extol the merits of protection in one breath and praise the free trade tendencies -little though they are-of the present Administration in the next; it was a feat for which his mental acumen is particularly well fitted. 'It was with a great deal of satisfaction that I noted the applause from the Government benches, which greeted every point he made in respect to reductions in the tariff. When he pointed out that the Administration which had killed1 reciprocity in 1911 and imposed an additional per cent tariff during the war, in spite of the oft-repeated assertion that the tariff was too sacred to touch during war time; when he pointed out that this same Administration had' reduced the tariff on certain articles to as low as 12 per cent, and placed many more on the free list; when he showed that the present Administration had gone even further than reciprocity, the enthusiasm of his followers and the satisfaction which they showed would almost lead one to believe that at this particular time they would like to have the country believe that they are the free trade party after all.
Then we have the venerable Eight Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), whose whole political life has been devoted to the suppoit of a protective policy, asserting that after all the indirect method of taxation is not the best for the country, but that there should be along with it certain forms of direct taxation. I have no doubt that the right hon. minister was speaking what he had learned in his own long experience, and that out of the richness of that long experience he is gradually approaching the position which -we hold and the policy which we advocate of a greater measure of direct taxation substituted in part for our present indirect system.
There are those who believe in a high protective tariff and who. have no hesitation in saying so. They would surround the country with a tariff wall as high as Hainan's gallows; keep out foreign goods and smother our trade; their idea is that Canada should be a self-contained country, independtent of other nations and developing her activities within her own borders.

To all those, I -would' simply say that nations, like individuals, must live and grow and develop by producing and trading, and to throttle a nation's trade is to strangle her life at its most vital spot. They are the extreme high protectionists, and although they are at present being kept in the background, I feel that we have too many of them yet in this country. It is quite obvious that the high protectionist is being kept in the background, but it is equally obvious that he is with us yet, and that his hand still guides the fiscal policy of the present Administration, as it has guided the policies of every Administration for the last forty years.
Much is toeing made of the fact that the 7J per cent duties imposed in 1915 are now being taken off. Much is also being made of the fact that all the benefits of the reciprocity agreement of 1911 have been granted, but nothing is said of duties which still remain at 30 per cent and 35 per cent, and which bear heavily upon many of the necessaries of life. Nothing is said of those duties except another of the annual promises of tariff revision, and although we are given to understand that the revision will be along the line of moderate protection, there is nothing to indicate that the coming revision-if it ever does oome-will be downward.
Now, what are we to understand by moderate protection? That expression has been oft repeated by members of the 'Government and their supporters. It is a very indefinite term, I have no doubt purposely indefinite, intended to assuage the fears of the consumer that further burdens may be added to the things he must buy; he is given the cold Comfort that those burdens, whatever they may be, will be moderate and on the other hand, it is intended to inform the protected interests that their welfare will be looked after and moderate protection granted them; moderate protection which means " such as we have had since 1867 ", which runs all the way from 15 per cent to 50 per cent.
Time was, and not so very long ago, when the tariff as it exists in this country was called a high tariff or high protectior . That was when our industries were in their swaddling clothes; when they were infant industries. In this connection, it is well to note that an industry which has been in the infant -class for forty years and has not yet learned to -stand on its own feet, should be given some more heroic treatment than to be fed on pap. Those indus-

tries considered the protection afforded them years ago as high protection. Politicians refer to it as high protection; the people regard it as high protection. Now that they have grown great and prosperous, it i-s only a moderate dose and we are given plainly to understand that the same policy of protection is to be adopted toy this Administration in the future as they have followed in the past.
Now, it is well to have the issue plainly before us. This House has a right to know, and'the country should be told in plain language, the issue that is before us and the issue that must be decided upon by the country at no distant date. It is the question of continuing the policy of protection, call it " Moderate " or " High ", as against the policy of reducing our tariff taxation until the point is reached where the protective principle may be said to be eliminated and the tariff designed for the production of revenue.
I'Ee Minister of Marine -says that -the question is quite clear. Moderate protection versus- free trade; if by free trade he means the entire elimination of all- tariffs so that no revenue will be collected in that way, then he is quite wrong in his statement of the case. The question of the future will be a tariff designed to produce revenue and not hamper trade, as against a tariff designed to protect our giant infant industries and enable them to continue to fatten -and prosper at the expense of the Canadian people. Protection. is to be the policy of the present Administration and you may call- it -moderate which means all the protection, you can get away with and impose on a patient and long-suffering people.
This, as I understand it, is the issue before the Canadian people at this time. It is not, as hon. gentlemen opposite would have us believe a moderate tariff versus no tariff at all. I am somewhat amazed to find how very moderate indeed hon. gentlemen have become in respect to their profession of belief in the tariff. They have no doubt been keeping their ear to the ground and have discovered a strong definite public feeling in the country demanding lower tariff duties. That may explain why they fairly tumble over one another in their haste to explain all that they stand for now, or -ever did stand for, or ever will stand for, is a moderate tariff. They would appear to be very moderate indeed in everything except their language of denunciation of the farmers and labourers of this country.

It has always been the policy of those who wanted to secure tariff favours to obscure and camouflage the issue if possible. This policy has been consistently followed in the past and in this debate we see the beginning of another campaign of the same kind, but if we are ever to arrive at any definite solution of this question, there is nothing to be gained by evading the real issue. We must face it squarely and decide it in the light of conditions that obtain in this country at the present time.
Many hon. members have wandered all over the continent of Europe and America for facts and figures and conditions that would substantiate their contention. That, of course, may all be very instructive and interesting, and it is quite 'true that there may be much to learn from the experience of other nations and yet it is quite obvious [DOT]that deductions drawn from those statistics and conditions that obtain elsewhere may be very misleading. In fact several different and opposing deductions may sometimes be drawn from the same figures. To illustrate what I mean, let me refer to the speech made in this debate by the hon. member for Fort William. He was quoting figures to show the wonderful development of the United States during the last forty years. He told us how production had increased enormously along certain lines. He was quoting the figures of the development of certain industries in the United States in an endeavoui to show how the fiscal policy of that country had developed production in United States industries and agriculture. The remarks to Which I particularly want to refer will be found on page 2632 of unrevised Hansard. I will not make a long quotation, but will simply direct the attention of the House to these figures-the increase in the production of certain articles in the United States from 1880 to 1917:

increase of lead, from 100,000 tons to 600,-00i0 tons ; of copper, from 27,000 tons to 840,000 tons ; of cement, from 2,[DOT]000,000 barrels to 91,[DOT]000,000 barrels. The production of corn increased from 1.700,000,000 bushels in 1880 to
3.000,	[DOT]000,000 bushels in 1917; of cotton, from
6.000.	000 bales to 11,000,000' bales; cotton manufactures, from $192,000,000 in 1880 to $701,000,000 in 1914 ; production of phosphate rock, from 200,000 tons to 2,500,000 tons; of zinc, from 23.000 tons to '584,000 tons. The export of manufactured cotton amounted from $10 -OOO.OOO in 1880 to $136,-0'0>0,000 in 1917. The production of wheat nearly doubled in the same period.
Now, that, I take it, is a fair indication of the development which Would be produced by a protective tariff policy, and the conclusion the hon. member wished to draw
from these figures Was that that policy was a good thing for the United States because it produced that kind of development. I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the increase in the production of manufactured articles, such as cement, cotton goods exported, and so forth, was anywhere from ten times to- in the case of cement-forty times what it was in 1880, whereas the increase in corn and wheat wts not quite double. Now that is just exactly the kind of development that would he produced by a protective tariff. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman. But I would just like to draw this other conclusion from his own figures, that that is not an all-round well balanced development of the various activities on the other side of the line; and I submit that that onesided development is 'a main reason for the present very high price of commodities- in other words, the high cost of living.
And the same condition obtains in this country. Canada is of such vast extent ,and possesses such immense agricultural possibilities that we have as yet hardly touched the fringe of those possibilities; and in addition we have incalculable natural resources in our mines, forests and fisheries. Looking at the statement made by the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech, we find certain figures of the values of our manufactured articles and of the products of our farms, forests, fisheries and mines. In that connection I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that those figures demonstrate that the products of our manuf actories exceed the combined products of our farms, mines1, forests and fisheries. That, I submit, is the kind of development that has been encouraged by the protective tariff principle, and in my opinion it is not a well balanced development of our national activities. To be building up large enterprises in a country like this at the expense largely of the consuming public and to the discouragement to a large extent of our basic industry, agriculture, is not conducive to our national welfare.
Now, my opinion is not a mere theory, it is borne out by the facts. The idea of a protective tariff is not to produce revenue but to protect industry and to build up large industrial establishments; and that is just exactly what it has been1 doing. It has made certain industries profitable largely at the expense of certain other industries, with the result that both labour and capital have been drawn away from those industries which cannot be protected by tariff and have been attracted to those industries

which are protected and are thereby profited. Our census figures hear this out and show that for the last forty years, particularly in the greater part of Eastern Canada, theTe has been a steady flow of our rural population into the large urban centres. The reason is that the farmers cannot compete with those engaged in other industries for the labour that they require, and they cannot use capital to the same advantage.
In order to further bear out that assertion I would like to place before this House a few figures in relation to the dairy farming business in Ontario to show the rewards offered to the dairy farmers of this province during the last few years of high prices. I have here the report of a survey made in the county of Oxford by the Ontario Department of Agriculture under the superintendence of Professor Leitch, Professor of Farm Management of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph. For the year beginning March 1, 1917, and ending February 28, 1918, ia survey was made of 437 farms in the county of Oxford, the object being to cover the . whole financial operations for the year:
(1) To determine the true financial condition of the dairy farming business.
(2.) To determine the cost of production of milk.
(3)	To discover the features of the business that have the greatest effect in raising- or lowering farm profits.
(4)	To give suggestions for the most profitable organization of the dairy farming business, based on the conditions found on the farms which showed the greatest financial returns.
These are some of the findings:
The cost of producing milk in the county of Oxford during that year-
And let me remind the House that this county- is perhaps the banner dairy county of the province.
The cost of producing milk is a subject over which there is a lot of different opinions even amongst producers. As a matter of fact there has never been until the present any organized effort to find the exact cost of the product on a variety of farms. The information collected from the farmers in this survey gave the look-ed-for opportunity for an investigation into the cost of milk produced during each month of the year. These farms were devoted to the production of milk as their main business, therefore, each farm was treated as a manufacturing unit for producing milk. The cost of production, therefore, was made up on each farm of the following items: current expenses (labour, repairs, seed, feed bought, taxes, etc.), depreciation on buildings and machinery, interest on investment at seven per cent and $5-00 for the labour of each farmer himself.
That was the labour income allowed to each farmer in counting up the cost of producing his milk during that year.
TMr. Kennedy.]
Prom this total was deducted the amount received for crops, hogs, poultry and other miscellaneous sales. The difference was the cost of producing the milk sold. Of course, in many instances there were considerable profits from the sales of hogs, etc., but the effect was to reduce the cost of milk produced.
This is what they found:-
The farms which were not strictly dairy farms had slightly smaller labour incomes than the dairy farms. Therefore their milk cost them a little more to produce. We are safe in assuming therefore that the cost of producing milk in Oxford- county during the year ending February 28, 1918, was $2.20 per hundred pounds. This just equalled the selling price which averaged $2.19-1 per quintal.
During 1917-1918, a year of high prices for dairy products, the farmers in the banner dairy county of Ontario were producing milk practically at cost, only being allowed in figuring that cost a labour income of $500 a year.
A little later on a similar survey was carried on at the other end of the province, in the county of Dundas, another excellent dairying county. I would like to ask the House to notice the rewards that were being offered to the dairy farmers that year on 278 farms.
